COTTON. 'Tis born of the burden of Toil, From the strength and the speed of the plough It springs from the heart of the soil, And the seeds that are glorified now. In the sot t•furrowed fields of the South, c It rules o'er the realms of the grain, us green through the gloom of the dreuth, 'Tis fair through the fall of the rain. With blossoms of purple and white, With leaves that are vernal in hue, 'Tie fed by the air and the light, 'Tis nurtured by sunshine and dew; It springs from the breast of the earth, 'Tis rife with rare colour and heat-- a starves of magical birth, "ris king o'er the corn and the wheat. The proceent pulses of May Beat under its ripening boll; And later it lives in the ray Of the light that illumines its soul. 'Twas known in the land of the East, Through ages long silent snd dead; With wonders of whiteness increased, To the warmth of the South it is wed. 'Tie gathered from valleys and hills; In opulent bales it is bound; With orient beauty it fills Vast acres of affluent ground. Though planted in darkness and gloom, 'Tis safe in the dust of the sod; It arises in splendours of bloom, It awakes at the whisper of God. Oh! lift a large pan of praise. As strong as the tides of the sea! Through lengths of laborious days And conquests of Commerce to be, This plant from the heart of the soil, In the pride of its purified fleece, With triumphs of glory and toil Shall reign in the rapture of peace. —Leeds Mercury Weekly. Wm. H. HAINE.

It is whispered by one who is not partial to card playing that it requires two packs to play a game—a pack of cards and a pack of fools. When a young lady offers to hem a cambric handker- chief for a rich bachelor, depend upon it she means to sew in order that she may reap. Somebody names, in the presence of a ferocious duellist, the name of one of his rivals—the most forraidable of them. "He !" cries the duellist; "I know him; I've been waiting /or him; some of these days I'll have to go and pull his ears." "What for ?" " What for? I don't know. If I did I'd go and pull them now." is infinite, there may be those who, having seen 4 go about to disparage it. The only answer that shall be made to this sort is a story from Tavistoek. There is ais ancient feud, half serious, half jocose, between Tavistock and the parts round about. It is said that a carrier of Tavistock was found on the moor by some Okehampton men struggling with a flooded stream, and that their comment on recognising him was, "Let en go, 'tis only a Tavistock man." It is a fact that a horse-dealer has been known to abate a seller's price by some pounds with the remark that the pony would be a good one but for having " Tatty- stock legs." In this usage of the name the first syllable is pronounced with a contemptuous emphasisis. Now Tavi- stock has nothing visibly contemptible about it, being a town of fair site, of convenient inhabitation, of ancient good fame, the birthplace of Sir Francis Drake and other worthies —including "manly Peeke," who, while a prisoner at "Sherries in Spaine," fought and beat single-handed with quarter-staff three spaniards with rapier and dagger—and to this day a dwelling-place of sufficient men. A certain man of Tavistock was asked if he could account for the general disparagement affected by the neighbours from Okehampton to Plymouth. His answer was concise and complete, and for my part I shall take it to extend to whatever has been or may be said to the prejudice of Dartmoor: Theu'm iealous.—The English Illustrated Magazine. MATTHEW AHNOLD.-:-Mr. Arnold is, of all his country- men, the most conscious of the national idiosyncrasies that endear him to the soul of the stranger. I may be doing him a poor service among his own people in saying this, I may be sacrificing him too much to my theory of the foreigner and, his longing for sympathy. A man may very well not thank you for letting it be known that you have found him detached from the ranks of his compatriots. It would perhaps be discreet on the part of the Frenchman or the American not to say too loudly that to his sense Matthew Arnold is, among the English writers of our day, the least of a matter-of-course Englishmen—the pair of eyes to which the English world rounds itself most natur- ally as a fact among many facts. This, however. is after all unnecessary; for what is so agreeable in his composition is that he is en fin de compte (as the foreigner might say) English of the English. Few writers have given such proof of this ; few writers have had such opportunity to do so; for to few writers have English affairs, the English charac- ter, the future, the development, the happiness, of England, been matters of such constant and explicit concern. It is not in the United States that Mr. Arnold will have struck people as not being a devoted child of the mother-country. He has assimilated certain continental ways of looking at things his style has a kind of European accent, but he is full of English piety and English good-humour (in addition to an urbanity still more personal), and his spirit, in a word, is anchored in the deeps of the English past.—The English Illustrated Magazine. WESLEY AND THE WASHERWOMEN.—We see the man more fully in his peculiar personal nicety in his el- couater with a slovenly washerwoman in a western farm- house at which he was entertained. A daughter of that house was the witness. She had left the parental roof, had married, and was, when I knew her, the mature mistress of her own farm. She would often entertain her Methodist visitors with stories about Wesley and his preachers, on -whom, as a girl, she used to think it an honour to wait. "Mr. Wesley," she said, "was very particular about his linen. There must never be a spot on it. Some of his preschers were the same in niceness. Thomas Ranken one day pointed to a spot on his shoe as he was going out and said,' Look at that! that is like a stain of sin upon the soul, it mars the beauty of the whole man!' Mr. Wesley was particular, too about giving as little trouble as possible in the house. And so he would never allow my mother to have any of his things washed in the house; they were to be put out at his expense. One day the washerwoman brought his linen and waited for her money. But Mr. Wesley found that his ruffles were so badly washed and so Smutted with the iron that he could not wear them. His ruffles had always been patterns of whiteness. The woman was called to look at the unwearable linen. 'I really believe,' said Mr. Wesley, 'that these ruffles are dirtier now than before they were washed.' The woman answered saucily, 'Dirtier, are 'em! an' spose they are! they are good enough for a canorurn!' The dear little man made no reply, paid the woman, and then looked at the ruffles again in a way which made me think that dirty ruffles were a greater trial to him than the washerwoman's abuse. He smiled at my mother and said, ' Sister Harris, I must ask yea to get these things made decent for me. Dear! dear! they really are the worse for washing!' Dear little man, he was so particular about his raffles."—Sunday Magazine. Tax Docsrou ix OLD TIMES.—The state of medicine in Henry the Eighth's England may be inferred from the pas- sages of the letters patent for establishing Linacre's College, which declare that heretofore a multitude of ignorant per- SOW, the greater part of whom had no insight into physic or any other kind of learning, were the usual advisers of the sick at moments of urgent peril, "so far forth that common artificers, as smiths, weavers, and women, boldly an acme- tomably took upon them great cures, to the high displeasure of God and destruction of many of the King's liege people." Nor was the ignorance confined to practitioners who could not have read a verse to save themselves from the halter. In truth the Tudors had long perished from reigning houses before the sick had better reason for trusting many a stately Court doctor than a rustic dealer in simples. An author of delightful books, William Bulleyn—a doctor of high repute in the reigns of our Sixth Edward and his sisters—dosed his patients with " electuaries " and "precious waters," compounded in ways as wonderful as their ingredients were numerous. For the preparation of his celebrated" Elec- tuarium de Gemmis," he says, with the seriousness nisei'', to a philosopher, "Take two drachms of wlafte perles ; two little peaces of saphyre; jacinth; Zorneline, emerauldee, granettes, of each an mance; setwal, the sweats roots don- nike, the rind of pomecitron, mace basal seed, of each two drachms; of reade corall, amber shaving of ivory, of each two drachms; routes both of white and red behen' ginger, long popper, spieknard, folium indicum, saffron, cardamon, of each one drachm; of trocb, diarodon, lignum of each,wh i llaalf a a small handful; cinnamon, gelinga, zurubeth, is kind of setwal, of each one drachm and a half; thin peeees of gold and silvkere, of each half a scruple; et as mk, half a drachm, y eilici, which is the fourth kind your electnary with honey nt moirobolans with roses, strained in squall pastes, as much a heaath cola diseases of ye brains, hartew, siltlomsua suffice. It is a This medicine proved against the remblynge of the harts, fant ing and souning, the weaknes of the stomacke, pen* Y- ven aolftarines. Sings and noble men have used this for their comfort. It causes them to be bold-spirited, the body to areal we!, and ingendreth to the face good colours." Who" such a mess was served to kings and princes to give them lightness of heart, personal fragrance, and a clear com- plexion, cheaper and more nauseous messes of half a hun- dred incongruous ingredients Were forced down the throats of the populace to bring them round from ague or typhus. --Leisure Hear. been the property of John Milton, and contained entries in his handwriting respecting his own birth, and these of his children and ether relatives. There are ten entries in all, and the " first eight are all in Milton's well-known hand- writing." The two last, Mr. Kerslake thinks, were written by John Phillips. The latter entries show evidence of the poet's failing sight, and there are several pages injured by burning, as books are sometimes damaged by persons of im- perfect vision who read by candle-light. The text at Romans xv. 6—" God even the Father "—is emended in the margin by the revised version, " the God. and Father." The Bible is a copy of the quarto edition that was printed by Robert Barker in 1612. The end cover contains the name of Elizabeth Elcock, who was probably a daughter of Jobe Allecock, of Nantwich, who was one of the executors of the poet's widow. There seem reasonable grounds for regarding this as a genuine Milton relic. The Bible appears to have been used by the poet in his darkening years, aid then after his death probably passed with his widow to her Cheshire home, and at her decease fell to the lot of her executor's daughter. The anecdote of its discovery and identification makes a curious addition to the annals et book-collecting.

Ale Ecoorrnic Irasmart.—Them wouli appear to be a I very eccentric farmer in Ohio. His flock of sheep is im- mense, but they have not been shorn for six years. The wool has grown over their eyes, and is so long that it drags on the ground. On being asked why. he.did not shear his sheep, Mr. Sellers (the farmer) replied, "God put the wool on their backs to 'My there and keep them warm, and I do not propose to interfere." Mr. Sellers never shaves, cuts his hair or finger nails. His hair hangs down his back, and has the appearance of never having been combed, his whis- kers are long and shaggy, and his general appearance is entirely different from other men. He has never bought any improved farm machinery, but all his tools are home- made.

BASIS OF VALUATION UNDER THB AGRICULTURAL HOLD- INGS ACT.—The following resolution was passed at a meet- ing of the Yorks and North of England Land Agents and Surveyors' Association, held at York:—" That, in the opinion of this meeting, it is desirable to adopt the under- mentioned scale of maximum allowances as fair and reason- able compensation under part 3 of the first schedule of the Agricultural Holdings (England) Act, 1883, to be substi- tuted by agreements for compensation under the Act, viz. , —For one-third of the cost of linseed cake, cotton cake, rape cake or malt calm, and one•sixth of the cost of corn cake, malt or other manafactured feeding stuffs of similar manurial value, which kave been consumed on the farm during the last year of the tenancy, and for one-sixth of the cost of linseed cake, cotton cake, rape cake, or malt culm, and one-twelfth of the cost of corn cake, malt or other manufactured feeding stuffs of similar manurial value, subject to the away-going crop being considered as one year's tenancy on the land upon which it is grown, and pro- vided that the quantity allowed for shall not exceed the average of the two next preceding years."

div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

Wort FRUIT TRREB.—Cuttings of these should now be it in. In a previous paper we advised, for reasons given at the time, to delay pruning, excepting black currants. A selection of the best shoots may now be made for cuttings, still deferring the pruning. The closer they are cut to the old wood the more likely are they to form roots. The end to be inserted should be cut even, and all the eyes or buds removed a length of 6in, from the base, for if left they become troublesome by throwing up suckers, which require removing annually. The top of the cuttings should be cut off so as to reduce them to a length of Sin. to 12in., accord- ing to the strength of the shoot, the strongest being reduced the least. The cuttings are generally put in rows if I. apart, 4in. to flin, distant in the row, and sin. or 6in, deep, and a trench to that depth should be cut with the spade, guided by a line. With one hand fix the cuttings in their place, and with the other press some soil against them to hold them in position till 6in, more is placed against them with the spade, and pressed firmly with the foot. The ground is then dug till a width of 18in. from the row is obtained, which is beaten with the back of the spade moderately firm. If it is not level with the starting-point, more soil must be added, and the line moved and fixed the required distance from the row, and the trench cut as before. When the cut- tings come to be trod, the advantage of beating the so with the spade will be obvious, for without this simple ex- pedient it would be impossible to preserve the cuttings in a straight line, as the ground at the back would give way. RHUBARB is, in consequence of the mild weather, starting to grow; it is so far advanced as to be liable to be crippled by frost, should it visit us. We have just covered ours with litter, or stock manure, about 41n. deep; failing to secure these, we should use ashes or any other protecting material. Low as the temperature of the soil is at present, it is several degrees higher than in frosty weather, and the covering will husband the heat round the roots as well as protect the crowns from injury. By this means the produce will be quite 14 days in advance of the unprotected. Anyone wish- ing to prove the soundness of our remarks can easily put it to a test by leaving a few roots uncovered. THB FRONT GARDEN.—Calceolaria cuttings intended for the front garden will be found to have made more growth than is usual or desirable for the time of the year; they are consequently in a more tender state than when Grit put in and liable to be injured by slight frosts. As much air should be given as possible, day and night, without taking the hand-lights or frame off. This will to some extent solidify their tissue and prepare them for the struggle they may have to endure before next May. Some protecting material which will exclude the first frosts should also be I. readiness.

ROCKWORIE is frequently attempted in the front garden. There can be no objection to its introduction so long as it pleases the cottager, and really plants will thrive on a stone with a little soil, or with their roots wedged between them, that refuse to grow in the ordinary way. We like te see the bit of rockwork in one corner, but should there be any hindrance to its being there, we should endeavour to keep it as far from the public thoroughfare as possible, and make it appear to be against the wall of the dwelling, though there may be some feet between them. There is an objection for any ground to be seen by passers-by between the rockwork and the house. We once assisted to make one in front of a villa, standing on a slight eminence. We began three feet from the wall, and about 2ft. high ; laid most of the stones flat, and by fixing some smaller rugged pieces on flattish ones, a natural, irregular appearance was imparted. One stone rested on the other with a gradual elope, and when completed it had the desired effect, giving the house the appearance of having been built on a rock. When the plants were put in the interstices purposely left, it had a charming look. The form of rockwork we like to see is exemplified in nature, where a group of stones is seen mingled with vege- tation. Nature's stony mounds are like her hills and mean- tains—irregular in shape, they project, incline, and recede. How different is this to the formal, conical pile of stories we frequently see in front gardens; or to one we have occasion to pass by at times, which reminds us of representations we have seen of Druidical monuments. The stones, 2ft. long or more, stand erect and isolated, like so many obelisks, con- veying an impression that the constructor must have gathered his ideas of a rockery from the headstones in some crowded churchyard or cemetery. Had they been laid flat, and the work begun at the bottom by allowing one stone to rest on the other, placing some so as to slightly overhang, as well as fixing other pieces rather more lumpy on the surface of a flat one, but slightly receding into the soil, the effect would have been pleasing. Any attempt at imita- ting hills or mountains on such a small scale as the limits of the front garden admit will only end in showing how ridiculous man's puny efforts are. We therefore say, hal- tate the stony mounds. Tics Wurnow.—To complete our remarks on the fern case for the present, we give a list of some of the most suit- able sorts of ferns for the purpose of planting. The best time for doing so is March, as the majority of them will be starting to make fresh growth at that time :—Trichomanes radicans or the Killarney fern, Asplenium marinum, A. trichomanes, Allosorns crisply; or the parsley fern-, Adiantum capillus-Veneris or the tree maiden-hair fern, A. assimile and A. affirm, Doodia aspera and candante, Onychium japoni- cum, Pteris cretica, and Albo-lineata. Many of the above are hardy in many parts of Envland ; they are consequently cheap. The Hymenaphyllumi Tanbridgense and Wilsonii are also hardy, and real gems for the fern case, but more ex- pensive; so are the species of Todeas, but they are not so hardy. Many of the mosses will also do well in the fern case.

SHARP WORC.—An American paper records with pride a feat recently performed by an inhabitant of Carollton in the presence of a large number of spectators. He invited them to see how quickly wheat growing in his field could be con- verted into bread and biscuits. Two years ago it seems the same enterprising individual had served round, to a party of guests, bread baked by his wife rust eight and a quarter minutes after the wheat was standing in the field; but on the recent occasion he determined to surpass his former achievement, and succeeded. At six minutes after four, we read, the reaper stood beside the growing wheat, men being stationed every few feet along the line of grain, ready to seize an armful as it fell, and rush off with it to the thresher hard by. The mill was just sixteen rods distant. At the "drop of the hat," the mules sprang to work; in a minute and a half a peck of wheat was in the sack and on the back of a horse, that set off at a gallop for the mill. Just one minute seventeen seconds later the flour was delivered to the agriculturist's wife, and in three minutes two seconds from the starting of the reaper the first griddle cake was eaten, whilst more than a minute later a pan of well-baked bissuits was handed round to the admiring spectators, who, adds the American paper in conclusion, intend presenting their fellow-townsman with a suitable testimonial for being a man of his word. FOOT AND MOUTH DISEASE IN GREAT BRITAIN.—We are now able to give a complete table of the Foot and Mouth Disease for the 52 weeks ending December 29th,1883. From this it appears that there have been 18,731 outbreaks during the year, and 461,457 animals attacked by the dis- ease. The wen showing the smallest number of animals diseased was the one ending January 13th, the number being 4,655, and the week of greatest disease was the one ending Sept. 22nd, when 87,519 animals were suffering. For the week ending Dec. 29th there were fewer outbreaks than any week since August 4th, and fewer animals diseased than any week since August 25th. From January 6th, when 5,187 animals were suffering, the disease gradually increased till it reached a maximum of 27,013 for the week ending March 17th. It then gradually diminished till for the week eading May sth, 8,804 animals only were affected. From that date it showed an almost steady increase till in the week ending September 22nd it reached its highest point, and 87,519 were registered as diseased, though the number of animals at- tacked reached its maximum about a fortnight earlier. Since that time it has gradually diminished till for the week end- ing December 29th, 36,070 were suffering. Thirty-three out of the forty English counties are now affected, three Welsh counties, and eight Scotch.-- Farram

THE AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS ACT IN CHESHIRE.-A Chester correspondent states that Mr. Denson, a tenant occupying 170 acres under the Ashton trustees, has received notice to quit under somewhat extraordinary circumstances. Mr. Denson says that shortly after the Agricultural Holdings Act came into operation the trustees of the Ashton estate sent round an agreement to the tenantry, and Mr. Wright, one of the trustees, called upon Mr. Denson and read the agreement over to him. The agreement, at described by Mr. Denson, asked the tenant to sign away his compensation under the act. For instance, under " drainage " the landlord was only to find tiles, while the tenant was to do the whole of the labour for nothing. Mr. Denson said he could not agree to that, and asked what he would receive for improve- ments made before the act came into operation, for he had spent nearly £3OO in draining and carting material for the building of his house. Mr. Wright objected to giving him a farthing, whereupon Mr. Denson said," Well, if you won't give me anything for what I have done before the act came into operation, yen will have to pay me for the improve- ments done now." Mr. Wright (according to Mr. Denson) then turned round, saying, "Oh, we will prevent that," and accordingly gave Mr. Denson notice to quit his farm. The case has excited a great deal of interest in Cheshire, where this seeming endeavour to drive a coach and four through the act is mach commented upon. The other tenants upon the estate have signed the agreement under similar condi- tions. TECHNICAL EDUCATION IN AGRICULTURE. - Mr. John Twentyman writes :—At Aspatria, Carlisle, Cumberland, is an agricultural school, founded a few years since to give practical and scientific education and training, at a mode- rate cost, to meet the means and demands of the middle- class. This school has, like the Bedford Science Classes, obtained let class certificates in the advanced stages of agriculture and its allied sciences, and even more, for it has recently taken two open scholarships offered by the Royal Agricultural Society of England. Professor Tanner reports on the papers set by him at the recent Christmas examina- tion :—" I am glad to report that the examination in the principles of agriculture and chemistry shows that some very good 7Prk is proceeding in the Aspatria Agricultural School. The papers on agricultural science give indirect evidence of considerable attention directed to the practical instruction on agricultural matters, and I cannot but think that some good field work is being done in addition to the instruction in the class-room." The past pupils are a credit to the neighbourhoods in which they reside, and show signs of progression, intelligence, and perseverance. The present students may be daily seen taking an active share in the fields, the byre, and the sheepfold, or attending the lectures and classes in the school. The insufficient endowment fund has prevented the directors properly advertising the school, for I cannot but think that were the advantages offered well known a large number of parents of limited raeans would send their sons to the school.—Gloucestershire and Wilt- shire have kindred institutions.

DANGERS OF A MILD WISTFUL—There is an old saying, "A green Christmas makes a full churchyard." Our statists of health tell us that the records of our death-rate contra- dict the prevalent opinion that frost conduces to human health. However that may be, it is as well for farmers to bear in mind that live stock—both cattle and sheep—may very easily be more neglected in a mild winter than in a severe one. Up to the present time, the winter of 1883-4 has almost failed to bring home to the careless observer the necessity of supplying other food than that which the pas- tures still give to the outlying live stock. But it is quite certain that there is a need of regular feeding with dry food to all kinds of sheep. Even if there be no actual disease resulting amongst ewes and hoggets from the fact that they ha-,e to get their own living on grass land, yet there is a lowering of condition, in itself an absolute loss, and likely to lead to farther loss. It is by no means bad weather for any kind of live stock, and the winter's expense of feeding has hitherto been remarkably light. It is, nevertheless, the worst of policy to economise too much in winter food be- cause the weather is mild and the grass green. There have been repeated and repeated instances in which farmers, nig- gardly of keep in the early months of winter, have found too late not only that their sheep were weak, Cut that their appetites were weak also, even when good food was at length available. To obtain this end 12 beasts were taken (eight steers, two cows, and two heifers); four steers and two cows were placed on one side and four steers and two heifers on the other side, All alike ,were given the same quantity of meal and cake. ----- Lord E. Cavendish, on Saturday, at the annual meeting of the North Lancashire Liberal Registration Association at Preston, and speaking at a luncheon afterwards, ex' pressed confidence in the Government, and said he hoped that in the coming session there would be a fair prospect of the Government carrying out some of the pledges given four years ago. A new Conservative Club was opened at Exeter on Wed- nesday by Sir S. Northcote. The right hon. baronet spoke briefly on the necessity of politically educating working men. Mr. E. Gibson, M.P., who was one of the speakers, appeared as the champion of the House of Lords, and, witb an eye to the rejection of the Reform Bill, protested against the assumption that the Peers were bound to act as mere recorders of the decrees of the House of Commons. THE OPENING OF PARLIAMENT. MINISTERIAL CIRCE. LLB.—The following circular-letter has been issued by the Premier to the Liberal members of the House of Commons: —" Hawarden Castle, January 14, 1884. Sir,—The Speech from the Throne will be delivered on the sth February, It is the desire of the Queen's Government to submit to the House of Commons on the earliest possible flay proposals of much public interest and importance. I therefore trust you may be able to give your attendance at the opening of the session, and I have the honour to be, sir, yonr most faithful servant,yl. E. Gunman"

_ Tun , Aluminum you Ileurax. Mr. J. Stansfeld and Mr. T. Shaw, the Liberal members for Halifax, addressed their constituents on Tuesday night. Mr. Stansfeld, whilst purposely refraining from a general recapitulation of by- gone political events, touched upon the Egyptian complica- tion, and said he looked forward with grave apprehension to what might result in that quarter. He anticipated, how- ever, that many of the reports of our intentions in regard to Egypt would prove exaggerated, and, as a friend and sup- porter of the Government, he preferred to wait for an au- thoritative statement before expressing any opinion as to the future. With regard to domestic affairs, the right hon. gentleman strongly advocated the inclusion of Ireland in the forthcoming Franchise Bill; in fact, he said, that was the only safe course that could be adopted. MR. MUNDILLA AT GLASGOW.—The Right Hon. J. A Mandella was entertained on Saturday at luncheon at the residence of Sir William Collins, Glasgow, at which many of the leading Liberals of the city were also present. The right honourable gentleman was afterwards presented with an address front the Educational Institute, and, in retAft said he hoped he had shown himself to be a friend to the teachers; but he would never surrender the interests of the children, either to the teachers, or to the school board, or to the department. With him the question had been, and would always be, " Education "—first and last. As to the position of teachers, he knew no country in Europe where the teachers were more honoured, or had a better social position or better reward, than in the grand old country of Scotland. Mr. Mundella left at night for Edinburgh. TORY Miettintenurrarroar.—At the annual meeting of the Rotherhithe Conservative Association, one of the speakers, referring to the dwellings of the poor, charged Mr. Chamberlain with possessing a vote in respect of one of the most dilapidated houses in Rotherhithe. The attention a the right honourable gentleman having been called to this statement he has sent the following reply :—" Board of Trade, Whitehall, January fl.—Sir,—l am directed by Mr. Chamberlain to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 2nd instant, in which you draw his attention to a state.. went made by a gentleman in course of a speech delivered at Rotherhithe to the effect that Mr. Chamberlain had a vote in respect of a dilapidated house in Paxton's-alley, Rotherhithe. In reply, Mr. Chamberlain wishes me to say that his statement furnishes a good illustration of the in- aecaracy of Tory speeches, as he has no property of any kind in Rotherhithe. Mr. Chamberlain's father had a vote ter East Surrey, but he has now been dead for some yeare, and Mr. Chamberlain does not know what his qualification as an elector was.—l am, drc.Llrionam B. LORD SALISBURY ON TEE EXTENSION Or THE FRANCIUM —Lord Salisbury, addressing a Conservative meeting at Dor- chester, on Wednesday, said nobody really cared very much for the extension of the franchise. Liberalsdesired to secure , in the future the preponderance which they had accidental'," obtained. He animadverted on the proposal to introduce 6 measures for the extension of the franchise and redistribu- ; tion separately, and said if this were done the disadvantages „ under which the rural population at present laboured would , be aggravated. In reference to the inclusion of Ireland ill r the forthcoming franchise bill, he said he could not conceive a more unfortunate time for introducing a reform bill which ; should distinguish between England and Ireland, and gave this as an additional reason for the postponement 0, ; the measure. He dwelt on the necessity for party organisa° Lion, and said we were on an inclined plane which led from ; the position of Load Hartington to that of Mr. Chamberlain. and on from that of Mr. Chamberlain to the depths over. ; which Mr. Henry George reigned supreme. The essential peril of the Conservative disposition was apathy. It migh.f ; be that we were entering upon a new epoch in which r would be necessary to show that the forces of self -preserve- , tion could be as active and alert as the forces of destruc• Lion. - •

M. BRADLAHGH AND PARLIAMENT.—On Tuesday night Mr. Bradlaugh addressed a meeting at Barnsley on his rela- tions with the House of Commons. Speaking of what he ehould do on February 5, he said : I shall be in the House of Commons before the Queen's Speech is read, and I will suppose that I swear myself in and take my seat. I sin not saying whether I shall or not. What will the House do 2 The House might expel wne. If it did there would have to be a new electiob, and I should be back again in a fortnight. The House might exclude me. Then I sipuld at once applY for the Chiltern Hundreds. The Government would grant it or they would not. If they did there would be a neW election, and in a fortnight I should be back again If the Clovernment thought it right not to grant it, I should announoe that at a quarter to four each day I should go to the House of Commons for the purpose of taking my seat' which I had already sworn myself into according to lavrt and I should go every day. Ido not know what would happen. That is for the House to settle. I shall call no more meetings. I shall assemble no more people. I Asa rely on the law and my right, and I will not give the Houle one day's peace until it either takes my .eat away from wet or lets me do my duty to ray constituents. (Loud cheers.) Resolutions in condemnation of the conduct of the House of Commons, and asserting Mr. Bradlaugh's right to his seat la the House were unanimously passed. Mn. IRELAND, Execterton.-eThe sentence of death pissed on Peter Wade for themurder of an old man named quina at Rattifarnham W 55 carried into effect within Kilmainham prison on Tues- day morning. From a balance-eheet submitted to the final meeting of the Parnell Tribute Committee iu Dublin, it appears that the total amount of subscriptions was £37,701. The advertising and other expenses were £1,100; a cheque for £35,000 was banded to Mr. Parnell at the recent banquet • and there re- mains in the National Bank a balance of £1,504. STREET RUFFIANISM IN DUILIN.—Ock Monday, at the Dublin Poblin Police Court, John Monaghan was remanded, Charged with a desperate aesault. It appears that as a Middle-aged man named Michael Cullen WAS returning home With his wife on Saturday night from marketing three roughs, one of whom it is alleged was the prisoner, came out of a lane and knocked him down and kicked him so severely that he now lies in hospital in a dying state. No reason is assigned for the outrage. Sceane In A Pooartouss.—At the Belfast Police Court, on Wednesday, two young lads, named Thomas Lavery and Patrick Hamill, were sentenced to five years in a reforma- lota' under peculiar circumstances. They, with over a hnn- dred lads, occupied a dormitory in the Belfast Poorhouse, and on Tuesday, after it was supposed they had retired to rest, they took the straw out of their beds and set fire to it, and while it blazed they lustily sang "There is a happy land." Fortunately, the masters extinguished the fire be- fore much damage was done. SCENE AT A DUBLIN COUNCIL MEETIND.—An extraor- dinary scene occurred at the meeting of the Dublin Corpo- ration, which sat on Monday till a late hour without dealing with any of the business on the agenda-paper. The time Was occupied with a discussion on the proposed increase of salaries to the city officials, and an unseemly wrangle oc- curred between the Lord Mayor' Mr. Gray, M.P., aad Mr. Mayne, M.P., during which Mr. Gray, referring to a ruling of the Lord Mayor being disregarded, said there was an end absolutely to order, and they had better come with bladgeons and revolvers to the next meeting, each prepared to stand by his own side. MR. BIGGAR AND THE 111.7iGNALISTS. -- MT. Biggar, ILP., on Wednesday journeyed to Blacklion, in spite of the Proclamation issued against the holding of any meetings at teat place. He was warned by one of the reeident magis- trates that no meeting would be allowed, but in the tern- Porary absence of the police Mr. Biggar snatched an oppor- tunity to address a hurriedly convened assemblage of his Nationalist friends, holding forth from the ear on which he had crossed the mountains. The hon. gentleman was inter- rupted by the returning police,. who stopped ell further pro- ceedings by the threat of "standing no nonsense." Mr. Biggar was escorted into Blacklion by the constabulary, who had some scuffles with the crowd, but ne serious collision occurred. DlntoNsrniertON ON MR. PARNIILL'S'FAIDL:OII Thurs- day a great demonstration was held on the demesne of Mr. Parnell, at Avondale. The occasion was the ploughing of SO acres by the farmers of the surroutding districts. At twelve o'clock 160 ploughs, with 320 horses, set to work, and amidst great enthusiasm commenced to plough the lands. The horses were decked in green leaves and ribbons, and in many of the ploughs small green flags were set. About 100 horses and earth belonging to the smaller farmers carried to the !farmhouse at Avondale the produce of six acres of potatoes. Mr. Parnell is at present in England; but he was represented by his manager, Mr. Kerr. Mr. James Graben and Mr. A. J. Kettle had charge of the arrangements. O'DONNELL'S ALLEGED CONFESSION. Mr. A. M. Sullivan, one of the counsel for the defence in the Carey murder trial, writes as follows to a contemporory :—" I have only just now seen the paragraph in your journal of the 7th inst. stating that the confession of 0 Donnell, as published in United Ireland, showing the crime to have been premeili- %tad, and that Carey was followed by his assassin all the Way from Ireland,' is generally attributed to me." "Kindly allow me to say no statement so false and so unjust M the deceased man could have emanated from me. Neither is the Journal you mention responsible for it. The Chicargo Z'eening Nerve of 17th December last compased and pub- lished the story, which was repudiated as apocryphal on the aPot by the only gentleman whose name was supposed to vouch it." "To that story you have yourself added the damning statement as to O'Donnell having followed Carey all the way from Ireland, vim., not one word of this being found in the so-called 'confession' which you say contains S,UPPOSED PLOT TO SHOOT A MAGISTRATE IN CHAPEL. --On Saturday evening an extraordinary discovery was made at the Romeo Catholic Chapel at Kitulla, a small vil- lage six miles from Loughrea, on Lord Dunsandle's estate. Some person, while walking round the church, found the door perforated opposite the seat which Mr. William Daly, a magistrate, occupies each Sunday and holy day during divine worship. The hole was made large enough to admit a revolver barrel. When discovered it was filled vrith,cotton, winch could be takenaway unnoticed. Mr. Daly, an enter- ing the church on Sunday, was placed under the protection- eight policemen. Extraordinary precautions were taken the police authorities. Two special constables were placed in front of the door which had boon Injured. Con- stables surrounded the building, while others were placed on the different roads leading to it. Mr. Daly, after worship, Was escorted to his residence by an extra force of consta- bulary. Seib-inspector Chambers, Loughrea, and a force of Police afterwards proceeded to the residence, close to Kitulla Catholic Chapel, of a carpenter named M. O'Halieran, and Searched it and aka his workshop. The search, which was of the minutest character, continued for several hours. At the close of the search the police carried away a large por- tion of O'Efalleran's tools. The search was made consequent on the discovery at the chapel.

OPENING OF THE VERDIN INsri- TUTE" AT MOULTON. An event not of every day occurrence has taken place at Moulton, a email town between Wiasford and orthwich of 1,200 inhabitants, which has grown up within the past 10 or 15 years, in connection with the salt works of Messrs. Joseph Verdin and Sons. Years ago they began to see that It was one of the responsibilities of property that their People should be well housed, so they laid out and built several streets of good substantial five or six-roomed cot- tagss with a few shops here and there. Then they gave land, and Canon Hayherat built and endowed a church in addition to the two.chapels for Primitives and Independents already there. Now they have gone still further and built, furnished, and completed an institute which the committee, into whose hands it was formally committed, on Monday last named after its founders " The Verdin Institute." The total cost of this munificent gift is £1,500, and warrants the rejoicing, holiday making, fi sg displaying, and decorations Which greeted one en entering this little town. The bands (hrass and fife) with more than a thousand men and women Inet the Messrs. Verdin and accompanied them to the new baildings, which were pronounced opened, and transferred to the following committee :—Messrs. T. Darlington, W. Rayner, C. Roberts, T. Marron, S. Sailer, W. Brogden, W. Barnes, W. Byrora, if. Broody, H. Watson, T. Hodkinson, Thomas Shaw, T. Marson' S. Hitchinson, Thomas Hitchin- ten' T. Gibson, George Buckley, T. Gleave, C. Keene, and John Whitlow ; T. Anderson, hon. treasurer; and Robert RrYning, hon. secretary, two of which hold the care of this property per month for the rest of their fellow partici- Pants Robert Verdin, Esq., LP , president; Joseph Ver- di; Esq ,W. H. Verdi-n, Esq , Rev. W. A. Hopkins, /ioe-preeidents. From the vast number who took tea on the occasion (near 700) the public meeting could not begin early. When the president took the chair he explained the reason of this memorial building to the memory of his father, its size cevering 1.,00 square yards enclosed by sub- mantial walls and embracing a reading room 54 feet long, 30 feet broad, and 18 feet high, with other necessary offices, all heated by hot water pipes, well lighted, and the walls adorned by fine oil paintings, engravings dm., with book- cases containing a library a well-bound first class books, d!aks reversible for seats and tables, chairs, and other op- -I)ilances for study, lecture, or entertainment, while in an Ordinary way there were billiards and other games when reading papers, &c., was not desired. He said the firm were Itatiefied with the architect, Mr. Joynson, of North- wich, the builder, Mr. Sergeant, of Wineford, and those who had completed the work for them. After detailing what other members of the family had done, he said nothing would give them greater pleasure than finding it proved a boon to the people, whe, having no public-house in the place, needed such an institute all the more.—On the Vicar taking the chair he moved that the best thanks of the committee and of nearly 100 members, as well as those for whom the institute was designed, and who should become such, should be given to the Messrs. Verdin for their noble gift. He spoke of their obligation to their father, whose business tact and unwearied exertions had been the foundationof their house, and their desire to honour that father had teen blessed of God. Their princely gift verould embalm the memory of Verdin in the hearts of the People of Idoaltea, who should rejoice in their success and nee it aright, &c.—The Rev. F. Carter (Congregationalist), Aeconded tha propural. He was sure that employers of la- bour only fulfilled their duly to their workpeople when they provided for the moral ant intellectual well-being of their people.—The Rev. W. Gellef supported the motion With pleasure, though dittle was left him to say, yet he could not forbear to speak of the privileges which arose from the !ight use of capital, which the Messrs. Verdin acknow- ledged and met aright (or the good of their employes.— Mr. A. Fletcher supported the resolution as an old school- rellew•of the senior member of the firm, and rejoiced in the good fortune of Moulton.—The resolution was put, and car- ried with acclamation.

FRANCE AND CHINA.

War between France and China seems to be imminent. The Viceroy of Canton has issued a proclamation in which he calls upon the population to unite against the French. Several thousand regular troops are being sent to Hainan, the important island which the French have expressed a desire to annex. From Tonquin it is announced that Admiral Coubert intends to push on to Bac-Ninh without waiting for reinforeemente. The Temps comes out with the usual announcement that French priests are being assailed by " furious mobs" of Chinese, who are instigated to deeds of violence by Mandarins. The Figaro stated on Saturday that fresh negotiations were going on between M. Ferry and Marquis Tseng, but the account appears to have been an invention. The Berlie papers published on Satur- day a document, purporting to be a decree of the Emperor of China, which, if genuine, amounts virtually to a declara- tion of war against France. The Marquis Tseng, in a letter to a German publicist, remarks that the French have ex- alted over the fall of Sontay as if it had been Metz or Strasbourg. EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. EVACUATION OF KHARTOUM. Severaltiplomatic agents have received telegrams from Constantinople, stating that a very sudden change has oc- curred in the relations between Egypt and the Porte, the latter manifesting a mere friendly feeling towards the Khedive. The Egyptian Government has received intelligence from Suakim stating that an understanding MS been arrived at with several chiefs of tribes hitherto hostile along the Suakim-Berber route to Khartoum. Confirmation of this intelligence has also been received by M. Barrere, the French diplomatic agent, and hopes are still entertained that it may be found possible to open the Suakim-Berber route, thus facilitating the evacuation of the Soudan. The Egyptian Government intends to deepatch Abd-el-Kader Pasha, the new Minister of War, to Khartoum by the Korosko route to superintend the evacuation. The Standard correspondent at Cairo communicates the following intelligence under date of Monday :—Advices have been received here both directly from Tripoli and through Constautinople that Sheikh Senowssi is advancing to join the Mandi. Streald this news prove true, Egypt would be in the greatest danger ; for the influence ot Senoussi extends not only along the whole North African littoral from Tripoli te the confines of Egypt, but—which is far more important—also throughout the Syrian desert and amongst the Arab tribes on the borders of the Sues Canal. It is only 15 or 20 days' camel march from Tripoli across the desert, either to Oongola or straight to Alesandria. A later despatch says :—The garrisons of Fashoda, El Reweh, and Deem having come into Khartoum, the White Nile is now in the hands of the rebels, who were reported to be marching on Messalamieh, on the Blue Nile, in order to cut off the gerrison of Sennaar. Accordingly, a steamer, was sent tip from Khartoum to relieve Sennaar ; but it broke down on the way for want of firewood, aad was obliged to return. •Presumably, therefore, the Sennaar troops are now izolated. It has now been decided, in view of the increased gravity' of the situation, to resort once more to the expe- dient originally proposed by Baker Pasha last year, and lately abandoned—namely, that of raising a Turkish con- tingent which shall be recruited chiefly in Albania and Croatia, and form a third brigade of the Egyptian army. It will be modelled after the first brigade, and officered by Englishmen. On Thursday the news from the Soudan was of a more hopeful character. General Baker has visited Massowah, end hopes to come to an arrangement with Abyssinia which would leave him at liberty to move into the Soudan, with the prospect of reaching Khartoum in June. Owing to the alarming news from Sinkat an effort will he made next week to relieve the garrison. Sir Samuel Baker has written an article with the object of showing that the wisest, as well as the baldest policy is to hold on to Khartoum at all risks. He advises that the circle of entrenchments should be contracted, and that good use should be made of the fleet of steamers—all of which can be armed—which are at the disposal cf,Colonel Coat- logon. If a bold stand is made, both breathers of the Nile can be cleared of rebel vessels, and the food -supplies of the garrison would be secure. If, on the other hand, the order should be given to retreat, Sir Samuel agrees with General Gordon that the destruction of the garrison woald be very probable in the waterless deserts of the Soudan. He urges that a division of Indian troops should be sent • at once to Suakim.

An explosion of dredamp occurred en !Friday in the Fer- fay coal mine, Arras, France, causing seven deaths. Twelve men who were injured have been rescued, but it is feared that five others will be found to have perished. A Ll7Cia SERTANT.—A. Paris telegram announces that 'the names of the prize winners ia the decorative arts lot- tery were made known on Wednesday. The first prize,, valued at £4,000, was won by Mddle. Josephine Daire, a, domestic servant at Montargis. AMERICA' JOURNALIST/ AND MR. IIiVING.—Mr. Henry 'lrving was on Saturday night entertained at a banquet by the journalists of Chicago, where he has been playing to erowded houses. Miss Ellen Terry has met with a sligkt accident. Her foot slipped upon a piece of ice-coated pave- ment and she fell, her head striking the ground. Her in- juries are, however, not of a serious nature. SALVATIONIST WEDDING IN FAnts.—A,curious ceremony took place in Paris on Tuesday in connection with a Salva- tion army wedding. The bridegroom was a Mr. Sinico, and the bride Miss Wallis, both Salvationists. ' The ceremony was performed by Miss Booth, and was of Avery remarkable character, attracting a large number of nercons. It Was the drat of the kind which has ever taken place in Paris. The Russian Minister of Finance has published his annual statement. There is, of course, a deficit, and the Minister proposes to cover it by the introduction of a stamp tax in Poland and "a tax of 1 per cent. on tke more important commercial and industrial enterprises." At the same time the Minister promises to observe the steictest economy, and Ito endeavour to adjust the public burdens to the means of the taxpayer. American competition in the corn trade is I assigned as one cause of the stagnation of the eevenue. ALLEGED GREAT 'FRAUDS —The case of Henry Boland was decided on Thursday morning by -the Liege Court of Appeal, to which the judgment of acquittal pronounced by the Tribunal of Marche was referred by the Public Prosecu- tor last June. The accused was charged with having in- duced a banker named Jacquemin to advance him 550,000 francs by various false pretences. He is now sentenced by the Court of Appeal to three years' imprisonment and a fine of 2,000 francs. The court ordered his immediate arrest. THE VIENNA MURDERS.—The Vienna police have ar- rested one Hugh Schenk, son of a Silesian judge, who is accused of murdering four servant glue. He is said to have lived comfortably of late years upon the savings of servants whom he enticed away from Vienna. promising to marry them, and whom it is alleged he murdered in out-of-the-way places. It is alleged that he has been two years in prison for swindling a servant of her savings. He has been married four years. His wife is ignorant of his crimes. The bodies of three of the supposed victim % were found at different times in different places. TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN AMERICA: TEBBE WOMEN BURNT TO DEATH A.ND SIXTEEN PERSONS IN- JURRD.—A shocking accident occurred on Tuesday on the Bradford, Bordell, and Kinzua Railway. A stream of waste oil lowing from a tank across the railway caught fire as a passenger train ran into it, and the train was in a moment enveloped in flames. The passenger car was filled with people, who made a rush for the doors at each end of the carriage. The heat from the burning oil was, however, so Intense that they were driven back, and had to jump through the window, landing fortunately in the snow. The train, in a mass of flame, ran on for some distance down the mountain side before it could be stopped, and by that Lime the fire had gained a complete hold of the carriages. Both the passenger coach and the baggage car were eventu- ally almost completely consumed. Though the majority ot the passengers escaped three women were burned to death, and sixteen people were injured, most of them from burns Some are badly hurt. At the time of the accident the track was for a hundred yards covered with oil, and it is supposed that the gas emanating from it, came into contact with the fire-box, the result being an explosion, which ignited the oil. TIMAGTC Loy' AFEAJR.—The ramparts of Cambrai have formed the scene of a tragic episode of love and devotion. The Petit Nerd relates that two young people, belongicg to good families in that town, who were devotedly attached to each other. met together by appointment in the Jardin Public. They had walked some time up and down the grand avenue, when eeekieg a more retired promenade they strolled along the rampart leading to the Paris gate. En- tirely absorbed in their conversation, they failed to remark that they were being followed. The individual who tracked their steps was the father of the young lady, a man of honourable conduct and greatly esteemed, who, rightly or wrongly, disapproved of the connection. Arrived at the spot where the soldiers' gardens are situated, the young people heard a suspicious noise in the fosse, and mounted the parapet to ascertain its cause. At the same moment the father, who had provided himself with a revolver, took aim at the young man and fired, but the girl, who Saw the movement, suddenly sprang before her lover, and, receiving the bullet in the face, fell dead at his feet. On realising the terrible truth, the young man also resolved to die, and precipitated himself from the ramparts into the fosse, whence he was lifted at the point of death. The affeir has plunged the families of the two lovers into the greatest dis- tress. It is thought the father of the girl will become insane through grief.

The reply of the Transvaal deputation to Lord Derby's Note of last week was presented at the Colonial Office on Thursday. The members of the deputation neither accept nor reject the frontier line proposed by the noble Earl, but they suggest another which they consider likely to effect a settlement of the question. EXTRAORDINARY DISCOVERY OF £4oo.—Oa Thursday while some workmen were repairing the flooring of an old cottage known as "the Ruins," Harwood. near Bolton, they discovered under one of the stones a large number of current coins of the realm, amounting altogether to £4OO. The last tenant of the cottage, Mrs. Howard, was killed recently by calling down stairs. The money is supposed to have been lets.
