THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 19, 1884. WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION. ADDRESS ON "THE NEXT REFORM BILL." The third of the series of public lectures in connection with the above association was delivered on Monday even- ing by the Rev. D. S. Prosser, in Brick-street schoolroom, on the subject of "The next Reform Bill." Councillor Platt presided. The scheolroom was well filled. The Cruanmes said he was glad to see so many of the Liberals of the North-East Ward there that evening. They expected to have seen a larger number of gentlemen on the platform, but at the last moment two of them who had in- tended to have been present could not attend. He had a telegram from Mr. Frank Roberts, who, as they knew, took such a deep and lively interest in the Liberal cause—(bear, bear)—who said that he had been suddenly called away and could not be at the meeting in time, which he very much regretted. He had also a letter from Mr. Councillor Broad- bent, who was unable to attend owing to illness. The object of their meeting there that night was to hear a lecture from the Rev. D. S. Prosser on the subject of reform. That subject ought to be one of the leading planks of the Liberal platform. (Hear, hear.) The Liberals were always ready to remedy aay abuses that might exist, whilst the Tories on the other hand were always for letting things remain as they were. There had been considerable discussion in the papers and elsewhere as to the subject of the next Reform Bill that would be introduced in the next session of Parlia- ment. He thought it bad been pretty well settled, by Liberals at all events, that the first measure which would be introduced into Parliament next Session would be the measure for the reform of the comity franchise. They were aware of the state of things at present. If they took as an instance their own borough and drew a line across Winwick-road or across any of the streets leading off Lovely-lane; on the one side of that imaginary line the householder could vote for a representative in Parliament, but on the other side of the line the person living exactly in the same kind of house had no vote at all. That was a state of things which had existed rather too long, and which no one could defend. (Hear, hear.) He could hardly imagine even Lord Randolph Churchill saying that that was a state of things which ought to continue. (Laughter.) However, they would find that the Tory party would op- pose the measure for county householders to have votes as they always did oppose reform on some pretext or other, and there was no deubt they would oppose the particular reform in question. Fortunately they had a majority of Liberals in Parliament, and strong enough to carry the Bill in face of any opposition which weight be attempted, aid it would not surprise him if in a few years hence after the Tories had done all in their power in opposing it, that they would turn round and say that it was themselves who bad been the friends of the Bill and did everything they could towards passing it. (Laughter.) They knew that the party had done such things before, and he had not the slightest doubt such a thing would occur again. Then they were told, and by Liberals even, that the Liberal party would lose ground in the country by the pass- ing of such a Bill, and they might do so in some parts at the outset because a great deal of ignorance and prejudice prevailed among the agricultural portion of the population. The agricultural labourer would vote as the squire and par- son told bins, perhaps, for a few years to come, but they must see that justice was done in the matter. Those people were as much entitled to votes as they were, and they must protect them. (Hear, hear,) They might take heart from the tact that edueation was making rapid strides. Education and Liberal ideas always went together. The people only wanted to be educated and to know the true state of off airs to find that the Liberal party were the party seeking for fair play in all matters affecting them. (Hear, hear.) They were also told that they were not to extend the franchise to Ireland. He believed that some Liberals had expressed themselves% to that effect, but in his opinion it would be a great mistake to refuse to give the Irish people the same privileges as they enjoyed in Eng- land. (Hear, hear.) It was said tbatdf all the householders of Ireland got votes that it would materially strengthen the hands of that party which sought to separate Ireland from England. That might be so, but, as he had said before, the Irish people were entitled to votes, and the policy of the Liberal party had always been a polioy of fair play and justice to everybody. (Applause.) As far as the Bill in relation to Ireland wae concerned they must take care that the people of that country, had equal rights and privileges with themselves in every possible way. (Hear, hear.) Whenever they took a step in advance they must take care that Ireland took a step in advance along with them. That was the only means by which they could hope to get Ireland happy and contented. (Hear, hears) He was very glad to know that there,was an improvement in the state of Ireland since they met in that room twelve months ago, and he trusted that such a condition of affairs would continue. That improvement, as they all knew, had been brought about by the wise aid liberal measures introduced into Parliament by Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) Mr. Gladstone was the man above all others who had brought about what was now comparative peace in Ireland. Ireland with peace and quiet- ness would enter upon a new era of prosperity. Peace and prosperity always went together. They could not • have prosperity without peace. When they the Tory Party were is Tower from 1874 to 1880 they were continually meddling with one part of the world and another, getting up little wars and devising scientific frontiers "--4laughter)—for which the British public had to pay. At last matters came to such a crisis that the country in 1880 came te the conclusion that they had had enough of Tory Government, and very wisely sent them out. (Hear, hear.) Since then they had had an im- proved state of things, and he hopel it would continue. With respect to the proposed redistribution of seats, the 'Chairman remarked that they were cognisant of the scan- dalous state of affairs at the present time, little boroughs with 200 voters returning a couple of members to Parlia- ment, and large boroughs such as Manchester being saddled with that " fancy" franchise which the late Lord Beacons- field called "the representation of minorities," and which only gave voting power to send one member to Parliament. That would hive to be remedied before very long. It would not come about until they had admitted the housholders of the county to the franchise ; then matters would be made more clear and redistribution of seats would follow. When that subject was brought forward perhaps it would be opposed to such an extent as to force the Liberal party to appeal to the country. If so they must do their best to place the Liberal party in a larger majority in the House of Commons than it had ever been before. Even at the election in 1874, when such a majority of Tory members of Parliament were returned to the House of Commons, the total Liberal vote throughout the country was very far in excess of the Tory vote, which showed that if the Liberal party had only had fair play in the distribution of seats they would have sent an immense majority of Liberals to the House of Com- mons, and have saved that six years of " bungling " which prevailed during the Tory administration. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, the Chairman impressed on his hearers the desirability of supporting those measures of reform which were to be introduced by the Liberal party. They were all satisfied that they never had a better head of the Govern- ment in the history of the nation than they had at the present moment, and they were also satisfied that the mem- bers of the Cabinet were the right men in the right place. (Applause.) He thee introduced the Lecturer. The Rev. D. S. Pnossma, at the outset, observed that his remarks would necessarily have to partake of prediction. One recalled the advice of an American humorist who said "Never prophecy unless you know." (Laughter.) They could not be absolutely certain of what some of the pro- visions of the anticipated bill would be, although there were some things about it of which they might be pretty certain. They knew they needed another reform bill, and they knew they were pretty sure of having such a measure at last laid on the table of the House of Commons. The measure needed and anticipated, would be what they liked to make it. Parliament enacted the laws, but the people make the laws, and hence by such gatherings as the one that evening the convictions of the people were made known to Parlia- ment, and such a healthy stimulus given to their Legisla- ture as might secure an efficient and final settlement of that ' important question. (Hear, hear.) The anticipated reform ' bill would not be the first reform bill of the century nor the second. Indeed, when the history of the 19th century came to be written from a political point of view, it would be known as the century of reform, and if at the year 1900 the constitution of Great Britain was compared with the constitution in the year 1800 it would be found to be almost ' altogether changed. It was said of a humourous Irishman that he once declared he looked back into futurity. (Laugh- ter.) There was wisdom and philosophy in that remark. He presumed the man acted upon the principle that history repeated itself, and that what bad been would be. If tney wanted to know really what would be the provisions of another Reform Bill, and the spirit and policy by whictr such a measure as they desired could be secured, it would be well to keep in mind past struggles and how the Reform Bills of 1832 and 1881 were brought about. They should turn back to the state of the country prior to the introduc- tion of the great Reform Act. A cursory glance would show that the condition of the people was very sad. Labour was exceedingly arduous, wages low, and taxation excessive. There had been great wars, and the burden of those wars had been placed in the greatest degree on the poorest sec- tions of the community. Most unjust and iniquitous im- posts were put on the necessities of life, and the Corn Laws raised bread very frequently to a high price. The people being uneducated in political economy thought, in many instances, that the introduction of machinery was the cause of their trouble, which in certain parts of the country was injured and destroyed. Disaffection and discontent prevailed, and the only remedy of the Government for this state of affairs was coercive legislation rigorously applied. Little by little, however, the conviction became impressed in the minds of the people that until they had a more ade- quate form of representation in the House of Commons it would be impossible to hope for any redress of their griev- ances or an improvement in their condition. When that conviction was impressed upon them in spite of discourage- ments they persevered until the Reform Bill of 1832 was the result. There were men at that time sitting for pocket boroughs and close corporations, whilst towns such as Bir- mingham, Manchester. Sheffield, and Leeds had no repre- sentation whatever. The lecturer proceeded to give an in- teresting account of the manner in which that Bill was combated before it came into operation, and coming to the Reform Bill of 1867 remarked that he thought they might fairly say that, looking at all the facts, that Bill was really provisions itohnes p? r o vI n i - the work of the Liberal party, and that it was the necessary and logical outcome of Liberal principles. (Applause.) sWioinths ovretryhafteßwilclhhaonwg.es they What werewere thoseliving Parliamentary boroughs they had what was virtually house- hold fr.mchise, but in county divisions they had 40s freeholds,

£5O rent, /31..0 copy bold, and £l2 ratal qualification, and the £l2 ratal qualificition Was a means-of shutting out a great mass of the agricultural industrial population. They would see how it operated. Their population in round numbers might be given as 35.000,000; now on the elec- toral register of the United Kingdom they had something like 3,000,000 names. There was a remarkable difference between 35,000,000 and 3,000,000, but that was an extreme way of putting it, and it would hardly be fair to put the figures in that way unless something was said in qualifica- tion. 'They took the 35,000,000, and might presume that half were minors, not having attained the age of 21 years, and the number was then brought down to 17,500,000. Of that number perhaps half would be women—(laughter)— and although he did not see why women should not be ad- mitted to the vote, the question came to this that they had some 9,000,000 adult men, and of that 9,000,000 there were only 3,000,000 on the electoral roll. They must ntt imagine too, there were 3,000,000 of district individuals, be- cause there were people who voted both in borough and county, and perhaps In two or three counties. He had heard of a gentleman who told the revising barrister that he had a vote in 25 constituences, and in some way he had managed to record his vote in 17 out of the 25 at the last general election. (Laughter.) It was to be hoped there were not many of his stamp. (Hear, hear, and laughter). Mr. Chamberlain, after ac- counting for removals, came to the conclusion that there were not more than 2k millions of persons who exer- cised in the four kingdoms electoral trust. There was a great contrast between 9 millions and 2i millions, and it was their desire in connection with the next Reform Bill to see that contrast lessened—he did not say removed—but lessened. (Hear, hear.) They were not prepared to go in for that which was not practical, as it was better te concen- trate their efforts on what they might fairly hope to accom- plish. (Applause.) They might take the number of inhabi- ted houses in the United Kingdom as a fair guide in pre- suming what ought to be done in connection with the coming Reform Bill. There were in England and Wales, they were told, something like 5 million of inhabited houses. There were, as they had seen, in the four kingdoms 2i mil- lion of voters. Every other family, therefore, if they esti- mated 5 to a family, might be said to represent a vote, and the principal of residential franchise equally operating would consequently double the electorate. That would be something they could scarce conceive ; it would be something most stupendous to double the number of those who had the privilege of citizenship. (Hear, hear.) At present he submitted that everyone who dwelt in a house who paid rent and rates, but who had not a vote, was an injared person. .Hear, hear.) Indeed, the deprivation un- der which he suffered involved the violation of one of the fendamental laws of civil society. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to bring to bear something like equality between every man who had had a house, who had a home, and who was at the head of a homestead. Under the present condi- tions a man might live in a borough such as Warrington where he had a vote, but for considerations of health or with a view to secure better employment, in the interests of , his family he might remove out a few miles and become a householder in a county division. He might live in a bet- ter house and be better prepared to intelligently exercise the franchise, but he was no longera dweller in the borough, and because he had gone to live in the country he was de- prived of what was bafere his right. (• voice: "That's Imy case.") That was the case not only of one, but of tens of thousands, and rankling under such a sense of injestice they had a very real and patent grievance. (Hear, bear.) He was told there were towns in that very county where on one side of the street a man had a vote, and on the other side he had not a vote. The property was of the same description, the rents the same, the class of tenants the same, but on one side of the street the houses were in the borough, and the tenants could vote, but the other side was in the .county division and the poor inhabitants had therefore none of the rights of citizenship. In a village just on the confines of England and Wales, it was said there was a house, one part of which was in the county of Shropshire, and the other part in the county of Montgomery. The man in that house was so particular that he put the bed in such a position that one side of the bed was in Shropshire, and the other side in Montgomeryshire. A warrant was out for him, and it was issued for Shropshire, and when the policeman came to exe- cute it the man rolled wrer to Montgonseryshire. (Laugh- ter.) He always thought that to be a bit of a tale—(renewed laughter)—but if they could draw any distinction between one side 'of the -street and the other, one could imagine a bed being in two counties. (Hear, hear.) He then gave a number of other instances of the inequali- ties and injustices misting between the counties and the boroughs, and said it was these injustices they wished to see redressed. The question of redistribution of seats, although they hopedit would not be confounded with ex- tension so far as the bill was concerned, must necessarily be taken into consideration when dealing with the franchise. He here instanced a number of the anomalies existing in the matter of the distribution of political power. One of the ernallest if not the smallest, county constituency was Rutland, where 768 persons returned two members to Par- liament. In their own division of Lancashire, he believed I they had 29,000 electors with only just the-came political influence in Parliament. Could such a state of things be justified? It was simply wonderful that these contrasts I had been tolerated. He thought it a very happy sign of the times that there was no disposition in towns having the franchise to have a monopoly of that privilege. It would be very strange if their Conservative friends op- posed the extension of the franchise to the agricultural population' because the agricultural population had been singulartyfavoured. They had not been expcsed like the masses in the towns to 'the pernicious influence of Dissent, and they had been under the benign influence of the clergy- men. The aristocracy and the parsons had cared for them, and sprinkled plentifully amongst them to exercise their beneficient influence. (Liughter.) If they were ignorant it was very strange that there should be such an objection to their being taught. One great difficulty that had faced the agricultural labourers had been the opposition of the clergyman and the squire. Wherever the agricultural libourere had combined to improve their condition they had met with discouragement from those who ought to have been anxious to see them in every way improved. But put the agricultural labourer besides his brother in the town and give him tbe same privileges and he thought they would find that there was the same desire on the part of both to obtain the information that should enable them to conscientouslv and intelligently discharge their privileges. He thought that the inclusion of the agri- cultural labacrer in the franchise would not only tend to their advancement and progress in political knowledge, but it would give a direct intelligence to Parliament ae to the wants of this class, and it would secure a better legislation in connection with those interests which directly affected them. There was another sense in which the extension of the franchise would have its influence: Constituencies would become in themselves necessarily so large that anything like corruption and intimidation would be impossible, and that would be better than a stringent Corrupt Practices Act. The Liberal party as a whole seemed to be thoroughly at one in connection with this matter of extension of the franchise. The Chairman had said "perhaps with some exception," but he (the speaker) thought that those exceptions might be counted on the fingers of one hand. The whole party seemed to be united, from Mr. Gladstone downwards. What would the Conservatives do? They would object that no measure for the extension of the franchise was satisfactory that did not provide at the same time for a redistribution of political power. Not that they wanted a redistribution of political power; no one dreaded that redistribution of political power more than the Tories did. Why then did they Insist that redistribution ought to go along with extension ? Because they knew that when they got to redistribution they got to a delicate question, to one that appealed to the selfishness of iudividuals and the selfishness of constituencies. It was evident that if they were to have a fair measure of redistribution of political power some of those , Liberal boroughs would have to lose some of their politi- cal influence on behalf of the principle of equality. Human , nature was very strong in theoretical virtue; it was very beginwent t uo pu eh , woodman,oneself. tjoustthebmutsejlayset s justice must crys t w tree !" (Laughter.) When it came to taking a member from their borough or when it came to taking away their influence it was not a very pleasant thing. The Tories , thought that by introducing the question of redistribution they would introduce jealousy and split up the Liberal party. Therefore they wanted to link together redistribution 1 and extension. He thought there was nothing to fear so far as the House of Commons was concerned. But after the Commons came the Lords. They would urge that '• We won't have part of the measure." That would be a time for the Liberals all over the kingdom to rally to the support of the House of Commons. It was possible for the Tories to dare too much, and it was I absolutely necessary for the people to show the Lords that they were in earnest about this matter. If the measures were thrown out they must be prepared for a battle; they must fellow the action of the people with respect to the old 1 Reform Bill. But he thought that the House of Lords would show that discretion was the better part of valour, and they would give way when they saw they were forced ,to it. lie was not only of opinion that it would be better for franchise to be dealt with apart from redistribution but he thought it would be better to have a dissolution be- fore the redistribution. That, however, was a question of mere opinion; let them centre their efforts upon the assimi- lation of the two franchises, and to seeing that only one vote was given to one man. Wealth gave influence, privi- lege, and immunity, but in politics let things be equal all round, let men stand upon the same platform, let them be shoulder to shoulder with their brothers, and let them feel that wherever they lived they had the same stake in the country. They must try to see that one man had only one vote, and when that was accomplished they would have the representation of the country on a firm basis. With regard to the extension of the franchise fer Ireland, he thought he might say that with very few exceptions the Liberal party were united in their desire that Ireland must go in with the rest of the kingdom. He thought the result ef the inquiries addressed by the proprietors of the Pall Mall Gazette to the members of the Liberal party should encourage them. Al- most without exception the replies received to their ques- tions were to the effect that Ireland must be included with the rest of the kingdom. It was also pleasing to note the remarks of W. E. Forster at Bradford on the subject. In , that matter at least no man had more opportunities of know- ing the condition of Ireland, and that the right hon. gentle- man should be prepared to say that he considered Ireland by all means should be treated as the rest of the kingdom was a very significant fact which should weigh not only with doubting Liberals but with Conservatives also. (Applause.) He asked them whether such sorrows and troubles would have betel the

sister isle if she had had proper representation, and would . not many of the ditficaltieb rhich they had been involved have been avoided. Let them know they could exercise their influence in the English nation and Parliament, as that would be the best way of curing discontent, and mak • mg Ireland peaceful and prosperous. So long as there was injustice in relation to Ireland the Liberal party must not fail to redress it, and show the Irish people ,that the latter were an important and integral part of the British nation. (Applause.) He then referred to some of the great benefi- cial measures passed since the Reform Bill of 1832, aril slid that now a number of greet measures were taking their place upon the horizon of practical politics, light was beit.g thrown upon these questions. We wanted a reform of county government. We wanted a reform in the land laws, bringing the uncultivated land into cultivation, secur- ing its easy and cheap transfer, and making it possible that it might pass into a number of hands in- stead of being held in settlement and entail. Then they wanted the question between Church and State put straight. (Applause.) They wanted the licensing question to be dealt with—(applause)--ind the vote in the House of Cemmons in favour of the principle of local option passed into legislation. And when they had got these great measures they would be better satisfied. The principles of Liberalism were the old principles of civil and religious liberty, and until the programme that they had now before them as a party was complete, until the sum of the happiness and content of the nation was appreciably complete, he urged upon tkem to be uaited in their efforts, and to give the Government all their support. (Applause.) Mr. M. BOWDON, in proposing a vote of thanks to, the lecturer, observed that the Rev. D. S. Prosser had given them a very clear and able address, and everyone would sympathise and agree with it. As the rev, gentleman pointed out, where there was any wrong it ought to be put right, and as Liberals they ought to aim in doing that. The great evils in this country and every country in Europe were caused through injustice, and if they were to escape from such evils they must do justice all around. They must carry out that principle "Do unto others as you would be done by," and if that was followed in their social and re- ligious life the world would be a better world than it was to-ff:ay.__ (Applause.) . .

Mr. HENRY ROBERTS said he had great pleasure in 1 seconding the proposition for two reasons. First, because he had been very mu.sh gratified with the lecture itself and the information it afforded them, and also because it gave him an opportunity of announcing the remaining lectures of the present series. On the 29th inst. Mr. James Jackson would speak on "The County Franchise: why it should be extended," on February 11th Mr. H. J. Leach (one of the lec- turers of the National Reform Union) would lecture en "The redistribution of seats ;" on the 26th an address would be j delivered by the Rev. R. Nicholls on ••Liberalism and the Working Classes ;" on March 11th Mr. W. B. Bannister (a working man) would speak on "The Pension List ;" and on the 25th Mr. Joseph Howes would lecture on that favourite subject, "The House of Lords.". (Laughter and applause.) Regarding the lecture, Mr. Prosser had spoken with refer- ence to the rating qualification that now existed in cmnties, aid an instance that came before his (Mr. Roberts) notice not long ago struck his memory. As they knew, and as Mr Piosser had told them, no man living in a house rated less than £l2 a year in the cocky was entitled to a vote. That meant he mast pay a rental of £l5 or £l6 a year, and they knew what that meant. If,they took Warrington, for instance, and gave the vote only to those persons 1 who lived in a house of £l6 rental instead of having 7,000 -voters as they now had, they would not have more than -2,000 or 2,500. It wail affected in a stronger degree in the country because the houses were of less rental than in the town. Then the persons who had to settle the question of rating were the overseers, and the overseers were sometimes the owners of the property, and where they paid the rates, in the selfishness of human sature,they kept down the rating as low as possible. In a revision court with which he had been connected there were six or seven claimants in which one paid £2O rent, another £l6, and the wholes of the others over £l5. Not one of those were oi the list. They sentin their claims to the assistant overseer who was a Tory, and he published a list of these claims, but when he

published it he wrote against each name th'e word " ob- jected." He (Mr. Roberts) wrote to him asking by what authority he did that, when the assistant overseer wrote back thatmo person whose rating was less than £l2 a year was entitled to be on the voters' list no matter what his rent might be. Mr. Roberts again wrote saying he was perfectly well aware of that, but as he (the assistant overseer) and himself knew not one person paid less than £l5 rental, and in one case actually £2O, and they certainly ought to be rated £l2 and be placed on the list. (Rear, bear.) They saw how it worked. The assistant overseer was a Tory, all the claimants were Liberals, and the owner of the property was one of the overseers who paid the rates. (Laughter.) It was a strange thing that nearly all the public appoint- ments were in the hands of the Tory party. It ought not to be but it was so, and they were not only officers paid by the town for their services, but they were also paid officers of the Tory party in the district. That was a state of things which ought not to exist, and if the franchise was extended and every householder entitled to vote it could not exist to anything like such an extent. The thing would then be too big to be mtnipulated. (Rear, bear.) In conclusion, Mr. Roberts said theta was nothing further needed to prove the cage which their Lecturer had put so *by before them that evening. (Applause.) The Lecturer baying replied to the vote of thanks, a similar compliment was accorded the Chairman, and the meeting then separated.

div.head: SHEPHERDS' ANNIVERSARY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SHEPHERDS' ANNIVERSARY AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday. the members of the Olive araneb Lodge (No. 1,120) of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds held their annual tea party and ball, when about 100 members, with their wives and sweethearts, sat down to a capital tea provided by the host, Mr. Edward Batley, of the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-street. Tea being over, a meeting WAS held, at which P.M. Edward Edwardson presided. In response to the toast of "The Loyal Order of Ancieat Shepherds," D.P.C.E. Edmund Wrigley said the order was making headway, and would -compare favourably with any other society. It was c mposed of some 100,000 members, wives, and widows, with a worth of £250,000. He hoped to see the day when the funds would be doubled.— P.P.C.S. A. H. Mather, in responding to the toast of "The Warrington District," said that in looking over the returns for the past eight years he found the district had paid the sum of £1,221 for funeral claims, fir distress cases £B2, and for fees for the purpose of educating poor children belonging to the district £l4 13s 11, leaving the district at the present time worth £517 13s Sit The members number 955.—P.P.5.C. loans Dr:Loose, in responding to the tout of "The Olive Branch Ledge," Hid many of the members present' would know that the past year had been the most trying year the lodge had had; by that he meant the heavy sick claims they had had to meet. The sum of £lO2 lOs had been paid for these claims alone, which is a heavy item considering the number of members in the lodge. The income for the year was £l6B 16s 741, and the expen- diture paid sick members £lO2 10s, district funeral fund .£3l 3s 7d, surgeon's bills £l6 Is, management expenses £lB Os 04 1, which, with a balance in the hands of the trea- surer, a balance in b ink. and £lOO in the Warrington Corporation, left the lodge £lO3 108 941 to its credit. Dur- ing the past year the sum of £42 193 Id had been lost. Thirteen members had been initiated during the year, mak- ing the number of members 115. In conclusion, he hoped the members would continue to leak with fresh zeal, so that by the end of next year he might be able to give them a better report, both numerically and financially.—" The lodge surgeon" was responded to by Dr. James Cennell. "The widow and orphans' fund and juvenile burial society" was responded to by P.P.L.S. James Deloeza, secretary, who stated that the widow and Orphans' Fund was the best fund in con- ' nection with the district, providing' as it did for the widow I and orphans, at the death of the member. It was approached by a email payment of 7d. per quarter with a small entrance fee, and the benefits were £5 for the widow and 103. for each child under 14 years of age. The Juvenile Burial Society was composed of some 1,200 members, with £350 to its credit, having during the past year gained the sum of £46 10s. 31. This, too, was an institution well worthy the support of every member of the society. The members then formed themselves into a quadrille party, and dancing was kept up with mach spirit until 10-30, when the company separated.

div.head: LOCAL PRISONERS AT THE
div.p: LOCAL PRISONERS AT THE

LIVERPOOL COUNTY SESSIONS. At these sessions this week the undermentioned prisoners have been dealt with as stated : SENTENCES. George Peacock, aged 47, labourer, for having, on the 10th November, at Halewood, stolen two tame rabbits, the property of Albert Grace, six months. Ann Kelly, aged 31, was found guilty of having at Prescot, on the 19th November, stolen a petticoat, the property of John Berry, and was sentenced to nine months' imprison- ment.

Ellen Hunt, aged 34, charged with having stolen a shill- ing from the person of Richard Prinley, at Widnes, on the 24th November, was sentenced to seven years' penal servi- tude she having been previously frequently convicted. Jolan Reach, aged 50, labourer, was sentenced to two days' imprisonment, for an assault upon Patrick Mannion, at Widnes, on the 20th October.

Frederick Anson, aged 42, Carter, ' for stealing a horse the property of Elizabeth Wiggles worth, at Sutton, on the 27th November, was sentenced to ten years' penal servitude, bay- ing been previously convicted. Daniel Sullivan, 20, labourer, for stealing a pair of boots, the property of Jane Siddall, at Warrington, on the 30th November, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude, and a further period of twelve months' supervision. He had been previously convicted. John Jones (36), collier, was sentenced to six months' im- prisonment for having, at Prescot, on the 1003 November, maliciously wounded one Henry M'Clarvey.

- ACQUIITALS. Margaret Dickinson (49) was acquitted of having, at Widnes, on the 22nd November, stolen £5 from Mvlesl Gaul. Margaret Morgan (34) arid Ellen Wheeler (39) was ac- quitted of having, at Woolton, on the 10th November, broken and entered the shop of William Butcher, and stolen therefrom thirty pair of boots, and also of having feloniously received the same. John Taylor (19), labourer, was acquitted on an indict- ment charging him with having stolen a horse and bridle at Tarbock on the let ult., the property of luau Prescott.

ENTIRTAINMENT.-Mr. W. Johnson gave another ot his interesting entertainments entitled " A Merry Evening," t •Dareshury, on Monday, to a crowded audience. He contri- buted several humorous songs and sketches, and was warmly applauded.

div.p: HALTON.

Martur. Ittritovituatqr Socmv.—The weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, when readings were given by Messrs. J. Faulkner, D. Barrow, and J. B. Houghton. The following members criticised the readings, viz., Messrs. J. H. Gamon, R. Hughes, W. Rowe, and Job Hancock. Rev. S. Mees presided. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL BIND OF HOPE.—OE Tues- day a free tea was provided for all members of the society under 16 years of age; the attendance was about 110. A public tea was proviied at 6-30, at which about 100 as- sembled. The following ladies presided at the tables:— Mrs Baguley, Miss Gamon, Mra S Hughes, Mrs E Looker, Mrs T Hankey, Mrs S Saunders, Mrs .1 Clark, Mrs H Bow- den, Mrs G Leathwood, Mrs J Heesom, Mrs J Tomlinson, Mrs N Tomlinson, Mrs J Hancock, Mns J Howard, Mrs J Barrow, Mrs J Houghton, and Mrs Gee. Subsequently, there was an entertainment. Mr J H Gamon was in the chair. Songs, solos, glees, Ica., were rendered by a choir of 50 voices, Miss Greenway, Miss Hinde, Miss Howard, Miss Grine, Miss A Houghton, Mr W Jukes, Mr L Fryer, Mr R Fryer, Mr W Hayes, Mr J Dale, Mr W &ape, Mr C Leathwood, and Mr Saunders. Recitations were given by Mr Hart, of Widnes, and members of the society. There was a very large atten- dance. Towards the close the Rev S Mees, resident minister, gave a very interesting address, and a very enjoyable even- was spent. Ten pledgee were taken. HATTON.

WESLEYAN Cturn.-00 the occasion of the annual foreign missionary meeting last Monday evening, the chapel was well filled, a larger congregation being assembled than for some years past. The meeting was presided over in a happy and effective manner by Mr. Littlemore. A report containing many encouraging facts respecting the work of the Wesleyan Missionary Society was presented by the cir- cuit secretary, the Rev. James McTurk, who also addressed the meeting. An eloquent and earnest speech on missionary subjects was delivered by the Rev. John Eglinton. The subscriptions and collections amount to £4 3s 6.1, being an increase of 25s on the year. A hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, and the singing of the Doxology, brought to a close a very succesafel anniversary. HIGH LEGH.

CONCIRT.-1. concert has been given in the schoolroom in aid of the funds of the Cricket Club. The room was filled by a most respectable and appreciative audience. The following ladies and gentlemen very kindly gave their ser- vices .—Roy. C. J. Winser, Rev. H. and Mrs. London, the Misses Lyon Bennett, Miss Walton, Miss Dignum, Miss Clarke, Miss Parr, Miss Hollingworth, Miss M. A. Taylor, and Mr. George Parr; Mr. Hudson acting as accompanist. They were, without exception, well received. The concert was followed by a dance and some excellent music, pro- vided volantarily by Messrs. Ralph Wheeler, Skilling, Grown, and Kirkpatrick, et Lymm, to whom a vote of I thanks was proplsed by the Rev. C. J. Winser, and heartily responded to.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

A CHESHIRE ROIICHL—On Tuesday, at Knutsford Court House, before Mr. E. Lewis Ashworth, a rough-looking man, who gave the name of John Madden, and stated that he came from Over, was charged, in custody, with being drunk on the Toft-road on Monday night. —lt appeared from the evidence of an intelligent young woman, a domestic servant at Mrs. Harrison's, that about 9 p.m. she was pro- ceeding towards the post-office with letters when the pri- soner rushed at her from near a gateway at the residence of Captain Price (Governor of her Majesty's Prison), and chased her as far as the railway station. Her screams at- tracted the attention of the night watchman on duty at the station, and he promptly went to the rescue, whereupon the prisoner used some bad language to this witness, and de- manded to know if he was the husband of this young woman, after which be decamped, but information having been given to the police, Sergeant Gunn subsequently ap- prehended the prisoner in the town. He was under the influence of drink.—The prisoner now begged for mercy, and declared he did not recollect anything of the matter, but the magistrates told him that it was intolerable that respectable females, having occasion to go out of doors these dark nights, should be subjected to such treatment, and it was fortunate for the prisoner that the night watchman had interfered before violence had been offered her, or the pri- soner would probably have been sent to Quarter Sessions. He would pay a fine of 10s and costs (8s), or in default he would go to prison for 14 days with hard labour.

div.head: RIXTON.
div.p: RIXTON.

Mr. Eva, of the above village, has had a merciful de- liverance from a shocking dam!). As he was mounting on his cart the horse started and he fell. The wheel of the vehicle narrowly escaped passing over him—just brushing his arm, but such a close shave as to necessitate sending for the doctor. He is uow recovering from the fright and shock to the system. A lad—a bright intelligent boy, about ten years of of age, on Monday morning last stepped into the house of Mr. Tongue, farmer. He took off his cap and respectfully greeted Mr. Tongue and family. He so won upon them that he stayed and had breakfast and dinner. When asked what his name was he said George Warrington. It appears that he was left a baby on a door-step in Warrington some ten years ago. He told Mr. Tongue it was the hest Christmas he had spent. In the afternoon the gentleman took him to the constable of Hollins Green village, whe saw him safely back on the way to Warrington Workhouse, which had been his home from the time he had been aban- doned by his unnatural mother. Being unknown he WAS called by the Workhouse officials the above name. It is to be hoped that he found his way back safely to the Work- house which he left at six o'clock on Sunday morning on his travels through the world. SOUTHWORTII-WITH-CROFT.

The monthly meeting of the School Board ought to have been held on Tuesday, but a quorum could not be found Ito proceed with the business. Only two members attended. I EgrzaTatiemErr.—A miscellaneous entertainment, on be- half of the Christ Church Renovation Fund, was given in the Board Schoolroom on Friday evening, January 11th, to 1 a good audience by Mr. Alfred Whittle, aided by the Misses Whittle, friends, and members of the choir. The decorations for the occasion were the same as at the previous entertain- ment. An overture "Light and shade waltz" by Mr. L. , Maudsley opened the programme. This was followed by a trio and chorus" Glorious Appolo " by the choir, which was well applauded. The following songs were then given:— " White squall " by Mr. J. H. Smith," Ehren on the rhino" by Miss E. Whittle," The blue Alsation mountains " Mr. 11. Brooks, " Mr. T. Marsh, and " The return of Spring" by Miss E. Whittle. The song " Sailiog " called forth a hearty encore, and Mr. Brooks received loud and well-merited applause. The choir then sang the favourite glee "Sweet and low," this bringing the first part of the programme to a close. After an interval of ten minutes Part It was com- menced by the comic song" Jolly laughing nigger," by Mr. F. Vernon. It was well sung and educed much laughter. Mr. J. H. Smith then sang "Take me home," and was fol- lowed by Mr. J. Stoddart, who rendered "Kiss me, and whisper good night" in a good style. The next, "Razors in the air," by Mr. T. Berwick, was vociferously encored. Mr. Marsh then gave "The midshipmite," and was followed by Mr. H. Brooks, who earned good applause by singing "Won't you buy my pretty flowers." The next, a banjo solo and song by Mr. Fred Vernon, caused much merriment. A laughable farce, "The wigmakers," by Messrs. T. Stod- dart, A. Whittle, and F. Vernon, was performed very suc- cessfully. The entertainment was brought to a close by the singing of the "National Anthem." A vote of thanks to Mr. and the Misses Whittle by the rector was heartily res- ponded to.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

THE DROVER AND His PIGS AT Wasrote.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Fellows, a young man, was summoned for committing a breach of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act. It appeared that on the 31st Dec. Inspector Hollingsworth discovered that foot-and-month disease had broken out on the farm of William Griffiths, Weston, and the district was declared infected. On the 9th January P.C. Price saw the defendant in charge of a cart at the Royal Oak Inn. He examined the vehicle and found in it six pigs. The defendant admitted that he had brought the animals from Terris, near Chester.—The defendant said he was not aware the district was declared infected, but the Bench informed him that he must exercise more caution, and fined him ss, and costs 11 6i. WINSFORD.

Tincritialscs ENTERTAINiLINT.—The Temperance Com- mittee connected with the High-street Free Methodist Chapel gave a successful entertainment in the schoolroom on Monday night, when the Rev. W. T. Symons occupied the chair, and the choir in their usual style gave excellently "When the bright sun," " ! the cryital spring," "Lift him up," and" Home ; "while Mr. Hough recited "Stolen" and sing "The teetotal car." Recitations were given by others, as Mr. S. Leech "Ruined by drink," &c., and Mr. R. Hatton spoke on the drink question.—The Hechabites' festival and dinner, with public meeting after, was held on Tuesday in the United Free Methodist Schoolroom kindly lent for the occasion. Capital speeches were given by Councillor Roper of Manchester, Mr. John Dimond of South. port, and Mr. H. Shsples of Manchester and other local gentlemen, under the presidency of E. Leigh, Eq., Mayor of Over. A vote of thanks was moved to the three first- named gentlemen by the Chairman, and to the president, I choir, etc. by Mr. J. tf. Massey and Mr. J. Buckley, which were'beth, carried with great enthusiasm. WOOLSTON.

A CAUTION TO LaNnLOßDS.—James Daintetb, landlord of tVßope and Anchor Inn, Woolston, WAS summoned to the lile arir ngton County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, for sell- ing intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours.—Mr. Draper appeared for the defendant.—Sergeant Pattinson said that about half-past eleven en Sunday, the 6th inst., he and P.C. Berry visited the defendant's house, and found two men, two women, and two children in the taproom, and there were four glasses of beer on the table. He asked them where they came horn, and one who gave his name as John Walsh said that he and his wife Came from Moseley, the other side of Manchester, but that they had stayed in War- rington during the light. Ha also said that when they were admitted they told the person who admitted them they had come from Warriceton. The other man gave his name as Owen Walsh, and said that he lived in Gandy-etreet, Warrington. He asked the landlady

if she knew they had only come from Warington, and she replied that her son admitted them' and thst they said they came from Moseley. The distance from where Owen Walah and his wife lived, at Warrington, to the defendants, I would be 2i miles.—Thomas Dainteth, the defendant's SOO, said that when the Welshes were admitted they said that • they all came from Moseley, and he believed them to be bona-fide travellers, or he would not have admitted them. They admitted after the police officers had gone that they did not tell him they had come from Warrington that day, and that in telling the officers they had done so, they had said what was untrue.—The case was dismissed.--Owen and Mary Walsh, of Gandy-street, Warrington, and John and Mary Walsh, of Moseley, were then fined 53 and costs for being found on the licensed premises of James Dainteth during prohibited hours.—Owen Walsh said that this was the first glass of beer he had had for two years, and that he was sorry he went into the public-house. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS. Cataluna RIFLB ASSO.NATIOW. -- The twenty- third annual meeting of thia association was held at Chester on Saturday, the Duke of Westm,nster pre- siding. The report referred to the death of Lord Egerton of Tatton, for many years a patron of the Ass,ciation, and then detailed the experience of the Mul line competition at Altcar, instituted by the late Colonel King, whic'i consists of squads of men tiring by command at unknown distances and at moving targets, each representing the figure of a man. Twelve squads of men, each from different companies, entered for the competition, and the winning squad, fro.n if Company, 3rd Cheshire Rifle Voluateers, made 36 hits on the target. The total number of competitors was 2,209, against 2,199 in 1882. The entries for the three principal competitions were as follow :—Volunteers 278, against 264 in 1882. All Comers' (Snider), 40), against 399; Sweet- hearts', 504, against 507. The winner of the Lord Lien- tenant's prize and the bronze medal of the National Rifle Association is Sergeant C, Preston, let Cheshire, with a score of 74 at 800, 900, and 1,000 yards. The total receipts were £1,043 3s 6d, and the expenditure £1,092 7s, showing a loss of £49 3s 61. The Duke of Westminster moved the adoption of the report, which was seconded by Colonel Htunberstone and carried. A vote of thanks to the donors of prizes and to the Duke for presiding soncluded the pro- ceedings. Tan CIIIOEIIIII Feamess' Crxn.—A largely attended gathering of the members of the Chester Farmers' Club was held on Saturday, at the Blossoms Hotel, Chester, the club head-quarters. Mr. John Roberts, of Well House Farm, Saltney (the president), was in the chair, and amongst those present were the Hon. Cecil Parker (agent to the Duke of Westminster), Colonel Hamersley (Chief Constable of Cheshire), and Mr. T. Rigby (of the Manchester and Liverpool Agr:cultural Society). A memorial was read from a number of farmers residing in the neighbourhood of Northwich, stating that they considered the restrictions issued by the Privy Council and the local authorities to be unduly severe, end not such as:were calculated to stamp out disease amongst their stocks. They were also of opinion that greater restrictions thonld be placed upon the importa- tion of live cattle from Ireland, &c., and that railway com- panies and others should be compelled to provide better ac- commodation for cattle on their boats between England and Ireland, and not be allowed to carry fat and store stock in the same railway truck. In the case of an outbreak of dis- ease they considered that the farm on which it occurred only should be declared the infected area. They also asked that the city and county authorities should act concur- rently. This memorial was generally endorsed by the chala. Mr. Storrar, veterinary surgeon, of Chester, next read a paper on foot-and-mouth disease—Resolutions were passed calling upon the Governmeut to stop the importation of live cattle from any country not known to be free from foot-and- mouth disease, and also to order that, as far as possible, the regulations should be made uniform for the United Kingdom.

THE COUNTY CORONERSHIP. A county court of freeholders, summoned by Mr. Ashton, high sheriff of Lancashire, for the purpose of nominating candidates for the office of eorener for the West Derby division of the county, rendered vacant by the death of Mr. T, W. Barker, Was held at Ormskirk at noon on Monday. There were from three to four hundred persons present, re- presenting the different districts of the division, which com- prises the whole electoral district of south-west Lancashire. Mr. Wilson, Preston (the under sheriff), presided, and after the customary preliminaries, Mr. S. Brighonse, Ormskirk, was nominated by Mr. H. L. Gregory (Southport), and se- conded by Mr. A. E. Wannop. Mr. H. L. Riley was nomi- nated by Alderman Cook (St. Helens), seconded by Mr. W. P. Clark (Southport), and supported by Mr. W. B. Walker (Earlestown). The show of hands was taken, and declared to be largely in favour of Mr. Brighouse. Mr. Riley ac- cordingly demanded a poll. MR. RILEY AT WARRINGTON. Mr. H. L. Riley addressed a large meeting of freeholders in the Corn Exchange, Blue Bell Inn, Horsemarket-street, Warrington, on Tuesday evening. Mr. Samuel Barlow pre- sided —The CHAIRMAN, in the course of his observations, said he found that since the last meeting was held in that room three at least of the candidates for the post of coroner had retired, and their reason for doing so was that they thought the expense would be so great in being obliged to have the poll at such an out-of-the-way place as Ormskirk, which was one of the towns of a by-gone age They thought that the freeholders of Warrington, St. Helens, Wigan, and Liverpool should have had an opportunity of recording their vote in their particular districts without spending a whole day in going to Ormskirk. He thought no too. (Hear, hear.) It was a state of affairs which he could not possibly understand. He believed if the poll had been postponed for a few days and a proper petition had been got up, that polling stations would hays I.,een erected at Warrington, Wigan, Ormskirk, and St. Helens, and he was there that evening to protest against the absurd and effete system in connection with the election of coroners for that division which had prevailed, for so many years. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. RILEY said if pol- ling booths bad been planted in St. Helens, Warrington, and other large commercial towns, Mr. Brighouse would not bays been a factor in that centeet. He contended that a coroner residing in that district would effect a ccnsiderable saving to the county, inasmuch as a large proportion of the inquests were held in that locality; and it would be also a ltanefit to the public in that there would be prompt action taken, opportunity afforded for collecting the facts prior to the inquest, and adjournments thereby nainimised."—Conn- cillor DIXON then proposed a resolution in favour of Mr. Riley's candidature, which was seconded by Mr. Moons.— Dr. SeAnxta SMETH supported the resolution, and expressed a hope that that would be the last time they would have to record their votes at Ormskirk, as he thought there should be polling stations for coroners on the same principle as they were arranged in Parliamentary elections. (Hear, hear. The resolution having been carried unanimously, Mr. Riley returned thanks, and took occasion to refer to the loss the legal profession in Warrington had sustained in the death of Mr. Moore, solicitor. In the deceased gentleman's private capacity he was greatly respected, and when he (Mr. Riley) was opposed to him in cases at the courts he could not be described otherwise than a good natured pro- fessional enemy. (Hear, hear.) The meeting then separated. THE POLL. The poll was opened at Ormskirk at eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, and was closed at to in the afternoon, and throughout the day the ancient market town was the scene of bustle and excitement only parralleled on occasions of county parliamentary elections in the days of open voting. Well-filled trains poured in contingents of voters from Liverpool, iVarrington, Wigan, Widnes, Southport, St. Helens, Prescot, and other places ; whilst every variety of vehicle, from the fashionable four-in-hand to the rustic spring cart, was employed in the service of conveying countrymen from the outlying districts. As a result ef the abnormal addition to the population of Ormskirk, caused by the unprecedented invasion of voters, the catering capabilities of the local licensed victuallers were excessively over-taxed, and even the supply of gingerbread, the stable commodity of the city of cakes, was soon exhausted. Late in the afternoon every hotel or tavern in the town was besieged by a hungry host clamouring to have their wants satisfied; and the whine of a famished freeholder, who had travelled 40 miles to record his vote and had to return home dinnerless, elicited but scant sym- pathy on account ef the number of his bucolic brethren who found themselves in a like predicament. This was the first contested election since the year 1851, when Mr. C. E. Driffield was appointed. It appeared to be a conflict between districts rather than between parties. The suc- cessful candidate received the support of the Earl of Lathorn Rioletyt's haedhse: St. and other influential neighbours, rents were said to be principally Helens and West Derby. Political considerations were not supposed to enter as an element into the struggle, whilst residentsM r he cordial sympathy of the Conservatives in but it was abundantly clear that Mr. Brighouse had t his candidature. A number of the active wire-pullers of the party were conspicuous in the vicinity of the polling statietband committee rooms. Amonget those who arrived the Liverpool contingent were Colonel Ireland Blackburne, with m.p.; Sir Thomas Edwards-Moss; Messrs. W.Radcl iff e, T. H. Sheen, D. Radcliffe, J. Parrington, John Houlding, ' Thomas M'Cracken, R. Bennett, T. E. Priest, R. Gardners, Luke Bagnall, &c. The few local Liberals present included Messrs. E. M'Cabe, Sam Campbell (West Derby), John Ahearn, and others. The polling took place at tfie Work- men's Institute, the under-sheriff (Mr. E. Wilson) presiding as returning officer. The open system of voting was in force, and such was the crowded state of the polling place from time to time that many were unable to record their votes. During the day the number ef gentlemen holding trusteeships for various places of worship in the division claimed to be entitled to vote. Mr. Brighouse's agent objected on the ground of illegality, but the presiding officer overruled the objection, providing that evidence of trusteeship was given. The votes were accordingly allowed, the usual statutory oath being admini- stered to those who claimed them. Beyond the collection .of curious crowds in the streets and the congested condition of the hostelries the election was devoid of exciting inci- dents. At the close of the poll it was generally known that Mr. Brighouse had beeo elected by a large majority, the figures Riley 757. given befog :—Mr. Brighouse 1,996, and Mr.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT A PAPER MILL. On Tuesday morning a fire broke out in the extensive paper works at Auchrnutv, near Markinch, Fifeshire, the property of Messrs. Tullis and Co., paper manufacturers. Owing to there being re fire engine nearer than Kirkcaldy, great damage NU done before the flames were checked. A store which con- tained 600 tons of esparto grass was destroyed, but the main building was saved. The damage is estimated at nearly £lO,OOO. AJMER' OF A GERMAN NOBLEMAN AT SHEFFIELD.— The Sueffield police en Thursday, acting on instructions Nan Bow-street, arrested Baron von Weissenbarg, a Ger- man, on a charge of conspiracy and fraud. He was arrested Sr Melbourne Villa, Walkley, and remanded by the Shef- field stipendiary, pending the arrival of a London detective. He is charged, together with Alienate Lindon, with conspir- acy to defraud Heinrich Huttsch, of Bethnall-green, London, of £6OO, or the strength of certain securities which are stated to have moved valueless. The accused, on hearing the warrant read, replied " That is net so." He was re- manded to London.

A SHAMTATHOLIC PmEsp.—The Anglesey magistrates on Tuesday committed for trial at the assizes a man giving the name of Patrick Maguire, and representing himself to be a Roman Catholic priest. In May last year the prisoner appeared at Holyhead and represented to a number of Roman Catholics that he was authoris d by the Nun of Kil- dare to collect funds for the erection of a convent at Knock. He received several small amounts, and successfully carried on the earns practice for some time in the county of Carnar- von. There he was apprehended on a charge of obtaining money under false pretences, and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment. At the expiration of his sentence he was arresteil on the present charge,

ATTEMPTED MURDER OF A SWEET,EAILT.—A young man named Slaughter is in custody at 6tratford, Essex, on the charge of attempting to murder a young woman nanaed Pole. They had been engaged," but a quarrel occurred, and the prisoner, by way of showing his exceeding fond- ness for the girl, attempted to blow her brains out. lie failed, and then fired at himself, but none of the shots took effect.

At a meeting held in Manchester on Tuesday of cotton manufacturers in Blackburn, Darwen, and Padiham a rase' lution was adoped declaring that it was" necessary in the interests of trade to continue the struggte to obtain reduction of 5 par cent in the weavers' wages." Seveysi employers who were present announced their inten- tion to join in the effort now being made to secure the reduction.

A BURGLARS' CAE/UM—At Oldham, on Wednesday'. James Collins, John Mulcrone William Murphy, and Julia Rochford were charged with burglary. They had broken into tke Canteen heerhouse and carried off a large quantiti of beer in bottles and jars. They had been carousing all night. Murphy was found in the cellar, close to the stillager drunk, and the others were hiding. The prisoners were coin. 'flitted to the assizes. -

Craggs, a constable, made a determined at- tempt on the life of a police sergeant named Best, shooting hint in the face and shoulder with a revolver. .Cragge then drowned himself in the Tyne. Re had been called upon to resign his place in the police force, and seems t 6 have attributed this to certain complaints about him which had been made by Best. It is stated, howeverp that the amount involved is not very heavy, and will be fully covered by his guarantees. Mr. Asquith had held‘his position many years. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 19, 1884.

MR. CHAMBERLAIN, the President of the Board of Trade, made a very telling speech at Newcastle, on Tuesday evening. Ireland, Egypt, and the franchise are the three great questions which at present occupy the public mind, and each of these topics the right hon. gentleman dealt with comprehensively and conclusively. With regard to the franchise and its proposed extension to the counties, there is a general concensus of opinion that the time for argument has passed, and the period of action has very nearly arrived The country has made up its mind that the dwellers in the counties shall be placed on an equality with those in the boroughs so far as the suffrage is concerned,' and it only remains for the Government and Parliament to give effect to the wishes of the electorate. As regards Egypt, the Government, as we all know, have undertaken there a task fraught with difficulties and dangers; but to the pledges they have given to other Powers they will loyally adhere. Our course must neces- sarily be shaped according to the develop- ment of events; still the facts cannot be too often insisted upon that our object is not a selfish one, and that we have no designs of annexation or national aggrandisement. As, however, we have made ourselves responsible for the good government of Egypt we cannot, much as we should like, withdraw from the country until its internal affairs are organised Upon a stable foundation. The portion of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S speech which will be read with most interest is, we are sure, that relating to Ireland. The President of the Board of Trade has always championed the rights of Irishmen, and shown himself anxious to redress the grievances under which the Irish people suffer; he has been at the same time careful to insist upon obedi- ence to the law, and cautious not to give any countenance to schemes of separation. Because -he has spoken out so boldly in favour of the ftanchise in Ireland being precisely the same as that in England and Scotland, he has excited the ire' of Sir R. CRoss and other Members of the Opposition, who hold that so long as it is necessary to govern Ireland practically by coercion it would not be wise to place the Irish people on an equality with the People of England and Scotland in the matter Of the franchise. We need scarcely say that With this view we have no sympathy. The fact that the Crimes Act is still in operation in Ireland is no reason why the franchise Should not be extended there; but, if it were a valid ground of objection, we do not think it would be very difficult to show that it is no longer necessary to continue in operation the provisions of that Act. Crime in Ireland has been for some time steadily on the decrease. In 1880 there were 2,580 agrarian outrages ; in 1881 the number rose t 04,459 ; in 188 z there was a change for the bettter, the number falling to 3,427 ; but last year there were considerably less than r,OOO outrages, fewer, in fact, than during 1879, the last year of the late Conservative Government. This im- proved condition of the country is, we admit, due in a measure, though very slight, to the operation of the coercion acts, but still more to the benefits accruing from the remedial legislation of the Government. The Presi- dent of the Board of Trade puts this view of the question very clearly thus :—"Tens of thousands of men, fathers of families, the tillers of the soil, who a few years ago were Without motive for exertion, without hope of , improvement, are now practically the owners of the land they cultivate—bound over to . keep the peace by recognisances stronger than any magistrate can enforce, by the 4 full enjoyment of their profits, by the security in their holdings which has been given them ' by the Land Act It is to these causes, it is to this remedial legislation of the Govern- ment, more than to the Crimes Act, that we owe the altered condition of things, and that law and order now maintain their sway in • districts which only a year ago were danger- ously disturbed." If we continue in the future, as we have done in the past few years, removing the causes of Irish discontent, we ' May reasonably hope for a much greater im- provement in the country; but it seems to us that if Parliament were next session to extend the franchise in the English and Scotch Counties and withhold it in Ireland then there would be a just cause for complaint on the part of the Irish people, whilst such an in- discreet act would tend more than anything else to undo all the good. that has SO recently been done. Though much

has been accomplished, much yet remains to be achieved before we can be satisfied. or before we can plead that we have done all that is necessary for Ireland. As Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN says, and in this he will have the cordial assent of all Liberals, "we will not think our task completed until we have secured for Irishmen every right and every privilege which legislation has secured or may secure for Englishmen. Until that has been done it is altogether premature to despair of a gradual union between the two countries, and to the gradual disappearance of those bitter memories which long years of injustice and oppression have stamped so deeply on the hearts of the Irish race." By this means alone can we turn the Irish people from conspiracy and crime, and encourage them to pursue peaceful avocations. We have too long treated the Irish people as out- casts; let us treat them as our equals, and assuredly we shall reap our reward, Sir R. CKoss and other Conservative leaders are also opposed to the extension of the franchise in Ireland because it would be the means of increasing the number of Mr. PARNELL'S supporters who are anxious for separation Here is an admission by Conservatives that Ireland is not properly represented at the present time; for if it be the wish of the Irish people that Mr. PARNELL should have a greater following, by all means let them have it. There is a great deal of force and wisdom in Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S remark on this point, and that is that if there are really so many people in Ireland anxious for separation, it is well that we should be aware of it, so that we may know exactly what we have to deal with. If the genuine voice of the Irish people is not to be heard throughl their representatives chosen from a fair electorate, and if their aspirations are to be suppressed in the manner advocated by Sir RICHARD CROSS, then we may expect a reversion by the Irish people to secret and unlawful organisations with the object of enforcing their rights. It is to be hoped, however, that the bitter, experience in the past of these organisations—whose influ- ence Lord BEACONSFIELD described as some- thing worse than " pestilence and famine" —will teach our Tory friends to act wisely in the future, make them amenable to a sense of I justice and right, and enable them to see their way to treat Ireland in the same way that they would treat England and Scotland. We sincerely hope that the Irish leaders will lay to heart the rebuke administered to them by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. He cannot i be accused of any want of sympathy with I the Irish people, for he has on all occasions proved their friend, and that being so he can speak with greater freedom of I the indiscretion of the Irish leaders. Never! has there been in power a Ministry which collectively and individually has done so much, or shown a greater desire to do more, to redress Irish grievances ; nor has there ever been at the head of affairs in Dublin officials whose loyalty; zeal, and devotion to I the interests of Ireland could be surpassed by any Irishman, no matter how high he might be in the estimation of his countrymen. That ' being the case, it must be admitted that it is as ungracious as it is undeserved that so much abuse should be heaped upon the Govern- ment and officials by Irish members. Intem- perate language can never do any good, but it may do much harm. It gives the Conser- vatives encouragement to offer opposition to the Irish demands, and on this and other grounds it would be better were such language not indulzes,.l PIG•KEEPING IN *WIDNES.—On Wednesday. at Widnes Petty Sessions, Francis Cooke, of Alforde-street, was sum- moned on a charge of having a nuisance upon his premises by keeping swine in a filthy condition.—The defendant ad- mitted keeping the pigs, but denied that they were a nuisance.—Mr. Dickson said that since the summons was taken oat the defendant had abated the nuisance, and if he would pay the costs the Local Board were agreeable for the case to be withdrawn.—The defendant agreed to pay the costs, Is 13d, and the summons, was withdrawn. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Danby, on behalf of the Widnes School Board, summoned the following persons for not sending their children regularly to school :—John Martin, Edward Lightfoot, James Traynor, James Cummins, Patrick Caine, John Dwyer, Henry Whitfield, and Thomas Smith. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each case. I Two children of Catherine Howard were committed to the I industrial school. Adam Green, James Smith, William I McNamara, Thomas Curley, John, Frahm, Patrick Burke, ; James Lynch, and James Crabtree were committed to gaol for non-payment of flees inflicted en previous occasions. PROPOSED GYMNASIUM FOR RUNCORN.—A proposal is foot to form a gymnasium for Runcorn in conneetion with the Young Men's Christian Association, and about a week ago a meeting of the committee with several members of the Football Club was held to discuss the best means of attaining the object in view. All present seemed warmly in favour of such an institution, the only difference of opinion being as to details. It was stated by the Chairman (Mr. S C. Beckett) that one could be effectively started for about LSO, and it was felt that with the support the public would extend to the movement, and with the subscriptions of members, a gymnasium might be successfully floated. THE QUEEN'S VISIT TO FRANCE. CABINET COUNCELS.—A COUNTY COURT CASE. BELT V. LAWES AGAIN. THE DOL} SHOW AT THE CRYSTAL PALA,CE.—THE LATE FRANCIS HOLL, A.R.A.—ARTHUR HUNT'S LANDSCAPES AT THE FINE ART SOCIETY'S ROOMS.—THE THEATRES. —MINNIE PALMER. LOTTA, AMERICAN TRICKERY. END OF THE FLORAL TRIBUTE CRAZE. •—• THE ACTOR'S MATINEE. BARNUM AND HIS vuurE ELEPHANT. LONDON, THURSDAY. Her Majesty's intended visit to Cannes is not to take place this season. It was rumoured that the Queen would I go there at the end of the present month. It was even ex- pected that her visit would fall in in point of time with the marriage of the daughter of the Count of Paris. But Her Majesty enjoyed so much her last years sojourn at Men. tone that that sheltering little watering place will be re-visited this year. The Queen's visit is fixed for the month of March. Mentone, 20 years. ago well-known as a resort of invalids, is now becoming one of tbe most fashionable spots on the riviera. This year it will be un- usually gay. The Emperor of Austria is also expected te wards the end of March.

Townl9 filling. The holidays of the Cabinet end with the week. The ministers must be all back on Monday, and on Tuesday commences the final series of Cabinet Councils. It remains that what has been determined on shall be put into shape. We are within measusable distance of the 6th, and the Queen's Speech will have to be considered. I have seen doubts expressed whether Her Majesty will open Par- liament. I think I may say on good authority that she will not. It is curious how London brightens when the holidays are over. The shops have at last recovered from the dreary fortnight sales that follow the Christmas glut.

County Court decisions are not often worth recording, but a case came on at Bloomsbury as to which the law was perfectly clear, the grievance unquestionable, and yet the aCtion without precedent in the Judge's experience. There are points in the law of master and servant which it would be very well for a servant to understand. The servant was in this case the defendant. She had hired on the usual terms of a month's wages or a month's warning, and pro- bably did not realise that these coalitions were mutually binding. Not liking her place,", she simply walked out of it. Her mistress bad the resolution to sue her •for a month's wages, and the Judge had not the slightest difficulty in giving a verdict for that amount. It often needs the bringing an action to establish the practical value of a right: This procedent is now likely to be largely followed. The Belt case is beginning to get a little complicated. There have been so many motions, and applications, and blunders, and expectations, and disappointments, that not a day pasees but the familiar title appears in the posters of the evening papers. The exact way in which matters stand now is thie. Mr. Lewes has refused to give Mr. Belt £5OO and costs. The costs are £4,000, or about that. Be it understood that this is only the amount of Mr. Belt's costs. Mr. Lewes' cheque to his own solicitor would certainly not be less. The plaintiff went to the Court of Appeal on Tuesday, and what his counsel said to the Judges amounted to this, "I have got judgment for £5OO and costs; in other words I have judgment for £4,500. Mr. Lewes appeals and you have stayed execution till the appeal is heard. Now, lam afraid I will lose my money, my £4,500 which the Court has awarded me, and I ask I that Mr. Lewes be ordered to pay that amount down now, to be paid to me if I succeed, and back to him if I fail." To this the Court of Appeal replies, 'You are really suffering no hardship; the hearing of your appeal instead of beieg postponed for months, as might be the case, will come on in a few weeks. At the same time if you can show us that your money really is jeopardised, that Mr. Levees is going to be a bankrupt or anything like that, then we will probably give you execu- tion, but otherwise not." So the matter rests—at least down to to-day. A population of 1,507 dogs of all descriptions and sizes made the Crystal Palace this week very lively. The dog show has become now quite a recognised event—as the number of sporting men in the building made very obvious to-day. There was almost too big a show, and though the average was very high it is a question whether it would not be well to confine the winter exhibition to large dogs, and have a second show for terriers in June. The blood hounds were very fine, and one in especial was so like Landseer's model at the National Gallery that it might , I have sat to the painter. Looking at the collies, it seemed difficult to believe that they are the nearest approach to the dingo or wild dog of South Wales, and that they are of all dogs the tribe whose tempers can be least relied on. These seemed the very perfection of intelligence, and in complete sympathy with human interests. St. Bernards have gone up largely in pubnc esteem since the show at Knightsbridge this spring, or rather last spring. Another dog that has become quit 3 a well-known figure in the Lon- don streets is the brinded Danish mastiff. A foppish young painter who goes a good deal into society made this creature fashionable some few years ago, and now the tribe takes its regular place at every dog show. The fashion can't last long. He is an ugly leggy brute with only average intelligence and an abnormal appetite. I pass over , the whole race of terriers to say a word about :the eccentric
