At the theatres, this week, not much has been done in the way of novelty. Minnie Palmer has COlll3 back with her style rather chastened by her provincial experiences. She has begun to learn that a boldness which in America may be attractive, in England is considered to be not so much artistic as vulgar, and she has profited by her lesson. She got an entirely loyal reception at the Strand, on Monday, and her tricksiness and quaint childish self-complacency delighted her audience. Meanwhile her rival tried her fortune with a new play at the Opera Comique, directly opposite. Lotta appeared as Little Nell which she did very indifferently, and as the Marchioness which she did very well. Chas. Dickens had dramatized for her his father's novel, and a house that has just been pulled down and was supposed to have been the original Old Cutiosity Shop, was reproduced as a background through the agency of the scenic artist and the stage carpenter. Lo:ta is undoubtedly clever and original. But what a gift is youth! Minnie Palmer copies her, at least the two styles, absolutely new to the London playgoer, seem to him identical. Lotta has most genius, but Minnie Palmer Is—the younger. There was a trickiness about both performances which deserves censure. A theory was got up by Miss Palmer that Lotta's friends were going to hiss her, while Lotta on her first night decor- ated her top gallery with a row Of substantial looking-out, unattractive police. In neither house was there the smallest semblance of a disturbance, and this bit of Yankee clap- trap has met with universal censure. At the Drury Lane pantomime, when oue of Cinderella's sisters (played by Mr. 11. Campbell) comes on, a basket of pumpkins and cabbages is handed up from the orchestra; and on the first night of Princess Ida, when a bouquet was flung to Miss 13raham, she ignored it. Other tricks for generating fictitious enthusiasm should be as sternly put down.
A very characteristic matinee WhS given on Tuesday at the Princesses. Mr. Wilson Barrett played to a house

filled with nothing but paper. It was an invitation to the actors to come and see the play. The leading members of the profession were in stalls and boxes, and up in Olympus were euphs and scene shifters. So many theatres now have matinees on Satur- days that this was the .only chance the majority of the leading actors had of seeing the play. I think I never saw an audience so critical and no appreciative, or a company play with so much fire or "go." An amusing study was Mr. Toole, sitting in a private box surrounded by his family and carefully treasuring up the recollection of every turn and gesture of his friend Barrett. Pan Claudian, the new burlesque by Burnand, will be given in a few dais, and while other actors were enjoying the play, Mr. Toole was minding Mr. Barrett's " business" and learning his part.

Tickets for the Zoo next Sunday will be at considerable premium if the white elephant should be on view. Barnum, who does everything on an enormous scale, seems to have arranged with nature to have the arrival of this deity pre- luded by a white rainbow. Both have been seen for the first time the same week. There is a popular idea, too, that the real exp!anation of all these phenomenal sunsets will prove in the end to have something to do with the great Yankee showman. This tricking his beams and flaming in the forehead of the morning sky is the biggest thing in the way of a novelty which he has yet brought out.

• WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the members of the South Divi- sion of the Widnes Liberal Association was held on Tuesday evening, in Oakland-street School; and there was a large ' attendance. Mr. B. Holden Davis had been announced to preside, but some untoward circumstances pi evented his attendance, and Mr. Joseph Robinson was voted to the chair. Amongst those present were Messrs. Wyse, J 14son, John Jackson, Samuel Jackson, J. Betney, C. Jones,,!'. Isceland, Myers, T. Andkers, John Evans, John Ankeis, Chrimes, Rickard, John Hartland, Alderson, W. Whitley (local secre- tary), and H. B. Shores (general secretary).. The CHAIRMAN said it was not his intentioa to attend the meeting, but he was specially requested to Oo so because Mr. Davis could not fulfil the position of chairman. He was glad there were so many present that night. He ,Jelired that was the largest meeting they had had in that division for the object they had in view. (Hear, hear.) He thought, therefore that they had a right to say that the Liberal cause was growing amongst them, and it afforded him great pleasure to see that it was a growing cause. At the same time, there was room for Improvement in that large populous district. The political world was likely soon to be agitated with many burning questions—the County Franchise Bill and other questions which he might mention were coming before the country with increasing force day by day. Tney might be on the eve of events that they had no idea of—nearer to a dissolu- tion of Parliament and a general election than any of them thought of. It therefore behoved them all to be on the alert, and watch the political signs of the times, so that they might be ready in the case of a general election to carry their candidates forward at the head of the poll—at any rate in that district. He thought they had made satis- factory progress during the year as regarded the south division of the Liberal A9saciation, and he believed he was right in saying that that division had always done itself credit as compared with the other divi- sions in matters of registration. The secretary had shown him the returns of registration, and he was quite gratified that by the Executive Commmittee, through the instrumentality of Mr. Shores, they had been enabled to gain so many votes on the register. It was also highly satisfac- tory, because the power they could exert at a general elec- tion depended upon the degree of energy which they put forth at the time the register was revised. He only hoped the other divisions of the Liberal Association in Widnet were doing like satisfactory work, so that they might have all their forces in the field. Mr. II: B. Seroags said with regard to the work of the Association at the revision court, we had the county secre- tary's statement as made out at Liverpool. That statement he might say was somewhat less than the statement of the local gain, owing to the fact that some of the property .owners for whom they had claimed in Widnes h4d property in other parts of the county, and were therefore what were termed dual voters, and their gain would be a credit to the county in which their vote first existed. Consequently, although they might obtain their votes in Widnes, they did not give them the credit for them. The statement of Mr. G. H. Powell was as follows :—Widnes: Struck off old register, 12 Liberals and 14 Conservatives; property claims allowed, 9 Liberals and 5 Conservatives; struck off £l2 list, no Liberals and 24 Conservatives—(hear, hear)—making, ac- cording to his statement, a nett gain of 30 Liberals. ( Ap- plause.) But, as he had said, they were entitled to count 6 more locally, making a total of 36. The gain last year was 122. They had been unable to repeat that increase this year, because their action was limited to Liberal pro- perty owner, and they could only claim for such as did own property. The coming year would be one of great impor- tance in the political world, inasmuch as they hoped it would witness the passing of the County Franchise Bill. Should that be the case, instead of Widnes having 900 odd voters he calculated that they would have about 3,500, and as they believed that an extension of the franchise would be in favhur of the Liberals they hoped to get a large accession to their voting , strength. (Hear, hear.) This year, too, would probably witness a redistribu- tion of seats. Under these circumstances, although Widnes with its 27,000 of a population was hardly likely to have a member of its own, it would come into greater prominence, as its population already exceeded the population of some six small boroughs that had members—that was six of these small boroughs put together would only have a popu- lation slightly exceeding the population of Widnes. (Ap- plause.)

The CRA/RMAN said he was sure they must find that a satisfactory report. If the County Franchise Bill. came be- fore Parliament and was passed irate law this sesaionf-Par- liamentary candidates would have to appeal. to quite a different social element in their midst; that wecto bay the electoral franchise would be carried down to 'a -lower point in the social grade. He thought tsUch a measure would come with the greatest - grace from a Liberal Government, and he hoped the time was far distant when a Liberal Government would fear to appeal to the free opinion of the masses of their countrymen. The Liberal idea of government rested upon the free expression of the people and upon the suffrages of the M4SSS of the community. If the franchise was extended it would cause a great increase in the work which the committees would have to perform next year. At this point Mr. Robinson was compelled to leave, and Mr. Wyse was appointed to fill the vacant chair. Mr. WHITBY moved that the thanks of the meeting be tendered to the retiring general committee and executive , committee, referring in complimentary terms to tbe labours 1 of Mr. Shores, the general secretary. Mr. P. IRELAND seconded the motion, which was carried.

The election of the committees was then pro- ceeded with, the result being as follows: General committee, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, S. Hall, R Shaw, H. Gasket', jun.' T. Snape, George Chrimes, T. Whitby, John Whitehead, P. Ireland, Thomas Hughes, John Ankers, John Betney, John Jackson, W. Priestnall, John Wvse. Thomas Makers, C. Jones J. Davies, T. Smith, B. Lock, John Anderson, Win. Scott, Samuel Myers, Jahn Evans Owen Owens, C. Evans, Henry Rickard, Adam Houghton, S. Jackson, J. Hartland. Executive Committee, Messrs. J. Coxon, W. Crabtree, Joseph Newell, Jos. Robin- son, Edward Knowles, John Hardee, H. N. Wharton, W. W. Gossaage. On the proposition of Mr. JACKSON, seconded by Mr. ALDERSON, Mr. T. Sutton Timmis was unanimously re- appointed chairman; and Mr. Whitby and Mr. W. W. Goes-age were appointed joint secretaries. Mr. SHORES said the association was this year making a special effort in the shape of lectures to organise public opinion. They contemplated having a lecture delivered in that room, on the 23rd inst. by Mr. Hampden Jackson, from Liverpool, who would enlighten them upon the subject of the county franchise. The chairman of the Finance Committee, Mr. Timmis, had told him that he thought it especially desirable that they should get all their Liberal friends to take some share in helping forward the cause in Widnes. He therefore suggested that they should ask for a sthall subscription, no matter how smell They should be glad to take le per annum, so that they could feel that they had a certain number of gentlemen who were. at the back of the committee, and not be obliged to rely simply upon the large subscriptions of the manufacturers—(hear, hear)—which to a great extent they had hitherto done. Mr. P. IRELAND said Mr. Whitby had served the party ably and well, and he believed all Liberals were in duty bound to give him their hearty thanks—(hear, hear)—and he begged to move a resolution to that effect. The motion was seconded and carried with acclamation.

Mr. WHITBY, in reply, said it give him great pleasure to do what he could for the good of the Widnes Liberal Asso- ciation, especially for the south division with which he was specially interested. He concluded by moving a vote of thanks to Mr. T. Suttdn Timms, the Chairman, for the way in which he bad always conducted the business of the As- sociation. (Applause.) His wise counsel and superior judgment they could always rely upon. (Applause.) Mr. ALDERSON seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamation, and the meeting terminated.

DRAMATIC PERFORMANCE AT HALE.—The residents of Hale had the pleasure of enjoying two very admirable dra- matic performances this week, the first being given on Mon- day evening and the second on Tuesday. There was a large and fashionable audience at each performance. The enter- tainments were given by the "Hale Strollers," who com- prise some really clever amateurs, anel they took place at the Drill Hall, kindly placed at the disposal of the "Strol- lers" by Lieutenant-Colonel Mewburn. The pieces repre- sented were Mr. Charles Dance's petite comedy, "Who Speaks First," and Oxenford's c:miedy, "Billing and Coo- ing," in two acts. The acting throughout was excellent, and the efforts of the amateurs were thoroughly appreciated by the audiences. The mechanical stage effects and scenery were designed and prepared by members of the company. Both performances were given under the patronage of Col. J. Ireland Blaciaburne, M.P., and Mr. E. Whitley, M.P. • Look out for dri2ith's Rune nm Alm macks for 1884. The,. are on the way. Over a ton and a halt weight. Call for One. --Advt.
ADULTERATED MILK AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Session, on Monday, before Mr. C. Reynolds, and Mr. G. Davies, John Anderton, shopkeeper, Church-street, was charged with having on the 6th Dec. unlawfully sold to the prejudice of P.C. Bossons milk which was not of the nature, substance and quality demanded. Mr. Burton apfreaged for the defendant, who pleaded not guilty. —On the 6th December Police Constable Bossons purchased a pint of milk from the defendant's shop, for which he paid 2d. Mrs. Anderton informed him that it was as she had re- ceived it. A sample of the milk vras forwarded to Dr. Carter Bell, who certified that it contained six per cent, of added water.—George Cooke. farmer, Halton State, and George Leathwood, deposed that the milk was delivered pure, and Mrs. Anderton stated it had not been tampered with whilst in her possession Cooke stated that the chemical gases of the district had a prejudical effect opt' the health of his cows, and upon the grasses, and last year he lost 14 head of cattle. De food had an effect upon the milk of the ani- I male, and his milk was not of the best quality. Before giv- ing a decision, the Bench heard a second case of a similar nature against Tickle. shopkeeper, Egerton-street. In this instance Cooke had also supplied the milk, but the analyst stated there was 18 per cent, of added water.—Mr. Burton, for the defence, pointed out that in all milk there was from 88 to 9ci per cent, of water, and be contended that the Manchesrer standard was too high, whilst analysts differed as to the component parts of pure milk.—The Bench ordered Anderton to pay costs amounting to £1 Bs. 61., and fined Tickle 103, and costs £1 Bs. 6d.

The annual meeting of the trustees and managers of the above bank, was held at the Bank Office on Tuesday after- noon. The Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A. presided, and there were present, Boys W. Preston, E. Williams. Messrs. W.' Simpson, W. Whittaker, John Brundrit J.P., W. Handley, W. Jones, and 11. F. Salkeld (actuary.) Mr. SALEELD hav- ing produced the auditors' certificate as to the correctness of the accounts, read his annual report. He said although several large sums had been. withdrawn during the past year, the amount deposited by investors was t little larger than when the last report was presented. viz : due to inves- tors on the 20th November, 1883, £23,847 Es 9d; same period last year, £23,769 15s 7d. The assets were as follows :—with the Commissioners of National Debt, £23,534 17s 3d; with the treasurer to meet calls, £365 4:4 id; total assets, £23,900 is 4.1, leaving a surplus of £52 12s 7d. Mr. W. WHITTAKEIC moved and Mr. W. HANDLEY seconded that the accounts be passed and the report adopted. The motion was carried nein con.—The CHAIRMAN proposed a vote of thanks to the treasurer, lie need not refer to what be had often referred before, namely, the great services which Mr. Simpson had rendered to the bank. They bed beard of heaven-born ministers, but he thought Mr. Simpson was the heaven-born treasurer, and he should be glad if Mr. Simpson's services were Continued. The Rev. E. WILLIAMS seconded the proposition which was carried unanimously. Mr. SIMPSON in acknowledging the vote, said he was glad that so many could meet together year by year. Mr. Brundrit was appointed one of the managers, he. (Mr. Thompson) was appointed treasurer, and Mr. Salkeld the actuary, all on the same day, and Canon Bar- clay was present in the chair. There were four of these I who had continued to meet year after year for 28 years. If it was not out of order, he should be glad to move a vole of I thanks to Mr. Salkeld. He and Mr. Salkeld had worked comfortably together during all these years, and he thought everyone most quite understand that Mr. Salkeld had the best interests of the Savings' Beak at heart. His whole character, and his regularity and punctuality, and hie remarkable correctness in connection with all cash matters, had been perhaps the greatest cause of the success of the Runcorn Savings' Bank, and he hoped he would be I spared to occupy his present position for many years to sgitne.—The Rev. W. PRESTON seconded the motion with great pleasure. There was no doubt the office held by Mr. Salkeld was an important one, and the welfase of the bank depended more or less upon him. It was satisfactory that the bank was making some progress. It was one of the in- stitutions in Runcorn which was not going back but devel- oping. It was also satisfactory to know that it was appre- ciated by those whom they were anxious to lead into ways of thrift—that they were bringing more money to the bank, so that when a rainy day came I they would have something to fall back upon. Although the percentage had been reduced from 3 to 21 the investments were somewhat larger, and this, he thought, spoke well for the habits et the Runcorn 'people at large. The good of the institution depended upon the secretary (Mr. Salkeld), not upon the ornamental head, the president; and the welfare of their institution was due 'to what he had done. He heartily reciprocated what had been said, that he might be long spared so that they might have the pleasure of meeting him from time to time, and also their worthy chairman. He rejoiced to see the chair- man with them that day, and he hoped they might meet him on several similar occasions.—The vote was passed.— Mr. Semorth returned his acknowledgments for the com- plimentary way in which he had been spoken of for his services. Twenty-eight years was a long time for a person to look lotck to, but it seemed a longer time to look forward to. Bat still during those 28 years his meet- ings with the gentlemen present had been of a cordial and agreeable nature without fault-finding or any- t thing of that sort, and they had been very grateful to his ' feelings indeed. He hoped he might be able to continue his services a little longer. He thanked them from the bottom of his heart for the kind and complimentary way in which the vote had been proposed and seconded.—On the motion of Mr. BRUNDIZIT, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY, a vote , of thanks was accorded to the auditors.—The Rev. E. WILLIAMS proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman.—Mr. HANDLEY seconded, and observed that they were all glad to see that Mr. Barclay was still able to take his public position so well and so ably. (Hear, hear.)—The motion was heartily carried —The CHAIRMAN said so long as he had health he should be happy to do what he could for the ' benefit of the bank and for every institution in connection with the town.---ahe meeting then concluded.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

Tsar.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. IMPORTANT TO BOAT OWNERS.—SamueI Bowyer, boat- man, sued Messrs. Simpson, Davies, and Ca., for lOs 6d, on account of freight, and there. was a counter claim for a guinea for damages sustained in consequence of delay by the plaintiff in delivering a cargo for the defendants. Mr. Burton appeared fo- the defendants and admitted the plaina tiff's claim, leaving the counter claim to be tried by his honour.—Mr. Burton said the plaintiff was a boat owner, or captain of a flat which belonged to the • port of Runcorn, , and the defendants were large merchants and alto carriers. ' Althmigh the sum in dispute was not large in value, there was a principle involved to all those engaged in the carry- ing trade. ORVW 3rd December the plaintiff asked whether there were any goods he could carry to Worsley and Leigh," I sod the defendants informed him there was a cargo that could be made up for him. He understood that the goods were required to be delivered with the greatest despatch, au ahe agreed te load. On the 3rd his boat was loaded except a email amount to be put on board the following morning. He left Runcorn on the 4th December. the boat being loaded with five tons of salt for Worsley and 35 tons of iron ore for Leigh, and he ought to have arrived at Worsley at noon on the sth. He, however, did not arrive ar that place until the 7th, and having delivered the salt, he went on to Leigh, where he arrived on the 10th Dec. This delay was a very serious matter indeed to the defen- dants,as their trade would be impaired if they could not have despatch, because they had to compete with the railways. Although the loss they had sustained was very heavy they only sought to recover nominal -damages of one guinea. The facts were proved by William Kudge, outioor foreman, and Hugh Rowe, clerk, and Richard Toft, agent for the Bridgewater Navigation Com- pany at Woreley, said there had been no storm or any sty- page in the canal to delay the plaintiff; and John Hughes and Joseph Gandy gave evidence of a comfirmatery char-. acter.--The plaintiff stated that he did his best to finish the journey quickly, but the water was low in the canal and he could not get along—llls Honour said it had been clearly shown that the canal was in its usual condition, and the plaintiff ought to have completed the journey in reasonable time. Judgment was given for the plaintiff for Ws 61 and against him on the Counter claim for £5.

AGED PEOPLE'S TREAT AT RIiNCORY. .I he annual treat to aged people, organised by, the. com- mittee of the Young Men's Chrietian AssocMtionetotok. place in Runcorn Public Hall, on Tnuesday evenizg. and was a complete iuebess. The oaly passpeart-/requirect for admis- sion to the excellent repast provided' was aro, and the com- mittee had fixed 60 years as the lowest limit. About 500 persons assmeled in the hall, which had been most taste- fully decorated, and their wants were attended to by the following ladiese-111 is. Beckett, Mrs. Bowyer, Mrs. Coven- try, Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Howard, Mrs. Humphreys, Mrs. Kniveton, Mrs. Lake, Mrs. Leatbwood, Mrs. Millinger, Mrs. PownalL Mrs. C. Pownall, Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Smith, Miss Bar- clay, Misses Booth, Miss Edwards, Miss Forster, Miss Gregory, Miss'Norman, Miss Owen, and Miss Peacock. lhe majority of old people present were women, and several had attained the age of 80 years, whilst there was one whose hair was silvered with the snows of 93 winters. At one table there were seventeen persons whose united ages amounted to 1,070. After tea an entertainment took place, under the presidency of Dr. Steele, who was supported on the platform by the Revs. Canon Barclay, M.A., 'F. M. Armson, and E. Williams; Messrs. J. Simpson, S. C. Beckett, F. A. Lake F. J. Norman, P. Briscoe, W. Whit- takerrT. Nornian, d. Randle; T. Howyer, and W. Pownall, jun. (hon. sec.) The Rev. E. Williams having offered prayer, Dr. Sleele'addreased a few suitable words to the as- semblage. A reference to . Cation Baxclay's long connection of thirty-sight years with the town evoked a hearty response, - and it was with regret the audience heard that in consequence of the feeble state of his health he could net raise his voice high enough to be heard over the building. Canon Barclay had, however, asked him to express to them his hearty good wishes' and a hope that they would spend a pleasant even- ing. The entertainment was then proceeded with, and seemed to be much enjoyed. The band of the F and G companies of the 2nd C.R.V., 'conducted by Mr. T. Woods, rendered several selections of music, as did also the Mersey Mission Band. The following also took Dart in the entertainment:—Miss Jones, Miss Leadbetter, Miss Jukes, Miss Horton, Messrs. C. Pownall, R. Morris, W. Pownall, T. Davies, J. Craig, and B. Knive- ton. Miss Jukes accompanied. UTTERING FALSE DECLARATIONS.

- A WARNING TO PIG DEALERS. • Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, Joseph Profitt, a pig dealer's labourer, of Latchford, was summoned for uttering a false declaration in order to evade the provisions of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act of 1878.--Mr. W. H. Jenkins appeared for the defendant.—lt seemed that the defendant, who was employed by a pig dealer named Hugh Bradbury, of Knutsford, sold some pigs to Thos. Massey at Warrington marset on-the 19th ult., and also gave him the declaration produced, which was false, allowing the pigs to be removed into an area which had been declared infected with foot-and-mouth disease.—Sergt. Harrington proved that foot-and-mouth disease broke out on the farm of Mr. Stan- ton, Tttelwall, on the 29th November, that the place had been declared an infected area, and that notices to that effect had been posted in various public places.—Mr. Jenkins' defence was that the defendant did net commit the offence inteationally, and in support of this be called the defendant, who said that he had no knowledge of the district being declared an infected area. Mr. Jen- kins quoted sub-section 5 of the Act which contains the words "unless he shows to a court of summary jurisdiction that he did not knew its falseness, and that he could not by reasonable diligence have obtained knowledge thtreof."— Toe case was diarnissed.—The defendant was then charged with uttering a second declaration which was false.—Ed- ward .Dennett stated that he bought two pigs of Hugh Bradbqry on the 29th ult. He told Bradbury that he lived in Cheshire and that he would want a declaration. Brad- bury shortly afterwards gave him the declaration pro- duced, which, however, was signed by the defendant.— Mr. Jenkins put forward the earns defence as that made in the previous case remarking that it would not be right for the d:fendant to be 'punished when he had unwittingly been made a tool of by Bradbury.—Tuis case was also dismissed.--Hugh Brad- bury Was then similarly charged to the last defendant in respect of two declarations, and he was fiiied £2 10s and costs in each case, which in all'amounted to £7 ss, the magistrates remarking that if he came before them again on a similar charge, he would be very severely dealt William Williamson Was fined 108 and 27s costs for a similar offence.

div.head: LATE MR. G. T. MOORE, OF LATCHFORD.
div.p: THE LATE MR. G. T. MOORE, OF LATCHFORD.

, A feeling of deep and sincere regret has been excited in the minds of his professional colleagues, and indeed her the public generally, in the death of Mr. G. T. Moore, solicitor, and ex-Town Clerk of Warrington, which sad event took place at his res Pence, Latchford Hodge, Latchford, on Saturday evening last, about seven o'clotk. The deceased gentleman was the eldest son of Mr. James Townend Moore, M.D., of Liverpool, and was originally intended for the Church (his father being a Protestant), but as time went on he was at his own request articled to Messrs. Woodcock, Part, and Scott, solicitors, Wigan, Mr. Moore being related to one of the firm, and adopting the religion of his mother, he because a Catholic, in which faith he died. Having served his articles he was duly qualified a solicitor, and was admitted on Nov. 14th, 1854. Shortly afterwards be married the eldest daughter of Mr. James Fairclough, of Wigan (the present Mrs. Moore), an extensive builder, a Catholic, and a magis- trate of the borough. Mr. Moore then settled in Warrington as a solicitor, he partnership with Mr. Shepherd, and they carried on business together up to a few years ago, when Mr. Shepherd retired. For about nine years Mr. Moore held the important position of town clerk of the borough, but he resigned a few years ago, and this enabled him to devote himself more fully to advocacy, in which he dis- played much forensic ability. The deceased was well-known in the police and county courts of Warrington, Newton Daresbavya.R -Runcorn, and Widnes, and his winning and genial manner brought him a large circle of friends. Mr. Moore, too, was a staunch Conservative, but he never played a very prominent part in local politics. About three years ago he had the misfortune to lose his eldest daughter, and this was a great shock to him. Mr. Moore at the time of his death was 54 years of age ; an I the immediate cause of his demise was, we understand, enlargement of the heart of very long stauling. Tne remains of the deceased gentleman were consigned to their last resting place in the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday. In the morning the coffin was removed from Latchford House to the chanel of St. Mary's, Litchford, where a service—attended by the relatives and friends of the deceased—was held, and which WAS taken part in by Fathers Thompson, Beauvoisin, Feeney, Furniss, Flanagan, and Barry. Subsequently the funeral cortege, which con -slated -of ,a hearse and six carriages, proceeded to Wigan. Seieral wreaths of immortelles were placed upon the coffin; and are a mark of respect to the deceased the blinds of the wiedews of tbe houses were drawn in the streets through which the mournful procession passed. On Monday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) said that before the ordinary business columenced he should just like briefly to pay a passing tribute of respect to the memory of one who on Saturday last passed from among them after a few days' illness. He alluded to Mr. Moore, the eldest local practi- tioner at that court, with whose face they were all perfectly familiar. He (the Mayor) did not hesitate to say that his heart was incapable of retaining eeen for five minutes a lingering recollection of any wrong which might have been inflicted upon him, and he believed that envy, hatred, malice, or uncharitableness could have no abiding-place ill Mr. Moore's heart. Therefore, it was with fellings of some little emotion that he alluded to him. Ha was sure they all , eympathised with Mrs. Moore and her family in their sad 1 1 bereavement—The clerk (Mr. H. B. White) s aid he was glad 1 to be able to corroborate anything that the Mayor had said with respect to Mr. Moore's geniality and kindness of heart. To what the Mayor had said he must add that he had been clerk to that court sixteen years within a few weeks, and he must say that there had not been a shadow of unpleasantness of any description between Mr. Moore and the. Bench, or between Mr. Moore and himself. Mr. Moore's cannectioes with that court had always been of an agreeable nature, and he was sure that as a court they would miss his presence very much. (The Mayor: Hear, hear.)—Mr. Bleckley, who sat on the Bench, at a subsequent part of the proceedings said that the sad news respecting Mr. Moore bad only just come to his knowledge, but he could not refrain from saying that they all regretted Mr. Moore's &vase. Mr. Moore had practiced at that court for a great many years, and they would all feel they had lost a man whose presence they were always glad to see in court. (Hear, bear.)—Yesterday, at the Borough Court, Mr. Percy Davies took occasion to refer to the loss the profession had sustained in the death of Mr. Moore. • Personally be felt he bad lost an old friend, and be was sure the magistrates felt it too. It seemed to him almost in- credible that they would never see Mr. Moore's genial and kindly face in that court again. He was certain the Bench joined with him in sympathising very sincerely with the widow and family.—The Chairman (Captain Reynolds) said he felt as much as anyone the death of Mr. Moore. He bad known him for the last thirty years, and they would always remember him as being a very pleasant man. On Thursday he paid the last tribute of respect to the deceased gentleman by following him to his grave, and he did so with a very heavy heart. They would never see a more amiable or genial man practising in their midst. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Ziba Armitage, who was also On the Bench, joined in the chairman's expressions of sympathy, observ. lug that they would miss the deceased gentlemaa very much. 'Hear, hear.) i. —....—...„—. WARRINGTON HIGHW 10ARD:

A meeting of the Warrington District Highway Board was held at the Bovd's Office, Sankey-street, on Wednesday afternoon. There were present—Messrs. R. Hought - (chairman), J. Fairclough, J. Stanier, E. Marsh, G. Lawto3 W. Royston, R. Owen, junr., J. Houghton, H. B. WV • (clerk), Longland (assistant clerk), tfd .1. Thompson (tsar- veyor.) . PROPOSED RAILWAY FROM Low"rox TO LEIGH. , The SURVEYOR reported that he had read a notice that the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Com- pany intend applying to Parliament for an Act empowering them to construct a new railway from Lowton to Leigh. He had examined the deposited plans, and found that the proposed railway would only interfere with the Board's district by crossing Common-lane, near to Mr. Ince's shop. The level of the line would be 16 feet below the present surface of the road, and the road would be raised two feet, the approaches having gradients of one in 30. The greatest inclination of the present road was one in 42, which he considered should not be increased. Be thought that if be SAW the engineer to the company the requirements of the Board would be readily complied with, as an altera- tion in the proposed gradient would be of little expense.— It was decided that the surveyor should see the company's engineer with a view to securing the alteration referred to.

THE BOARD AND THE SHIP CANAL. The SuRVEYOR reported that he had examined the plans of the proposed Manchester Ship Canal so far _as they related to the Board's district, and he found that it was pro- posed to divert a portion of the river near Willgreare's Farm, Woolston. It would therefore be necessary to have steps and hand-rails on each bank. Al- though the bill provided for steps and hand- rails on each bank of the canal at that point, nothing was said about providing similar accommodation on the banks of the proposed diverted pot'. tion of the river. He thought that the omission was an oversight —The CLERK was instructed to consult with the solicitors to the company with a view to securing the in- sertion in the bill of a clause providing the additioual ac- commodation.

CROFT AND ITS LIABILITIES. The CLERK said that all the calls had been paid with the exception of that of Croft.—Mr. OWEN said that he saw it in the newspaper after the last meeting of the Board that the Assistant-Clerk had had some conversation with the Overseer of Croft, and that the latter had told him that he could not get the money in. When he saw that he imam- mediately went to the Overseer to see if the statement was correct, and the Overseer told hire that all the calls were paid, and had been some time. He thought there must be some mistake some- where.—The ASSISTANT-CLERK produced the book containing the accounts relating to the .question, and said that the last call which was paid by the overseer for Croft was paid in August., and he did not see that any call had been paid since.—Mr. OWEN: He told me all the instalments were- • paid in Who was the person you had the conversa- .•. , „ ton with r—The ASSISTANT CLERK: Mr. Brimelovr.—Mr. Owme: Well, he said he hadn't seen you for 12 months. (Laughter.) I may say for ,Cfaft that I think we pay as soon as anybody, and I don't think it is right for Croft to be pointed at like that.—The Caelnetati remarked that there must be a mistake between the oy•rseer and the Assistant Clerk.—Mr. OWEN: tie distinctly told me that he had paid in all the rates be had received.—The CLERIC remarked that it was possible the overseer had paid the account to the treasurer, but be (Hie _clerk) could not mark it off until be sarha tthief t ;tees timreerr'ssereerphiapdts—areTdbme Cu cHhA fortrtulkb said be thought character be would, when he saw the obeervation in the papers, have called upon the Clerk tease that the matter was set right.—lt was decided that the Assistant Clerk Avid communicate with the overseer on the question. There was no other business of public interest.

ISLAND REVENUE PROSECUTION. A LTTEXI GENLLEmix HEAVILY FlNED.—Yesterday, at Lymm Petty Sessions, Charles Farnsworth, The Hollies, Lymm was summoned for employing a man servant on the 25th 'September without having a licence; further, with keeping a carriage without a licence; and also with keeping a dog without a licence. —Mr. W. H. Jenkins appeared to prosecu.e on behalf of 'the Board of Inland Revenue.—The defend mt did not ap- pear.—lt seemed that in 1882 the defendant had licences for two servants, two carriages, and two dogs, but in 1883 he only took out licences for one carriage and two dap, although he still employed one man servant, kept two car- riages, and bad on this occasion four dogs. Previous to these proceedings being taken defendant had been communicated With by the Inland Revenue oflicers several times respecting the matter. When the four dogs were found on his pre- mises he stated that one dog was not six tn. ntbs old, and that another belonged to a Mr. Sennett, and was on his pre- mises "on approval." Mr. Bennett was seen and be stated that the defendant had bought the dog and had paid for it. When the defendant was told of this he admitted that he bought the dog, but said that be bought it en the condition that it was able to do is the field all that he required it, adding that it could not jump. On one occasion when a visit was paid him by Mr. Ray, supervisor of the excise at Warrington, he said that be was sorry that the licenses had not been taken out, and that be had omitted to do so owing to the pressure of business. He also said that he thought that those licensing laws had been repealed.—The defendant was fined £5 and costs in each of the two first cases, and. '1 13s. and costs in the third case, in all £l6 Sa. 6.t.

FRUIT FARMING. Sir,—Referring to Mr. Gladstone's speech at the annual rent audit at Hawarden, will you kindly allow me to reply to that portion which refers to fruit farming? I will take the points in order as reported. Mr. Gladstone says that the number of acres of fruit grown in this country has only increased by 27,000 acres in the last ten years, and that i 24,000 out of the 27,000 acres has been n five counties only. I have no doubt that this is quite true, and the counties referred to are those immediately around London. Other counties at a further distance from London go in for only partial cultivation of fruit, say Cornwall, Devon, Gloucester, Worcester, Hereford, Shropshire, Cheshire, and Norfolk; but a large proportion of other English counties do not grow fruit to any extent as compared to the acreage under culti- vation of other products, and I, as one of the largest la:Hemmers of English fruit in this country, am compelled to draw very large supplies from the counties immediately round London, of which tiovent-garden and other London markets are the centre. I have for many years been of opinion that if the British farmers would put an increased portion of their soil under the cultivation of gooseberries, raspberries, strawber- ries, black currants, plums, and damsons, it would pay them much better than their present mode of working. In the manufacturing counties of Lancashire and the West Riding of Yorkshire there is a very large consumption of jam, and I am quite certain that there is an adequate supply of good agricultural land available in these and other northern and midland counties which might be most profitably brought under fruit cultivation, and would find a ready market within a comparatively short distance of the growing districts. I support Mr. Gladstone's statement that what are considered ae the most ungenial climates in the whole of this island are favourable to the growing of delicate fruits suitable for the manufacture of preserves, thus proving that the farmers in the North of England are just as likely to improve their income by fruit-growing as the farmers are in the famed county of Kent. Mr. Gladstone is right in stating that the manufacture of fruit preserves is beginning to take a new position in this country, and is now being largely used. He is, however, in error in stating that jam is charged from 7d to 9d a lb., and also that this is owing mainly to the energy of the French, Belgian, Dutch, German, and American fruit growers. No doubt the first four countries do give a supply of )sorne kinds of fruit for the manufacture of jam, principally plums, but I am not aware that America sends us any fruit whatever for jam-making. By far the largest proportion of fruit used for the manufacture of jana„is, I believe, grown in this country; and, personally, I may be al- lowed to say that the gooseberries, raspberries, strawberries, black currants, and damsons used by me are entirely English -neforeign whatever being used-and to prove that the quan- tity is not particularly small, my usual season's make is : Gooseberry, 300 tons; raspberry, 300 tons; strawberry, 200 tons; black currant, 400 tons; damson, 500 tons; black- berry, 100 tons; and they can be bought retail from any ready-money grocer at the following prices: Gooseberry, 5d to sid per lb.; raspberry, Od to 6d; strawberry, 8d to 811; black currant, 50; blackberry, 54d; plum, 4d. Mr. Glad- stone is therefore in error in stating that the jam consumed in this country is not English-made jam. I speak with a large experience of the trade, and I have never seen a single package of French, Belgian, Dutch, German, or American jam offered in this country.—Yours, , Ww. P. HARTLIIY. Bootle, Liverpool, January 10th, 1884.

EMMANUEL CHURCH TEL PARTY. Sir,—lS is truly pleasing to read the account of the Emmanuel Church tea party as recorded in your last week's issue. It is truly pleasing to hear of the growing prosperity of the Church. It is exceedingly pleasing to see that in their noble stand for conscience sake they have not only tile sympathy of all the Nonconformist bodies, but also the sympathy and support of their eiangelical brethren of the National Church, thus manifesting to the world that a true spirit of Christian unity may, can, aod does exist without an absolute uniformity. But according to the old proverb, no rose without a thorn. The Rev. W. Mules must have been inspired with the spirit of irony when he said that he almost asked the Chairman to offer himself for the work ef the ministry, because it is too evident that the white tie and the empty pocket are not the only lacking qualifications. No doubt the worthy Alderman is useful in his day and generation in the sphere which he occupies; but really his animadversion upon the character of Solomon reflects little honour upon him as a student of Biblical literature. But he is comparatively young; as he eta older he may become more and more reflective he may again look at the books of the Kings —he rn ty again look at the Book of Provers, the teachings of which are all in keeping with the one which reads "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom," and "The departure from evil is understanding." He may look again at the sublime song of songs, and reflect upon it in the light of the latter-day dispensation. Anel last but not least, he he may look again at the Book of Ecclesiastes, the teach- ings ef which are all in harmony with "Remember thy Creater in the days of thy youth ;" Christian men be. ware. Ye are yet in the flesh, your probationary'state is not ended. Ye still belong to tbe Church militant, each one of yen carry in your bosom the evil heart of unbelief, the natural tendency of which is departure from the living and life-giving God. If David and Solomon, men eminent for Godliness, were liable to fall, so are ye; if they fell or fall, they did most grievously, so may ye therefore be not high-minded but fear. "Backsliding Christians dispair not! feavid and Solomon were restored, and so may ye." David's restoration is explicitly declared, and the restoration of Solomon is implicitly portrayed in the Book of Ecclesiastes the last sacred production of his pen.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, OBSERVER. Warrington, January, 1884.

div.head: LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL
div.p: THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL
TRADE.

In the iron market business continues qeiet, and there was but little doing on 'Change, on Tuesday. There are, however, inquiries in the market at low figures, and at the minimum rates there .are buyers for long forward delivery. In some cases pig iron makers are showing a disposition to give way to meet buyers, and for local brands quotations have been reduced to 44s for forge and 4.5 s for foundry, less 2, delivered equal to Manchester, but these figures do not bring forward orders. Some of the district makers still hold out for full late rates, but where business is done it is at about is per ton less, and sales have been made on the basis of 43s 10d to 443 101, less 21., for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered equal to Manchester. In manufac- tured iron very little is being done except where makers are disposed to give way on late rates. Some of the leading Lancashire and Staffordshire makers are still quoting £6 2e 6d for bars delivered into the Manchester district, but for good specificAtiens £6 is being taken, with hoops to be got at £6 78 6d to £6 108, and sheets at £7 53 to £7 lOs delivered.— Since the commencement of the year business in the coal trade has been exceedingly dull, and it is only in excep- tional cases that pits have resumed work on full time after the holidays. A quiet tone is necessarily given to the mar- ket by the mildness of the season, which is keving down the demand for all descriptions of round coal for house fire purposes. Common round coals have been moving off mo- derately fer iron making and steam purposes since the re- sumptioa of operations at the various works after the holi- days, but the demand is without animation. The shipping demand for steam coal has been quiet, with sales pushed at low figures. At the pit mouth the average quoted rates are without change, beet coal averaging 103 to lOs 6d, seconds 8s to fis 61, common lime coal 6s 6d to 78, and steam and forge coals ns to es 81. There is, however, a good deal of underselling, which is giving a downward tendency to the market, and for shipment Lancashire steam coal delivered either at Garston .m Liverpool can be bought readily at 83 per ton. The strike in the cotton trade Is affecting the de- mand f i ar engine fuel n some districts, bat Apart from this 48 9d to 58, best slack 33 9d to 48 3d bargy anl slack appear to be moving off fairly well, good burgy fetching ordinary qualities 38 3d to 38 6d, and common sorts, good about 35 per ton at the pit.

The men of the first class Army Reserve have received orders to present themselves at their appointed stations for medical inspection. They tell a capital story in the Temple of ex-Chief Baron Pollock, that one who wished him to resign waited on him, and hinted it, suggesting it for his own sake, entirely with a view to the prolongation of his own valued life, eto. The old man arose, and said, with his grim, dry 'gravity, "Will you dance with me ?" The guest stood aghast as the Lord Chief Baron, who prided himself particularly on his legs, began to caper about with a certain youthful vivacity. Seeing his visitor standing surprised, he capered up to him, and said, "Well, if you won't dance with me, will you box ' with me?" and with that he squared up to him, and, half in jest, half in earnest, fairly boxed him out of the room. The old Chief Baron had no more visitors anxiously inclair- ing after his health and suggesting his retirement. COAGULIXE.—Cemeat for Broken Article.. 61., is., 24 poi- tage 2d. CHAPI'BR LXVI.—"No Moult DBLIISIONS, MOTELBR ?" "Dear, sweet girl!" ejtculated the Countess as she re- viewed what had passed, conscious of the fearful effect upon Miss Vandeleur if once more there should be disappoint- ment; but fortifying herself as she best csald for her next task—the demand she had said she would make upon Lord Harlaxton. It was then that Stephen drew near, and discovered she was alone. She heard a step behind her, turned, and saw him ; and her face lit up with joy and new confidence that since he was here all must and should go well. Advancing to meet him with open arms, she stopped, as if struck with paralysis, at the sight of his cold, severe face, and forbidding gesture. And when he spoke hie words gave intensity to his as- pect and manner. "I learn on my arrival that Miss Vandeleur is to be mar- led to-day ?" Lord Harlaxton hopes so, Miss Vandeleur fears so, but "No more delusions, mother; lain sick of them!" "Do you dare thus to speak to me ?" responded the Countess indignantly. "I dare to tell you the truth, if you are not afraid to listen to it," said Stephen. "I will listen if it kills rns!" cried the Countess, half .closing her eyes, as if to shut out the world and all pertain- ing to it, while she did listen. "Truth should cure, not kill!" rejoined Stephen; "when the disease is the suppression of all truthful and honest life, as I have too late discovered. To break away from such a life, and replace it by a better—an independent one —I have exposed myself to the most infamous of all punishments. I whisper it once to you, then seal my tongue for ever. I have narrowly escaped being flogged; supposing that is, I could have found no means of taking myself oat 0 the world's way beforehaad!" FARN WORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

OPENING OF THE NEW BUILDING. SPEECHES BY LORO WINMARLEIGH, MAJOR CROSS, MR. E. K. MUSPRATT, MR. TIMMIS, AND MR. F. H. GOSSAGE. The Grammar School of Farnworth was on Thursday again launched upon a career of usefulness after being closed for a period of six years. Before relating the cir- cumstances that led to the stoppage of the operations of the school we may briefly refer to the history of so venerable an institution. It is indeed one of the most ancient gram- mar schools in South-West Lancashire, having been estab- lished at the beginning of the 111 h century. Dr. William 'Smythe, Bishop of Lincoln, who was born at Coerdley or In one of the adjacent townships, is generally credited with being the founder. In 1507 he gave to the Monastery of Launde £350 towards the purchase of the rectory of Rs- theme, and coupled with the gift the condition that £lO per annum should be paid out of the rectorial tithes towards a sufficient and honest priest "teaching grammar freely at a free school at Farnworth, in the county of Lancaster.' The abilities requisite to fill such a post are shown by the reser- vation that the priest must be "a Master or Bachelor of Arts, or a Master of Grammar" at the least, and as he would have under his care the sons of the squires and the wealthier yeoman for miles round, Warrington being the nearest place possessing a similar institinion, it was necessary .that he should be a man of culture. About 1530 the rectorial tithes of Rostherne were transferred to Christ Church, Oxford, and subsequently they were leased by the Mainwaring family, of Peover Hall, Cheshire. Sir S. T. Mainwaring now pays the.n to the governors of Tarn- worth School. Up to tile year 1623 the school appears to have been to a great extent under the control of the Mayor and Corporation of Chester, who had vested in them the right of appointing the master. In that year, however, the control ceased, and since that time the inhabitants of the parish of Farnworth have elected ten trustees, in whose hands the management of the school has been placed. Naturally such an institution was made the recipient of various benefactione, and in 1574 Matthew Smythe,who was fist principal of Brazenose College, Oxford, and who was related to the founder, bequeathed a tenement and lands in Sutton to William Smythe his nephew, who was "Parson of Barton-in-the-Clay, Bedfordshire." This property Was chargeable with 20s. a year to be paid to the usher of Farn- worth Grammar School, and that sum is now pail by Mr. Michael Hughes, who is the present possessor of the estate. In 1630 Henry Plumpton 'of Rainhill, bequeathed to the school a field in Rainhill of about eight statute acres, which have since been sold for £1,550, and the money invested in the official trustees of charity lands. The dividends are now paid half-yearly to the governors. At a sub- sequent date J. Plumpton willed to the sclrool a farm in Penketh containing nine statute acres. The rent was to be divided equally between the master of the school and the minister of Farnworth. The farm was recently sold, and purchased by Mr. Bolton for £1,650. At the same time an allotment on Greystons Heath, owned by the same proprietors, was sold to Mr. Wareing for £3OO. In both cases the proceeds were invested in the official trustee of charity lands, and the dividends are received in equal proportions by the Grammar School and the Vicar of Farnworth. On °Jae of the benefactor's tables in Farnworth Church various sums of money amounting to about £l9B, are recorded to have been bequeathed to the school from time to time, and it is supposed that part of this money was in 1760 invested in the purchase of a copyhold house in Farnworth-street, Farnworth. The house has since been pulled down, and the site leasad for a period of 70 years to the executors of the late Mr. Lockett at £8 per annum. By a bond granted to Thomas Kidd, on the 18th June, 1872, and bearing interest at the rate of 5 per cent., a sum of £96 ' was secured on mortgage of the tolls of the turnpike road 'leading from Warrington to wigan. When the turnpike trust was abolished the bond was surrendered for £3B Os and the money has been invested with the official trustee of charity lands. Through various fluctuations of fortune the Grammar School has existed for nearly four centuries, and many eminent men have within its walls felt the first prompfings of genius. It was here that Richard Bancroft, who became the Archbishop of Canterbury, and was elected a Privy Councillor and Chancellor of the University of Oxford, re- ceived the rudiments of that education by which he at- tained to the highest dignity both in Church and State. iThe school has not, however, always bad the same habita-1 tion although the name has changed not. It has been re- moved from time to time to meet the requirements of the , neighbourhood. Mr. James Raven, who was appointed the head master in 1862, erected himself a suitable build- ing. When he resigned his position in 1877, the governors were unable to obtain the premises on what they considered fair terms, and they found themselves in the unique pre- dicament of having scholars without a school. It was ulti- mately decided to temporarily suspend the operations of the, school, and at some future time reorganise it upon a new basis. On the 14th August, 1879, the Queen sanctioned a scheme drawn up by the Charity Commissioners. By thie scheme the school Was made of an entirely unsectarian character, and placed under the control of ten governors, two of whom were to be selected by the Widnes Local I Board, two by the School Board, and two by the local justices. The other four are termed co-operative governors, and these are Major Cross (chairman), Mr. S. Broadhurst, Great Sankey; Mr. W. W. Tipping, Bold , Hall; and the Rev. George Bond, M.A., vicar of Farnworth. The Local Board is represented by Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., and Mr. E. Carey; the School Board by Mr. T. S. Timmins land Mr. John Brock, J.P.; and the justices by Mr. Holbrook Gasket', jun., J.P., and Mr. Henry S. Hall, J.l" The scheme provides that nobody shall be admitted into the school under eight years of age, or remain there after 16, except by the special permission of the governors. The tuition fees are £8 per annum, or 133 4d per term. The course of in. struction includes Latin, French, mathematics, English grammar, composition, and literature, natural science and the usual elementary subjects, besides book-keeping and vocal music. Upon the receipt of this scheme a piece of land 9,000 square yards in extent, situate near Farnworth Central Railway Station, was purchased, and the governors , forthwith issued proposals for the erection of a new school I at a cost net exceeding £2,000. The designs of Messrs. F. and G. Holme, architects, Liverpool, were accepted, and the general contract was let to Messrs. Brown and Backhouse, of Wavertree, and building operations were commenced last summer. With the exception of a few minor details it is now completed. The structure is built externally with grey bricks, and is handsomely ornamented with terracotta panels of quaint design. Over the staircase window are the arms of Bishop Smythe, who founded the school, in terracotta, and in- scribed in quaint letters under the window is the name of the school and the date of the foundation. The school is entered by a central porch facing Peel House-lane, the door of which opens on a large vestibule or staircase hall. On the ground floor are two class-rooms capable of accommo- dating 80 scholars; while on the first floor is the main schoolroom, approached by a staircase from the vestibule. It is 40 feet by 22 feet, and capable of accommodating 90 scholars. Half way up the stairs, to the right, is the mas- ter's room, and a flight of steps from the main room leads to the storeroom. The interior ef the school has a most pleasing effect, due in a great measure to the design of the staircase. The roof of the building is formed of red tiles, which harmonises with the rest ef the building and is most picturesque. We ought to mention that the school is de. I signed to form a large group of buildings, with principal's residence, and numerous class-rooms for scientific teaching, for which it is needless to remark there is a large plot of land available. The playgrounds are very extensive. The terracotta and red pressed have been supplied by Messrs. T. C. Edwards, Ruabon, and the heating apparatus by Messrs. J. R. Cooper and Sons, London. Mr. J. Hough, Widnes, provided the school furnture Although the Widnes people have no Cause to complain as regards the education provided for their children, they will welcome this addition to the educational forces of the neighbourhood. There is no doubt the grammar school will fulfil a want long felt by the middle and upper classes, in that it supplies a higher class of education than can be given either in the well conducted Board schools or the ex- cellent establishments maintained by voluntary aid. The curriculum of the grammar school includes a variety of subjects, and a master well qualified to teach them has been engaged in the person of Mr. Walter A. Watts, M.A., who is assisted by Mr. H. V. Black, M.A. The endowment of the school only amounts to £75 per annum, but the governors have guaranteed the head master a salary of £350 per annum for the first two years. The institution is, however, intended to be self-supporting, and whea the extensive population in the immediate vicinity is considered, there is no reason to doubt it will be so. No accommodation has been provided for boarders, but with the permission of the governors the head master can arrange for any students that may apply. As we have stated, the opening ceremony took place on Thursday afternoon in the large hall of the new building, which was well filled. Major Cross presided, and amongst those present were Lord Win- marleigh, Captain Brunner, Revs. Canon Penhryn (Hay- ton), G Bond, W Stewart (Hale), J Wright Willams, J C Brawn, S A Spooner, J Holden; Dr. Cooper; Messrs E K Muspratt, F H Gossage, J.P., T S Tiininie, J Brock, J.P., E Carey, II Gaskell, jun., J.P., W W Tipping, J W Waring, Jataes White, Robert Kidd, A E Smith, Joseph Morrison, Joshus Midwood, D Wright, T Handley, S Sadler, W Gil- , body, Inspector Wood, S Owens, R Webster, T J Peters, 1W A Watts, H V Black, and R Lewis (hon. secretary). Major Cross, in opening the proceedings, gave an interest- ing sketch of the history of the school, relating the facts embodied in our introduction. There bad, he observed, been a great deal of dissatisfaction in that district from the fact that the Charity Commissioners had done away with the old custom of a number of free scholars being chosen by the township and sent to the school. With this the Governors had nothing whatever to do and could not help it. The Governors hoped before long, however, to be able to give a certain number of free nominations to the school. (Applause.) If that were done it would be for the benefit of the whole of the scholars of the district in the chapelry of Farnworth. That was to say, there would be some ex- amination by which a child educated in any school of what- ever class or denomination in the chapelry compete, and, passing well, get the free scholarship. (Hear, hear and applause.) The Governors hoped- to make the school a thoroughly efficient high class grammar school for the dis- trict. (Applause.) When the new scheme came into force the Governois had to provide suitable premises, and they set about doing so and (the building in which they were now met was the result. The total number of scholars for which the building was adapted at present was 60, and they had got something like 20 scholars in at- tendance. (Applause.) He might say that the Charity Commiseionere out of their funds gave the money to buy the site, but they refused to go any farther, and the eon-

sequence was that the building was to be provided for out of private subscriptions. Something like £2,000 was re- quired to complete the building and furnish it. Of this, £l,OOO had been subscribed, and he was perfectly sure that when the trade improved they would very soon get the other £l,OOO. (Applause.) So far, however, he must say that very little had been received towards it—(laughter)— but he hoped the opening of the school would induce those who had not subscribed to do so. (Applause.) The gover- nors had appointed Mr. Watts, who was well known in the district from his having had for a long time charge of the art and science classes in Widnes as head master— (applause)—of the school. He was assisted by Mr. Black so that he thought they might congratulate themselves' upon having first rate teaching element to commence with. (Applause.) He need not say that in a district like this very great attention would be paid to subjects more im- mediately connected with the industries of the country. The natural sciences would be made a prominent feature of the teaching of the school. He then called upon Lord Winmarleigh to declare the school open, observing that a more appropriate pers in could not have been chosen. (Ap- plause.) Lord WINMARLEIGH, who was loudly applauded on rising, said it was in obedience to a request made to him by the governors of the school, conveyed to him by his friend the Vicar of Farnworth, that he had come to discharge the duty of opening the building. It had been great pleasure to him to do it for many reasons. First, because the reritiest was conveyed to him by the son of one of his oldest politi- cal friends, to whom in the earlier stages of his political life he was deeply indebted for the active suppart which he gave to him in the' northern pert of the county, and he did not like to refuse the request of his friend's son. Secondly, there were family associations with F anworth which made him take at any rate an indirect interest in everything that occurred there. His family had been connected with Fern- worth for centuries. Although he had tiO connections with the place either by property or otherwise, he had buried in the church yard of that parish ancesters who lived two centuries ago. But there were nearer family connections than these which induced him to take an interest in any- thing that occurred there—(applause)—and which made him come there under some little difficulty on account of. the state of his health. The noble lord then referred to his political connection with the county, extending over a period of half a century, and went on to say that there was no movement that had excited such interest in the public mind, or upon which there was such an unanimity of opinion, than the educational movement of the present reign. (Applause.) This movement, which commenced some four years ago was now in full activity throughout the kingdom, and there was no doubt that if the object with which all these im- provements were undertaken was carried into effect, the generation which was now rising would be better educated: than any generation which had gone before. (Applause.): George 111, the grandfather of the present Sovereign, ex- pressed a wish that before he died every one of his subjects might be able to read the Bible. That aspiration was never' realised. At that time the System of education was in a veryl imperfect state. He could recollect when only two or three out of every ten of the labouring population in the district where he was could read the Bible. He believed that before the reign of Queen Victoria was ended every one of her subjects would be able not only to rea4 their Bible, but would have been educated tq such an extent that they would be acquainted with till history of their country, and with the elements of the natural sciences. They would, in fact, have an education that would enable them to take advantage of all the oppore tnnities which many offer by which they could rise in the, scale of society. (Applause.) When the history of the' present reign came to be written, amongst the many momeni. teas events that would have to be recorded the educational movement would form an important item. (Applause.) It I might be recorded of them that while they had their politi- cal differences, their religious dispetes, there was one sub. ject upon which they had been united, and that was the determination of every Government, whether Censer-1 vative or Liberal, to promote the education of every class of her Majesty's subjects.. (Applause.) It was quite true they had not all agreed upon the mode of doing it. But if they reviewed the history of the different Govern- ments of this country for the last 50 years, they would find ' amongst the main objects they bad in view was the iini. provement of the education institutions of the country, ani more or lees they could all claim the credit of having one ginated and supported the present movemeet. (Hear, hear.) Aneougst the schools which required perhaps more assist- ance thao any other were the high class schools to which Farnworth belonged. Ile did not believe that the elemen- tary schools could be much improved beyond what they were at present as regarded the system, but the higher claim schools might be made more serviceable to the districts in whicli they existed than they hitherto had been. (Ap, planets.) He was delighted to hear that they had intro. duced at Farnworth the subjects of French and German, and natural science, and thus that school would fulfil the position which it ought to occupy in the general scale to which he had alluded. Referring to gratuitous scholarships, the speaker said he had in the House of Lords opposed theEr discontinuance in the grammar schools, but he was beaten by men on both sides of the House with this argument, to which he attributed great weight, that the Government were giving out of the taxes of the country two and a half million pounds towards education in elementary schools. Ile knew that the taking away the advantage re- ferred to by Major Cross bad been deeply felt in one or two grammar schools in the country—Warrington and another—in whiuh - tz2,7416,44.11, Eitetettta, ut he thought the exhibitions _ , ea: up to competitive examination were doing as much good as was done under the old system. His Lordship then touched upon the impor- tance of scholars obtaining a knowledge of the modern European languages, which were of great advantage in cons- mercial pursuits. He also alluded to the founder of the I school, Bishop Smythe, who, he believed, came not from Cuerdley but the very village of Farnworth. He was one of the greatest benefactors to education in this country. He founded one of the first colleges in Oxford, Brazenose College, to which Lancashire was much indebted. (Applause.) It was a college at which more Lancashire men had been educated than any other, or any other University. He knew dis- tinguished men who attributed everything they had in life to the education they received at Brazenose, a college founded by an inhabitant of Farnworth. Archbishop Bancroft was also educated at that school, another instance of what could be attained be sedulous attention to duty, but though he did not believe they could all be archbishops, he did be- lieve that if his life were prolonged he might see some of the scholars in that school fulfil high positions in this country. His Lordship gave some excellent advice to the boys assembled, and referred to the great and honourable men that had been educated En the public schools,such as Eton, Harrow Rugby, and Winchester, mentioning Canning, Fox, and the present Prime Minister—(applause)—and expressed the hope that from the building he bad that day opened would issue many distinguished and noble men. (Applause.) Mr. E. K. MIISPRATT said he had been rather unex- pectedly called upon to say a few words on that occasion.' His Lordship had referred to the great revival of interest in education during the reign of her present Majesty. The former revival of learning, and he might say the foundation of many of our grammar schools, dated back to the reign of a former Queen of England—the reign of Queen Elizabeth. The revival which had taken place during the present reign had been caused by the feeling that if education was to be made national, it should be absolutely nsectarian. It was to this feeling that we owed the Education Act of 1870, which had givers the nation for the first time a national •system of education. In the reconstruction of these old endowments, the Commissioners had insisted upon the fact .that they should be made unsectarian. That school, as Major Cross had told them, was going to be worked on those lines. In this way they would gradually obtain a national system of education, beginning with the hoard and other elementary schools of the district, followed with secondary schools such as the Farnworth Grammar School, and then in the city of Liverpool they had a University College which would form the third rung in the ladder. He expected that they would see the time when the children who entered the board schools would be able to obtain a univer- sity career. This path was, he believed, open to many of of the pupils who would enter the Hall, in which they were then assembled, for he hoped that under the instruction of the head master, Mr. Watts, they would be fitted to take a high rank and many of them wpuld proceed to the Uni- versity College at Liverpool. Beth in the higher and lower education of the age they had found that it was absolutely necessary that the teaching of natural science should be in- cluded. (Hear, hear.) They found this to be necessary, because, as practical men, they saw that other nations were rivalling England in her manufactures and becoming great competitors. And why was this the case? Because in Switzerland, and Germany, and now in France there had been established a system of elementary education followed up by a system of secondary education in which natural science was included. For the last 40 or 50 years natural science had occupied a high place in the education of Ger- many, owing to the education given in the universities of that country being of so high a character. He understood from Mr. Watts that the division was to be equal in that school—that was to say, that Latin, the natural sciences, •and mathematics, and the other branches of learning which would be taught there were to have an equal share of atten- tion. There had been a great discussion throughout the country as to the respective educational value of the science. and the classics. For his own part he looked upon perfect education as necessarily including both. (Hear, hear.) Unfortunately their schoolmates had been ben taught in schools where science had not been taught, and the great difficulty which their public sehooltnasters had was in finding competent teachers of scieuce. However, in connection with the school they were opening that day, they would have the great advan- tage of possessing in the head master a man who was him- self competent to teach science. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He, therefore, thought that he might auger well for the suc- cess of the Farnworth Grammar School On aecount of its having as its head master one who was thoroughly imbued with the necessity and proper way of carrying out scientific teaching. (Applause.) Mr. T. SUTTON Timms said, as chairman of the Widnes School Board, he welcomed on behalf of himself and his colleagues that addition to the educational facilities of Widnes with very great pleasure. They certainly possessed some excellent board and voluntary schools ; but as re- garded secondary education there had long been a great want felt, which he believed the, Farnworth Grammar School would supply. There were a number of people resi- dent in that district who ranked above the position of work- ingmen, who did not feel inclined to send their children to the board schools, and he knew as a fact that many of the

Am I Versau ? Am I Barrisre ? Ate I EAPPIIII? Wiser ? That is to say, more self•controlled, less the slave of my passions, less Irritated by small vexations, brayer in bearing misfortunes, more careful to live for eternity ? Better ? More forbearing towards others, more forgiving, less uncharitable, more reticent in exposing the faults of others, more solicitous for the happiness of those around me?—Happier? That would mean more contented in my station of life, striving tio derive all possible benefits from it, to beautify rather than to alter it? Have I more faith in God, and more calmness aad resignation in all the events of life?

- 91iLLING TIM SCIENTISTS.—One day, at the Academy of Sciences, they had a long and tiresome session. Arago thought he would go out and take the air. At the foot of the stairway there was leather bowl, upon whichlhe rays of the sun were beating. Arago turned the bowl round, and, rushing upstairs, told the distinguished assemblage that he had just met with something very mysterious. "That leather bowl," he said, "at the foot of the stairway, is cool upon the side which presents itself to the sun, but warm upon the other side." The scientists descended in a body, and substantiated this assertion. They took the inclination of the sun, the hour, the minute, the second, and a vast array of other details. They made calculations; and seve- ral weeks afterward each of them presented a paper explain. ing the phenomonon, Arago himself taking care to send in his explanation with the rest. There is no knowing how far the discussion might have gone had it not been for the doorkeeper, who, having seen Arago turn the bowl, and pitying the worthy gentlemen who were so much worried, cleared away the mystery.
