div.p: fmen of the middle class bad had to motto outside in order that their children might obtain that education which they felt to be necessary. That school might also supply another want. It was quite possible that some bright genius might be discovered in the beard schools, and when he got to the sixth standard he could not go any further in these schools, but if the child could be sent to a secondary school be would get a more perfect education, and from thence pass on to the University College. Under such circumstances these bright intelligences would not be lost to the country. It was also quite possible that some of the men educated under improved conditions would be the means of developing new industries and new processes which with their present edu- cation they were unable to bring to perfection. They had got a small council of education in Widnes, and it had been decided to offer prizes with the object of stimulating the at- tendance. At the time when the matter was discussed it was suggested that some portion of the funds should be devoted to establishing scholarships. He must say that be took the lead in opposing that proposal, net because he did not appreciate scholarships but because he thought that some of the manufacturers in the district might establish them. Now that times were improving he had every hope , that some scholarships might be founded so that the child- ren obtaining them might get an education that would , allow them to pass on to a University. (Applause.) He I concluded by proposing a vote of thanks to Lord Winmar- I leigh for his presence that day in complimentary terms. . Mr. F. H. Gosseon (who was greeted with applause), se- conded the motion' observing that they all owed a debt of gratitude to Lord Whemarleigh for coming there at that season of the year. The prosperity of Widnes had been re- ferred to several times that day, but in soliciting help for , the school he had been told that the times were bad, and they could not subscribe. He had had, therefore, to go away empty handed. But he had not been discouraged, be- cause he always had faith in Widnes, and he bad always I felt that when trade improved tha institution would receive I the support it needed. (Applause.) I The motion was carried with acclamation, and his Lord- ship suitably responded, expressing the hope that the ' talented head master would succeed in the object he had I undertaken. is The proceedings then terminated.

MP. LYIIISI CONGREGATIONAL CHURCII. ANNUAL TEA MEETING. In connection with the above church the annual tea and meeting were held in the schoolroom, on Wednesday even- ing. The room was beautifully decorated. There was a large gathering, about 150 ladies and gentlemen being pre- sent. The following ladies presided at the trays : Mrs. Bedell, Mrs. Astley, Mrs. Chandley, Mrs. Bowen, Mrs. Merchant, Mrs. Rowson, and Mrs. Frangleton. After tea the public meeting was held, the Pastor (the Rev. J. Beddell) presiding, and supporting him on the platform were the Rev. John Yonge, the Re'. Thomas Jenkins (Bucklow Hill), the Rev. Thomas Rippon, Messrs. Nichols (Altrincham), Woodburn (Partington), R. Dobson (Man- chester), G. N. Ford (Ashton-on-the-Mersey), and G. Wood (Bowdon). The Rev. CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said he had to thank those kind friends there for the sympathy and the kindness and the patience with whisk they had treated their pastor. If anyone had to speak of always being surrounded with loving friends he had. He thought that meetings of that kind were in every way good; they brought a blessing with them, and gene- rally, if not always, left a blessing behind them. He thought that those present ought to thank God that they had been spared to meet together that evecing. Mr. Woomenstre than addressed the meeting. He referred to the pamplet entitled "The bitter cry of outcast London," and said that he did not know of any pamphlet that had produced such a sensation in the country for many years past as that had done. Evidently its revelations were of a sad character indeed, and now the cry was "What is to be done ?" He had recently heard an excellent paper on " The duty of the Church in relation to the poor." The poor were in our midst, and their was no use in their denying the fact; it was patent to every observer. The great Teacher said " The poor ye have always with you," and were they to give them the cold shoulder ? No ; but they were to sympa- thise with them and to help them. There were two classes of poverty. There was the poverty which was the result of intemperance, improvidence and idleness, and of all poverty this was the worst. But there was another class of the poor, and if they were to trace their ancestry, their great-great grandfathers were poor, and they lived in" Poor-street," and the probability was that they would remain in " Poor-stri et " as long se they remained in this Vale of Tears. With these they greatly sympathised. He quoted portions of scripture showing that Christianity was adapted to all conditions of men, and said that it was the great panacea, the great care- all. They talked about social reform, and he would go in for social reform and better furniture, kc. He believed in political reform—(applause)—and be hoped they would all be included in the coming Reform Bill. (Applause.) But, after all, self-reform was the truest, the noblest, the wisest, and the best reform a man beginning with himself in self-know- ledge, self-control, self-reverence. "A man who conquereth himself is greater than a man who taketla a city." Let them each tied out what their particular sphere a life was, and then move in that sphere. (Applause.) Mr. GEOHGH WOOD then gave an humorous, but earnest, address, urging upon his hearers to make it a practice to attend a place of worehip regularly. The Rev. JOHN YONOH said he was very much inclined to sympathise with the remarks which were made in Lymm a week or twe ago. Speaking at a meeting in connection with the Methodist Church, his good friend and neighbour, Mr. Rippon said that he thought that newspaper reporters and Methodist ministers were the hardest worked people in the world. He did not know about newspaper reporters, because he never was a reporter, and, therefore, he did not know the strain of work that rested upon them from time t, time. And, again, he noticed that news- paper reporters never made speeches about their own performances, but he did know something about Methodist ministers and Congregational ministers. He had some very dear frinds among the Methodist minis- ters, and he looked upon his brother Rippon as one of his best friends in that Church. He always laughed at Mr. Rippon when he came to see him because he was always complaining of how hard the Methodist ministers had to work. He (Mr. Yonge) had a sort of envy of Methodist ministers, because one sermon of Mr. Rippon's could be made to go 13 times as far as one of his. They knew what he meant by that: Mr. Rippon had 13 places of worship to preach at, and if he liked he could take one sermon round to all those places. He (the speaher) preached in his own pulpit every Sunday. If they took into consideration the sermons they had to make and the meetings they had to attend he believed it might be a revelation to some there that Congre- gational ministers had to work very hard. He was verf glaa to be present to express his sympathy with the Chair- man that in a recent hour of danger a merciful Providence watched over him and kept him from more serious harm and injury in that fearful storm. He confessed that he pitied very heartily those poor Hebrews they read about in the Book of Exodus who in Egypt had not only to make bricks for very long hours, but had to make bricks and find their own materials for making them. That was a somewhat similar position to the one in which he was placed in com- ing there that evening. It struck him that con- gregations sometimes treated their ministers very much like the Egyptians treated their Hebrew slaves. That was to say, they expected good work out of them, and still they witheld the materials for the right-doing of the work they expected from them. Every , congregation in the land he supposed expected its minister , to give two sermons every Sunday. In all congregations he thought they would find that there were a considerable number of persons who absented themselves from their places in church upon the Lord's Day, and he contended that people who were in the habit of doing so were withold- ing from their ministers very valuable material for the right- doing of their work. He thought empty benches were very bad conductors. They could not expects minister to get any inspiration or help in his work from empty seats. He had this fact—and he had to a certain extent this experi- ence—that a good congregation would nearly always make a good sermon. They might depend upon it that a man would speak better to a full house than to an empty one. A great deal of the success of the pulpit rested with a few. There must be an opinion in the minds of some people that . all the prosperity and usefulnese of the Church , rested entirely ia the hands of the man who , occupied the pulpit, for how frequently was it the case that members of the Church ; left the ministers and the deacons to make all the arrange- ments and carry cut all the work of the Church. The Church ought to be a hive of constant and indefatigable industry. [ The souter they got to realise that the sooner they would realise Church happiness and prosperity. It would be a [ very easy matter to preach a long sermon on the indo- lence of Christians. The people who really enjoyed their religion were the people who were most earnest and most . faithful in the work in connection with it. But those in- dolent Christians did nothing, and they enjoyed nothing; and besides that they hindered everything, and threw a damp upon every good work. They made people of the world soy "what can there be in their faith ?' and they die- , honoured the Master whom they professed to serve. In conclusion, he would join his voice with that of Mr. Wool , in hoping that during the absence of their minister they would not neglect to carry on the work of the Church and Sunday school, so that when their minister returned he would have no occasion to regret his forced absense from their midst. He was sure the desire of all their hearts wal . that he might be brought back with renewed energy and , vigour. (Applause.) , The Rev. THOMAS JISMINS, in an earnest address, paid , a high tribute of praise to the chairman, and gave Borne , excellent spiritual advice. The Rev. THOMAS Rio re next addressed the meeting. He said that he had reason to be thankful to God forth' ; influence upon his mind and heart of Congregationalitant [ and his contact with Independent ministers. He had rsecti , some good men in that ministry who had helped him, a.,!1, he, en the principle of reciprocity, had helped them. ne , thought there was reason now to do what in them lay t° remove from their midst anything like bigotry, selfishnesis, r and narrowness of heart. He was disposed to preach in an): pulpit that might be open to him; he would be very gl„ad_w,„ , preach for the Roman Catholics if they asked him: hear.) If they dealt in positive, dogmatic truths. in trutue . which had served to mould their own lives, if they the selves had sat at the feet of Jesus Christ, and declared Di •, truth as they believed it, it would do good. (Applause.) , Mr. R. Dobson, Mr. G. N. Ford, and other centlemn liii e , dressed the meeting, which was brought to a closeiii usual way.

div.head: COUNTY QUARTER SESSIONS.
div.p: COUNTY QUARTER SESSIONS.
The General Quart; Sessions of the Peace for this divi- sion of the county commenced on Monday, at St. George's Hall. Sir. R. A. Cross, M.P., presided. RATES.

On the motion of Mr. BLBCILY the following rates were ordered :—Main Roads: The West Derby Hundred, 3.16 d, estimated to produce £1,864 Is 9d. Police Rates: West Derby, 2d, estimated to produce £2,573; Bootle 2id, esti- mated to produce £2,171 44 7d; Ormskirk, id, to produce £1,047 5s 10d; Prescot, led, to produce £3,020 13s 3d; Warrington, Id, to produce £1,300 4s 4d; and Wigan, Id, to produce £1,338 es 4d. THE LATE CORONER. In the report of the Finance Committee, which was Ac- cepted by the court on the motion of Mr. Bleckly, the fol- lowing reference was made :—" The committee regret to re- Port the death of Mr. T. W. Barker, the late county coroner, who was accidentally killed at Pemberton on the 29th vecember last. CRIME IN THE COUNTY. The Chief Constable of the county (Colonel Moorsom)

Presented- the return of crime kc., ior.the quarter ending 31st December last, from which it appeared that the number of apprehensions was 4,773, compared with 5,516 in the cor- responding quarter of the previous year, and 4,456 in the 4orresponding period of 1882 ; the decrease in the former case being chiefly from vagrancy, drunkenness, and thefts of fruit, and the increase in the second case being in apprehen- sions for drunkenness. The summonses by the police were 5,468, as against 5,931 in the corresponding quarter of the previous year (the decrease being shown in drunkenness, Offences against the Licensing Act, and vagrancy) and 5,033 in 1882 (the increase being due to drunkenness and pro- ceedings under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act. POLLING STATIONS UNDER THE WEW scr. , A petition was read from the township of Atherton pray- I ing to be detached from Tyldesley for the purposes of Par- liamentary election/J.—Mr. Heywood appeared in support of the petition, and said that the request was made under the 47th section of the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Act, 1883, which provided that every county should be divided into polling districts, and that the places assigned to each should be distributed in such a manner that, so far as was Practicable, every elector should have his polling place at a distance not exceeding three miles from his residence, pro- viding that such polling districts contain not less than 100 *lectors. Atherton was a township and a local board dis- trict, having a population of 12,602, and containing 2,377 houses and 294 electors. Hitherto the electors of that dis- trict had been obliged to go to Tyldesley, of which the nearest point to Atherton was a mile and a half, while from Some points the polling station was as much as four miles distant. There were no railways, and, now that no con- veyances were allowed to be used at elections, the four miles would have to be travelled on foot. There were con- I venient offices at Atherton for the purposes of polling, and he was prepared to show that both political parties were united in the request which he made. The court acceded to the petition, and, on the motion of Mr. Bleckly, it was resolved "to appoint a committee to consider the question 'of making new polling divisions under the Corrupt Practices iset in the parliamentary division of South- West Lancashire, and report thereon at the next sessions."

FOOTBALL. s' Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. Sr. Pain's CHOIR V. ORFORD EXCELSIOIL—The return match Was played on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and ended in a victory for the home team by 2 goals, 2 tries, 12 touchdowns. 1 dead ball to nil. WESTON Ponse v. WIDNES RECREATION The return match between these stubs was played on Saturday at Weston Potut: A. hard game was played, resulting in favour of the visi,ors by two touchdowns to nil. RI/IMPISH VICTORIA V. BOOTLE CALEDONLANS.—This match wee played at Bootle on Saturday, and after a good game it re- gretted in a win for the Victoria by one goal one try and three minor points to nil. E. Woodward, J. Christie, H. Lancaster Obtained the try, and P. Bibby kicked a very neat goal. RYNCORIT WRITE STAR V. WARRINGTON ST. ELPHINS.— This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday, and resulted In a draw in favour of the Warringtonians. It was a very ex- alting and pleasant game, the backs on both sides receiving many rounds of applause from the crowd of spectators. WILILY WASPS (Iwo) V. PAGNIFIELD (INB). The above teams met for the first time on Saturday last on the ground of the latter. The visitors had not been beaten this season, and they evidently thought there was going to be another win for them, but to their great surpriae and chagrin the home team lowered their colours by one try and tour minor points to four Minor points. Sr. JAYBS' Y. NEWTON (A TEAK).—This match was played eat the ground of the former. Newton won the toss and chose to ploy with the wind in their favour. During the first quarter 'of an hoar play was pretty even, although tit. James's man- aged to score. After the change of ends the home team had the Play all their own way, the visitors never getting the ball near their opponents' goal. At the esti of time St. James's were victors by three goals to nil. TRUE BLUES V. HALTON.— This match was played at Halton Oil Saturday. The Blues winning the toss elected to play Mainst the wind. The Halton captain started the ball, Houghton returning it Tickle getting the bail obtained a try, and Booth scored a goal. At the call of half-time Houghton started the ball, and Hayes folio% ing it up obtained another ttiry- No goal was got. Time being called, the scores stood as follows :—True Blues, 1 goal 2 tries and 6 minor points; Hal- ton nil. Halton played a good game, considering it was their first year. WARRINGTON RANGERS V. WARRINGTON WANDERERS (2ND), —This match was played on the Wanderers' ground at Arpley ou Saturday, and this being the only match in town, there was a very large number of spectators oa the field. The Rangers. after a very good Ana stubbornly-contested game, were the victors by 1 goal and 4 minor points to I try (dis- puted) and 5 minor points. The goal was kicked by Hill from a try obtained by A. Ratcliffe. Bill, Lightfoot, Whitfield, and Wright, from behind the scrimmage. and T. Lawless, Rat- cliffe, and Hardman (forwards) played well for the Rangers. /alms( V. Avristurcfsaas —Played on the ground of the foi mar tia Saturday. A g ,od game ended In a victory for the visitor, by one goal (kicked from a disputed try by Carlson), one try (Harrison), and one minor point to nil. Teams—Altrlnctam 111 Rustige, full back J A Drinkwater, J Smith, and IC Grisota (captain), three-quarter backs; F Wright and J W Harrison, half backs; R Smith R Kenyon' W Mills, T Rustige, H Pear- son, J WatkinsOn, W Whitehead, H Wright and A Blease, for- wards. Lymm ; P Holt, full back; T Clegg, A Duo, and T H Masters (captain), three-quarter backs; H Clegg and E Hoyle, half backs W Hoyle, F Dun. J Crawford, W B Masters, J Pearson, T Obend ler, J Edelston, H and J Morris, forwards. ILAYDOCK TEMPERANCE T. OUPKTRINGTON, NEAR LYMM (ASSOCIATION).—This match was played on the ground of the former, a goodly number of spectators witnessing the game. The leather was set in motion at half past three o'clock, the ball being driven on to the Ouglatrington territory. The Tem- Perance men, hiswever, did not appear to be in form for scoring, Which made the game quite a monotony for the spectators; but it was relieved by the ball being sent through the uprights by C corner kick sent by Paul Twist, of the home team, who thus scored the first and only goal during the game. The play of 4. Harrison, P. Twist, J. Carter, and T. Hatton, of the Temper- ance may here be remarked as very good.

div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess. Bumalfn CASE.—Wm. Searle Hyde, the boy who was found on the premises of Mr. Greaves, pdwnbroker, Church- street, under suspicious circumhtances, was handed over to the care of his parents. MONDAY —Before the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison) and Mr. Bleckley. The business of interest will be found reported elsewhere. TITESDAT.—Before Major Cartwright and Councillor Monks. The business is reported in another column. WIDNESDAY.—There was no business for disposal. THURSDAY —Before Alderman Webster and Captain Litton. The business will be found reported elsewhere. FRlDAY—Before Captain Reynolds (in the chair) and Mr. Ziba Armitage.' A WOMEN'S D/SPUTI.—EIIen Cotton, summoned for avault- ing Sarah Ansbury on the 14th instant, was bound over to keep the peace.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAL—Before Mr. Peter Stubs and Mr. Ziba Armitage The business will be found reported in another CO:WM.
LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. TElDAY.—Before Messrs, Dewhurst, T. r Morris, H. Stanton, _ _

. _ and W. Long. Richard Hall, grocer and provision dealer, of Rnutsford, was summoned for having on the 3rd lust, without hoving & license, used a dog for taking game, but the case was dismissed. John Buthern, of Lymm, was ordered to pay 13s 6d for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart on the 28th ult. Thomas Groak and John Mann, of High-street, and William Taylor, of Lymm, were each ordered to pay costs and be bound over for committing breaches of the peace by fighting. James Collins, of Lymm, was ordered to pay 8s 6d costs and be' bound over to keep the peace for using threatening language to William Johnson, on the 10th inst.—George Rowell, a boy re- siding at Lymm, was fined 4s 6d for damaging shrubs, on the 28th ult., belonging to Samuel Hodson.—Merbert Sinister, an intelligent-looking young man, who has been employed as as- sistant to Henry Shannon, pawnbroker, of Altrincham, for atout four months, was charged with stealingtwopawntickets, the property of his master. The case, however, was dismissed;

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. G. Davies. 4iIINTERANCE OF A PARENT.,—J hn Smith was summoned to show cause why he should not contribute towards the sup- port 0 his aged mother, Ann Dolan, who is chargeable to the ',ammo's fund of the 111A:in.—Mr. Houghton, the collector to the Guardian.), stated that the defeniant's mother was in re- ceipt of 2s Bd per week.—The defendant stated he wes only in receipt of 19s. per week, out of which he had to keep a wife and two children. He would willingly contribute towards his mother if he contd.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay Is 6d. yer week. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Beore Captain Willis (chairman) and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. Munurrxmous.—Michael Henry was, on the evidence of P.O. Thompson, convicted of sleeping in Efutchinson's chemi- cal works, on Tuesday night. and he was sentenced to a month's Imprisonment. Inspector Wood stated the prisoner would not work and had been before the Bench on numerous owasions.— Matthew Burns and James Mcßeogh were charged with com- mitting a breach of the peace by fighting on the 14th Instant, and they were bound over to keep the peace for a month.— Richard gee, a youth, was sum mened for obstructing Mersey- road, on Saturday night. P.O. Blackhall gave evidence of the I obstruction, but admitted that although lee bad warned the defendant on several previous occasions he omitted to do so on this occasion. The Bench dismissed the case, but gave the de- fendant to understand that he would be severely dealt with on a future occasion if he again offended. A STRAY Swum —John French was charged with permit- ting his horse to stray in Waterloo-road on the sth January.— The case was proved by Inspector Wood and P.O. Barker, and a fine of 5s and costs was imposed.

STOCK AND SHARE. MARKET.

Messrs. Jo—s;pii—ii: and W. P. Baines, share i brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Marketestreet, Manchester, write (Jan. 17th):— Weakness, in which most descrip lore of securities have par- ticipated, has characterised the market during the past week. The arrangement of the account has engaged attention during the past few days, and this with declining prices has restricted new business, a large portion of the transactions reported being doubtle,s the curtailing of ace unts. Traffic returns have not been calculated to arrest the downward tendency, and as political affairs abroad and to some extent at home are not very tranquil no beneficial help has been afforded by these influences. Foreign Funds are Mwer In the majority of cams only, Argentines and Spanbh allowing better figures, whilst Egyptians, notably Unified and Daira, Mexican Three Per Cents Turkish Stamped, and Peruvians are all more or less declined in value. Mexican Railway Stock moves about a little, and with another traffic decrease (27,800) the balance of movement is adverse about 1 on the week. ' Miscellaneous shares have changad hands to a greater extent than for some time past; still the volume of business is by no mewls large, and quotations do not exhibit a decided general tendency. Banks show a moderate number of dealings, and full rates still rule. Beyond a few changes consequent on quotations belog now ex dividend, the only alteration (save a partial one, viz., an advance of by buyers of Manchester and Live,pool District) is a decline et 1-16th in Consolidated.

CIIESTHRE AMB ER- OF- AG RIC ULT [IRE. " DISCUStION ON' THE ; AGRICULTURAL HOLD- INGS ACT. sdeciat meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agricul- ture was held yesterday at the Crewe Arms Hotel,Crew2. Mr. H, J. Tollemache, M.P., was voted to the chair. 'The main business of the meeting was a discassion on the Agrieultairat Holdings Act, 1883, introduced by a paper _earthen by the secretary to the Chamber, Mr. Thomas Rigby. At a foiling meeting, of the Chamber Mr. Rigby read an introductery paper on the subject, and he' now replied to some of the views expressed by others at that meeting, and extended hie treatment of the subject to a consideration of the Act in practice. Mr. Ream, in his paper, said that the utility of the Act was to his mind proved by, the amendment it made in the conditions of holding land. It created a general and legal right for the first time itt favour of occupiers to compensa- tion for Improvements made ' on their farms on quitting. Compensation to :some extent, .in, many cases to. e full extent, had prevailed in Cheshire more than in most other counties; but on no estate was there ever, as now, a legally-defined tenant right. The effect of compensation being promised oragieed.to-be paid by aeree- meat had had a stimulating effect upon outlay and enter- prise on those estates on which it had been the rule or cus- tom to allow it; and it would be, readily allowed that where the principal was not recognised, or where there was doabt of its being recognised, there had been less improvement made, less money expended, and generally worse farming. It must be so from the nature of the case. Capital was one of the most sensitive things ina aginable, and it was more ad- versely affected by insecurity than aught else. Skill or faculty for management required promise or probability of success to encourage its application and development. This Act of Parliament secured the tenant's advantage by law in all cases, and fixed compensation on quitting tenancies upon the just basis that it shall be "such sum as fairly repre- sents the value of the improvement to an incoming tenant." This clearly established its utility as encouragement to improved farming, and a sure guarantee of compensation. It might be that some of the directions laid down he the Act to regulate estimates of improvements seemed to direct valaters to proceed upon lines that would reduce the amount to be awarded as much as possible. Yet he would argue that where the spirit of the Act was recognised, it must, and would in practice, make its force so evident to valuers that they-we-add have to be guided by it both first and chiefly %and emu though it were argued that the Act itself might be nullified by both landlord and tenant agreeing to ignore it, he would point out that the act of doing so would be unwise on the part of owners, and foolieh on the part of tenants. Such an agreement would be illegal, and despite it, if made, there was the highest ahthority for saying the Act could be enforced. The Act provided compensation upon quitting holdings for improve- ments execated before the commencement of the Act (the first day of this year), under cartein conditions, as well as after its becoming law. He recomnaended his brother farmers to seek the advantages of the Act by diligent, mare enterprising, and more intelligent practice. , He need not point out that the Act of itself would not make it easier to live on farme, or to become better farmers. Crops would not become heavier, stock more healthy or more profitable, seasons more favouraole, or land more easily'kept clean and made fertile, because this Act of Parliament had been passed. There would always be necessity for labour and thought, for ,care and economy, and for skilful management and increased know- ledge of both the practice and science of agriculture to produce this; but there was now no excuse for parsimony in outlay or indifference as to results, and no justification for not doing their best to their farms, if this part of the Act were worked in the spirit advocated, and valuations be made in accord with its principle. He readily allowed that great progress had been made in farming in the county, and that as much improvement during the last 30 years could be shown in Cheshire as in any of the coun- ties; but he had the impression there was now less emula- tion and enterprise than formerly, and that they required a mere stimulating effort. The two chief agents of improve- ment in the past have been draining and boning. Both of them partook largely of the character of permanent improve- ments. Draining was the basis of nearly all improve- ment, but it was expensive, and required years to realise all its benefits. The Act recognised this by providing compen- sation for the outlay. in special and alternete ways. The tenant might have to leave his farm in a few years, after spending a large sum of money in draining, and the Act said he should be compensated if he did to the extent the land had been improved by it for subsequent tenancy. He might not do it himself at his own cost if the landlord pre- ferred.to.do it, and to charge him not more than five per cent. on the °atilt)? ; nor do it himself without giving notice to his landlord, and trying to agree with him if .he wished' to have,part in the work, or satisfying him that he would do it in good workmanlike manner, and in accordance with recognised-principles; but he might do it, or have it done if he willed to have it so, and on equitable lausiness:ike terms. These two features are new in their joint character, and ought eto stimulate to the drainage of much land that still wanted draining. The same might be said of boning, and of tl.e ap- .plieation of similar manures, or of food consumed on the hold- ing other than that grown on the farm. The consent of the . landlord, however, was not required to the use of these im- provers. The practical knowledge of the tenant and his free action had full scope, and if the result was improve- . 74 ment of substantial value, his reward was provided for whenever he became a retiring tenant. These facts rendered it incumbent upon them to try to raise more produce and becomeletter farmers. In garden farming there was much to be learned and much progress to be made. The limitation of the law of distress to one year instead of six would have a healty influence for good tenants with means and of char- acter, as it would constrain landlords and agents to look more at the competeccv of the men they accepted as tenants and into the fairness of the rents they asked, and the pro- bability of tenants being able to pay them. This new system would clear the course for honest competent runners, and make it more difficult only for the inefficient men who sue- I needed in nothing unless it were in making the work more difficelt for the fair minded and hard working. Mr. G. W. LATHA-M said he WAS prepared to say what he had said before regarding the Act, that it was of no use to the tenant farmer. . Mr. Rigby told them that the benefits of the Acts would depend on the heartiness with which it was received ,by landlord and tenant. If cordially accepted and acted upon, it was capable of fulfilling- its mission. Now, these were very brave words, • but he would like Mr. Rigby to apply them, say, to an Act for stopping burglary. If an Act for stopping burglary were accepted in such a spirit by the parties concerned, most people would consider it of precious little use. As he thought, an Act should be, not for the porpose.of enabling a good landlord and an im- proving tenant to agree together as to what im- provements should be done, .and how they should be computed, but to put a bad landlord in the position of a good one and enable the soil to be cultivated Whether the nnimproving landlord wished or not. We wanted laws not for the good or well disposed, but to prevent the bad from doing whet was wrong. How did this Act operate in that respect? Take the schedules. How on earth did these put them in a better position than they etre ? First of all, there was a list of 14 improvements to the consent of tho landlord was required. That was WAS not tenants' work, but land- lords' work, and what he wanted was to let the tenant do it I and get compensation for it, and do it in his own time and way. Comieg to the clause' relating to im- provements for which the consent of the landlord was not required; they found that the tenant should receive j the full value of hie money; but.,—there was always a I " but" in this Act—the valuer had to consider "the in- herent cap ability of the soil." It WAS impossible, unless they had a land court with scientific judges over it, that such a clause as the latter could ever be made to work. What would be the result of this? There would be so much uncertainty in these awards, and it would be so ex- pensive to have scientific witnessee and costly analyses, that every farmer would have recourse to the clause which said he might substitute a fair and reasonable compensation by agreement. Looking at tha expense .and difficulty of arbitrating with regard to the inherent capabilities of the soil—and he took it that almost any agreement would be considered by a court of law as fair and reasonable if it kept the tenant out of the litigation which must ensue upon that • clause—they came back to what they thought they had got _d of. No tenant had a right to Come under this Act unless he was a tenant for a year. How, if landlords were ,o let their farms for 364 days, would this Act apply? He bad a strong 'opinion that it would not, but then there would be most probably an amendment of the Act if such were the case, ley far the most dangerous thing was thattwhich. Mr. Willis Bond pointed out. He said that the _landlords were , in a perilous state, but there was one secret- which he could show them. Every tenant who wished to .est be compensated for improvements wee . bound to give two months' notica to the landlord before the termination of his tenancy. Every tenant was under cer- tain covenants, as they knew in Cheshire—covenants not to sell hay or stritir, not to glp g thousiuld things. They

l!knew they were seldom put in operation unless the tenant was going to leave the farm, but they were held over his head. Here, on the breakage of any of these covenants, the lanyllord had the right to re-enter, and by re-entering ttle tenancy was terminated. With regard to notice to quit,* 1 tenant might substitute six months for twelve. Mr. Shaw Lefevre pointed out in the Nineteenth Century that formerly a landlord had to give notice when he contracted out of the Act, but now landlord and tenant hid to consult and agree that they should reduce it from twelve to six. If they did not agree to give up all their privileges, they received notice to quit. That watt the result of it all, and if the result of .having such an -Act was only to be that a man who was independent enough to stand to his rights and claim to be under the Act was to receive notice to quit, then he said the Act was rather a curse to the country and a curse to independent men than a blessing to them. They wanted an Act which should ren- der it impossible for a non-improving landlord to contract himself out of the Act. (Hear, hear.) The Act was so weak that there was only one thing which was compulsory, aad he thought that was as bad a thing for the tenant as was possible. It made the limit of distress twelve months instead of six Tears. Hitherto, under the old law of dis- tress, an indulgent landlord cDuld allow his tenant to go on without paying his rent for an almost unlimited time, but now it would be necessary as soon as the tenant wis in arrear to diatrain, because he would not be able to distrain for more than twelve months, and so he would put in distress at once instead of waiting as he did. He totally disagreed with Mr. Rigby's idea that with hiving only twelve mouths instead of six years landlords would he more careful in selecting their tenants. It was the fact of the landlord hay- ing a preferential claim at all which was important' and not the difference in the period. He though he had proved that the Act was not of the slightest benefit. It WAS not compulsory, and did not effect a large number of im- provements, and would lead to such litigation as would make every wise man anxious to c nitract himself out of it even to his own loss, because he dreaded litigation. He could see no good it could possibly do except one thing. It would have brought agricultural matters into such a mud- dle that it would be necessarvto have a new Act in order to get out of it, and he hoped that when they had a new Act brought forward farmers would bestir themselves to have a proper and satisfactory Act pissed. Tais Act was passed entirely through the fact that the farmer remained quiet and did not exert himself. He hoped tee former would see that if in any future Act he wanted a good thing he would have to put his shoulder to the wheel, or he would not get it at all.

Mr. WILLIS (of the Dairy Farmers' Association) was disposed to think that if they did Incept the Act In the spirit Mr. Rigby advised, there was msiderable beneft to be drawn from it. both- for the landlords and tenants in Cheshire.
Mr. C. EDWARDS thought SORIEI of Nfr. Litharn's state- ments rather overdrawn. With regard to letting a farm for 364 days, he did not think any farmer wound take one 011 those terms.

Mr. RIGBY, in replying to Mr.,Latham's case of an Act to suppress burglary which he had supposed for comparison with this Act, said that it would not hold. The cmditions were altogether different. In regard to the Act they were discusiing, he-pointsct out that both landlord and tenant were interested in it, and the Act assumed that there would be croperation in its working. The supposition of Mr. Latham seemed to him to be—he was going to say mon- strous, for it would be entirely to disregtrd public opinion and all rules of necessity and self-preservation for the land- lord te act in the way which he had supposed. He thought they might cordially accept the Act as an instalment to- wards the settling of. a question which would be further advanced by their cordially accepting it in good faith and seeking to act upon it. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Rigby for his paper, said he did not take the desponding view of the subject Which Mr. 'Latham did. , Mr. LATHAM seconded the vote of thanks, and said he hoped the Act would turn out better than•he thought. The motion was then carri,d. anti the meeting dissolved. WARRINGTON IN FIRMARY AND DIS ?ENS ARY.

The Assembly Rooms at the Lion Hotel presented a gay aspect on Tuesday evening, on the occasion of the annual ball in aid of the funds of the above deserving institution. That the Infirmary is worthy of generous support from the inhabitants of Warrinzton and the district is evidenced by the fact that "upwards of 4,000 poor persons receive medi- cine and advice at this institution annually. Many of these are lanourers, who are employed in the agricultural districts of Lancashire and Cheshire, but have to lad their homes and aid in time of sickness at Warrington. The new In- firmary and Hospital is now complete, and in constant use for the reception of patients; and as the expenses of the institution are heavy and increasing, donations and sub- scriptions in aid of the funds are earnestly solicited." The large room, decorated by Messrs. Johnson, of Rylands- street, presented a -very pleasing and tasteful appearance. Dancing commenced shortly after nine o'clock to the strains of Johnson's Manchester Assembly Band, and was kept up until " the wee sin? hours." A recherche supper was supplied by the manageress of the Hotel, Miss Hart. PAPER BY MR. MORRIS, OF WAitRTNGTON.

On Thursday evening tha menbers of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society met in the lecture-room of the eduseuin in Bold-street, whin—Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S , read a piper on "The geological and inanufac:uring, history of a galvaidsed, bucket." In the absence of the -president (the Rev. Canon Dodd) Mr. Charles Broadbent (vice- president) occupied the chair. There was a fair attendance and the paper was listened to with rapt attention. Mr. hionars read as follows:—The paper I have ventured to...prepare for you is a sketch of the history of a buckee Humble as iny subject is,.the more I thought of it, the greater did its importance seein, and to my mind the more worthy was it of an able expositor. - Still, to have turned , my back upon it would have been un-Eaglish, so I kept plodding on till I had 'Completed what I have pleasure in hying before you, and Shall be amply repaid for my labour if no one tarns his back upon me with remorse that he has by listening to me wasted an hour of his life. Without doubt iroa has been oqe of the components of this earth ever since it made its grst revolution round the sun, or upoa its own axis, but what form this mass took when it came bath space no geologist of our day or philosopherief olden times has ever been able to tell U 3 clearly. So-called philosophers of a century or two ago gave expressioa to some extraordinary wild notions and theories. For instance, Werner's theory was "that all the superficial parts of the globe were once in a state of aqueons solution, from which the .materials were at first separated by chemical deposition in a crystalline state and formed a thick mass of granite round the globe." Wood ward's theory was that the deluge was occasioned by a momentary mispension of cohesion among the particles of mineral bodies, the whole mass of the globe was dissolved, and the soft paste became penetrated by shells. Whiston fancied that the earth was created from the atmosphere of one comet, and deluged by the tail of another. The great Leibnitz, like Descartes, amused his Imagination by conceiving the world to be an extinguished sun, or a vitrified globe upon which the vapours coadensine• as they cooled, formed seas, and afterwards deposited calcareous strata. Buffo° imagined that the mass of our earth, together with those of the other planets, was struck off the sun in a liquefied state by a cornet at the same instant. Kepler, one of the greatest astrono- mers, considered the globe as possessed of living faculties and a circulating vital fluid, and that all its particles were alive. So much for ancient ideas. Modern geologists seem to have had more discretion than speculation on how the en-theme into existence, but they all agree that gra-lite is the oldest known rock. Page tells us that the graniticerocks are highly crystalline; and from the circumstance the granitic rocks are held to be of igneous origin ; and, so far as geologists have been able to discover, they are the most deeply seated of all rocks. Jakes, one of the ablest geologists of our own time, says that granite is the oldest rock that has been defined. lie also goes carefully into the composition of this and ' other rocks, describing the agencies that decompose and re- compose. In fact, all modern- geologists are agreed that granite and the granitic series, comprising micaceous and porphyritic compounds too numerous to mention and very hard to pronounce, are the oldest known rocks. Accepting the theory of the principal modern geologists, that this granite is the most ancient rock, I shall endeavour to trace the origin of the material from which the galvanized bucket is manufactured. There is not much doubt that metallic iron existed at the remotest period. Gold, silver, and plantinum, and all metals found among-the -old rocks are found the most pure and unalloyed, arid are Cho least susceptible to decay or decomposition ,from any atmospheric influence. - Iron, on. the contrary', Is the most sensitive of this class'of metals, it having a great affinity for oxygen, and the rusting (oxidation) of iron is woaderfally promoted by the presence of acid and vapours.- This pro- perty in great measures has bsen the cause why iron is so universally diffused over the face of the earth. When some

granitic rocks have been long exposed to the influence of rain, rivers, tides, and the action of frost, snow, Lo., the lime and potass in its constituent parts are acted upon by water or carbonic acid, and the oxide of iron, almost always in its least oxidated state, tends to combine with more oxygen; therefore the feldspar decomposes, and likewise the mica, but the firzt most rapidly. The feldspar, which is the cement of the stone, forms a tine clay; the mica, partially decom- posed, mixes with it as sand; and the undecomposed quartz appears as gravel or sand of different degrees of fineness. Feldspar and mica are compound substance. In the feld- spar there is usually lime and potass ; in the mica, lime and magnesia, whilst both contain silica, alumina, and oxide of iron. Without further preface, I ask your attention to the diagram I have had prepared, showing the analysis of one of the oldest iron ores found. Chemically, as you will _see, a greet chanals has taken place between it and the granite; mechanically a most gigantic one. Here you have granite :

Lime Llme Magnesia Maguesia The above is not much unlike on algebraical formula with iron ore for the unknown x, and puede illy speaking it is one, for in working to find out the origin of this early formed red hematite, I came across the components given under No. 3; following on! found these had been wrapt up in quartz, feldspar, and mica, No 2; and Osey in turn had sprung from the parent known rock granite No 1. There are many varieties of granite, differing not so much in their composition as they do in colour and texture. The bard close grained is taken advantage of by the architect and the builder whenever they want a building stone for heavy or ornamental structures. The soft and decomposable has given ths potter the finest kaolin, or china clay. Indus- trially, these rocks are of prime importance. It is not my province to discuss whether these rocks are of igneous origin or not, but my desire is to be as lucid as possible in tracing out the origin of hon. stones. Now if his plain to us from the formula that clay. sand, and limestones have been formed through the decom- position of granite, it follows that all that was soluble in that rock must have been carried away to other fields, and deposited elsewhere. And as there is no such thing as an- nihilation, everything that has or has had an existence is in existence now, in some form or other. Hence the iron that existed in the form of an oxide in the original rock must, after the dissolution, have taken up partneranips with other minerals, o' in other werda, saturated other material, so completely as to bring there under the notice of the, mineralogist. Neither does he leave the latter here, for he. has classified them, and given them such names as the youngest student can understand. If over 20 per cent of iron he calls them ironstones. If under he de- nominates them flues. For instance, the hema- tite ore is sb called (although of different -varieties), owing to its prevailing reddish colour.; argilla, ceous ironstones from these being found among the clays and shales, and having alumina as a component of the coal measures ;-.siliceous, because of silica being a large compo- nent, and calcareous because of lime being a large con- stituent. Of these ores of iron there are many, but as only the four named are principally need in the manufacture of cast and malleable iron we shall omit alhthe others in our attempt te prove where the material has come-from to make the iron of the bucket. Geologists have. been pleased to call the period the early hematite ores were laid down the "Transition and Primary." The ore of which the analysis is shown is from a sample taken from the eastern part of Cornwall, and is what is termed a siliceous ore, and is just one remove from the parent rock. In addition to these hematites, with which these formations abound, the magnetic exide of iron is found, not so much ia England as it is in Norway, Sweden, France, Germany and other European states; Australia and New Zealand also abound in it. When this is pure it is com- posed of one atom of the protoxide and two atoms of the peroxide; or decimally of iron 71..79, oxygen 2821. In proof of the antiquity of these rocks no trace of life, either. vegetable or animal, is found among them. In the next system of rocks, which is called the "Old Red Sandstone and Silurian system," fossils are found. It was thought at one time that these rocks were deposited before the dawn of life upon the earth, but it was found that in the North- American States veins of fossiliferous ores and hematites existed in conjunction with veins of limestone and shale. The ores found in these systems are of various descriptions and qualities. Still, the deposits of valuable ores appear conhned to a few districts. Time old red sand stone rock derives its colour from an admixture of peroxide of iron, of which it contains from five to seven per cent. Calculating at this amount the entire thickness of the system, it ap- pears that the quantity of iron so dispersed amounts to imagination to comprehend how the same ageneies that above a million tons per acre. It needs no stretch of the woreoci &comports the granite and recompose it late .lays, a ande, limestones, and all ~tht. RlSltifari,.... -.taus—these tahierr asnyds twe ma t eorf, Ar'oogBd. In this syeteen ie found numerous layers of argillaceous or clay ironstone—for instance, the Earl of Dudley's ten yard seam of coal, together with the mountain. limestone, ,t is these three sad the men that lived on this iron _coil which made South Staffordshire ' the most famous ironmaking district in &trope ' at one time, and I question, notwithaanding all the eulo- gies we hear of steel-making, whether the day is not far 1 -distant before all the laurels will have faded from South I 4taffordshire. Alto in this system are -found the calcerons ' or shell limestone .iron ores, the working of which now and i during the last few years is bringing some Darts of Derby- shire and Lincolnshiee to the front as a pig-iron making district. The great black band ironstone of Scotland was laid down during this period also. And when one looks at this irodstone, with its numerous shells, its hard, dull, coal- like appearance, its analysis, which shows that in its com- position there exists Barna BO to 35 per cent, of carbonic acid, and come eight to ten per cant, of organic matter, the mind sees, as it were, the weather- worn granite rock which now forms Ben Lomond and his brethren undergoing decomposition. The muddy-looking- streams running' hither and thither, carrying the iron in solution only to deposit it on the rank , vegetable mvsliv soils of Lanarkshire, where some 82 years ago, that famous metallurgist Musket found these valuable:l iron MIL, .- -Since the commencement of converting them into pig iron, Scotland has never ceased climbing the hill of ISOIIPWISTs-And to this day rules the selling rate of pig iron .-.•- ~
