in all the markets of Great Britain, if not of Europe. In this system of rocks also are ' found all the principal coal' fielde, and nearly all the foseiliferous ironstone measures, together with limestone in abundance. In fact, to England and its people, especially to thole who are in any way con- necee4 with the iron and coal industries, it is the most interesting system in the earth's forma- tion. Before bidding adieu to the geological part of my subject I mast ask you, dry and uninteresting to many as it is, to bear with me a few minates while we examine some epecimens of the most important rocks and ores I have named. Here were shown and cainineuted upon the granite, quartz, felspar, and mica—(as regards clays, sande, ana limestones, you have only to see a .hole dug in the ground from a few inches in one piece to a few feet in another in depth, and the delver will show you one or the other)—iron sand ; the argilleceous, cerbenate, fossil lepido- fiendron, belonging to the club moss tribe; the calcereous foesil shell from the Lincolnshire iron fields; the siliceous, especially the lepidodendron and calcareous ore, a sort of hematite iron ore. There is not the slightest doubt about the sheet iron being manufactured in South Staff rd- shire from which the first bucket was made, and this will be my reason for describing the treatment and passage of the ores found in this district to the very useful domestic article under consideration. The first step taken after this clay iron ore is brought out of the pit is to make it up into heaps with roughly- *tint sides. Is this form it lies for a time to weather the action of the sun and rain causing a large amount of ad- hering useless muter to fall from it. It is afterwards cal- cined, a process technically called "roasting." This con- sists in the application of a moderate heat, whereby the more volatile comeaments of the ore, such as carbonic acid, sulphur, dec., are expelled. This is eff,cted by spreading on the ground a stratum of coals to a depta of about eight inches, over which is laid a layer of ironstone to a depth of about six feat, interspersed with small cinders and coke dust, and Covered with small coals. The coals being set on fire, combustion will go on for nearly a month, when the cementation is complete. The modern method of perform- ing this roasting process is in a kiln, the coal and iron- stones being put in at the top, and the roasted ore taken out at the bottom. The next operation is the conversion of the celeined ore into metal by, the applicatioa of a white heat in a furnace. This process is called smelting. As will be readily understood after what we have said on ores of iron, after the roasting process they consist of an oxide of the metal, combined with some earthy matter in very various proportions. If these ores were fused alone, anyone having the least knowledge of chemistry will at once perceive that they would be formed into glasses, the properties of which will vary with the com- position of the ore, but retain no metallic character. The me- method of proceeding, therefore, to intermix the ironstones with such substances as during the process of fusion will combine with the oxygen and earthy matter of the ore and leave the metal free. The early metallurgists knew no fuel but charcoal, but this was fast getting exhausted when Dud Dudley, of South Staffordshire, in the year 1650, or about that time, got letters patent to use pit coal. Ever since then the ordinary coal when converted into coke has been found to .be the most useful and economic fuel. From the great affinity of this coke or carbon for oxygen, it is selected as the proper substance for separating the metallic base from the oxygen. The nature of the other substances to be employed in separating the earthy matter of the ore are determined by the species to which that earthy matter belongs. In the cese before us limestones are used, they being the best flux to form glasses or slags with the earthy matter of this argil- laceous ore. To give the corstruotion of a smelting furnace , will be out of place, It will be sufficient to -say that the ores, coke, and flux are charged into the top, and are acted upon by the heat rising up from the lower part of the fur- nace, the combustion being accelerated by air being blown Into the furnace under pressure. The oxygen of the ore combines with the ctrben of the coke, the limestones with the alumina, silica, dec., and a pertion of the carbon with the metal, which being the, heaviest falls down to the lowest part of the furnace. There are suitable openings in the lower part of the furnace, one at the bottom of the hearth which is opened at fixed periods to allow ths molten iron to run out, and one at the top of the hearth or " bosh," as it is called, from which the slags are continually flowing. Whilst this lowest part of the fur- nace is filling with iron by the fusion of the ores the men are engaged in making rough moulds in send to receive the metal, which when cast is commonly known as pig iron; by metallurgists it is called the carburet of iron. Thus, what it took nature myriads of years to form is converted in a few hours by the knowlgtige and handiwork of man into the most useful metal known. Useful, because the ironfounder can make finished castings from any design the engineer may think proper to have the pattern made, from the largest to the most delicate Dina of mechanism; because he can make with it the column with the statue on the top of it; ,or the finest trinket a woman may wear; be- cause he can and does shape it into a million forms for the uses of the millions of the people. However it is the finished and sheet iron maker that we have now to do with. For a few minutes we will follow him and see what he does with this useful metal. It is of no moment to describe the puddling furnace, only to say that this is the first stage the finished iron maker passes it through, and that the furnace has two compartments, one called the grate, and the other the hearth, the two being divided by a bridge composed of iron plates, with firebrick to that side of them next the fuel part, and on the other side where the metal is put a lining (or fettling) of a re- fractory material the latter being blackbend ironstone after being 3alcined, or any other rich oxides of iron. This pud- dling process is the mast interesting and one of the most laborious in the manufacture of iron. Consisting as it does of chemical action and mechanical application, it has fairly worried hundreds of inventors, who have tried to produce good iron from inferior pig, by adding their patent drug to the melten iron during the working of the charge; or, to save labour, and economise expense, have introduced re- volving furnaces, oscillating and rotating furnaces, moving rabbles, rocking furnaces, &c., itc. With all this the pro- cess in Warrington to-day is the same, with very few ex- ceptions, as it was in South Staffordshire 40 years ago. Thera is no into to whom the puddler owes a debt of grati- tude worth recording except Nastnyth. Before the intro- duction of the Naemyth steam hammer the puddler had to drag the ball of iron after him to the hammer, and throw it under, whilst it was going up. This operation required no smell practice and anxiety on the part of the puddler befere he could manage to do it well. Now he is relieved of this by sanding the bell to the hammer on a trolly to the hamrnermart. To resume, the furnace is made hot, and the charge is thrown in, consisting of slags and scales from previous workings at the hammer and rolls, and some 4801 be. tee 5601b5. of pig iron. The opening through which the charge has been thrown is closed by a• door in which is a small hole, through which the workman can see and work the iron. Whilst this part is being closed to keep all .air out, the grate is being pertly filled with coal to melt the iron. At the expiration of 25 or 35 minutes the iron will lie on the bottom or hearth of the furnace a liquid plate of metal covered with the melted slags, the former having a thickness of about IM., and the slag about tin. The puddler'e assistant, with an iron bar, moving from back to front and side to side, stirs every part of the iron ; in a short time the carbon of the mettl unites with the oxygen of the silicates, and as a carbon is emitted the atoms of the iron expand until the specific gravity of the iron is no greater than that of the silicates. At this period a sort of bailing goes on of the whole mess; carbonic oxide is thrown off, with its characteristic blue flames. The work- men all the time continues stirring, and is careful that every particle of iron gets its equivalent of the purifying oxygen. This being done, the iron comtnences to knit and agglutinate, assuming a consistency like a sponge. New the silicates that were the lightest are the heaviest, and take the place of the iron when first milted. The puddler collects the eisily yielding iron, forme it into balls, which he takes from the furnace, and sends to the hammer by his under- hend. There tho hamtnerman (called a " shingler,") who .ia clothed with strong leather round the lower part of his body, Ms legs being also covered with sheet iron to protect the leather, and a fine wire gauze-blind to protect his face from the burning sparks, takes it in hand, and by a few dexterous movements of the mass of iron under the repeated blows of the hammer shapes it into what is celled a bloom," draws it from the anvil, and delivers it to the forge roller, who passes it through the rolls, each time elongating it until he gets it to the size wanted by the fore- man. It is then drawn away from the rolls, allowed to cool, weighed, the weight being entered in a book to the name of the puddler, and put on one side convenient to the man who has to cut it into lengths for the sheet mill. This man, who is called a "cutter down," cuts the puddled bar into definite lengthe, wheels them into the mill and piles them up, generally five bars high. The heater takes hold of them, puts them on a peel one at a time, and charges them into a furnace, the bottom of which is made of sand. This operatio“ is not much unlike a baker putting his loaves of bread in the oven. When the piles have been in the fur- nace some time, the layers of each pile are welded ; they are then drawn from the furnace one at a time, and passed through a pair of grooved rolls (the grooves being the same width as the pile), until it is the right thickness to make two sheets the length wanted, and lone enough to cut two sound lengths from, both being three t'e; ' four inches longer than the width the sheet is required they are intended for. So soon as these bars (they are celled " moulds" now) are cut, they are taken to a pair of chilled cast iron cylindrical rolls that have a very hard, smooth surface, and passed through sideways. Each time the two have passed between the rolls a screw is turned, that is fixed over the rolls in the frame in which the rolls revolve. This screw prevents the top roll from rising beyond a defined distance, consequently the iron is thinner each time it passes through. When the pair are rolled out until they are about one-sixteenth of an inch thick, they are taken from the rolls and the bright smooth sides made by the emooth rollers are put to each other, doubled over bee bringing all the -four ends together, the middle flattened, and again pat into another furnace for a second heating. Each pile that was put in the fist heating furnace passes through the same operation just described. and suppoeing 20 piles were charged in the first heating fur- lace, there will be SO sheets in fours in the second heating f urnace ,w hen all the charge is drawn. When these packs of four sheets'ere heated to a bright red heat they' are taken mem' the furnace and pa.sed between the rolls again, until they are as long and am thin as required. They are then oaseed on to a man called a "shearer," who puts the pattern ic has to shear them to on each pack, runs a piece of soft elate along the edge of it, which leaves a mark he can see, ind which he must so guide while shearing that the top cut- ,er shall come on the mark and take off the rough edges that are made during the rolling process and leaves the eve, vitt clean edges and proper dimensions. He after-

_ wards *pens and exam Mes each sheet to see they are free from defec s, and makes thin up into parcels of about 112 lbs. In this parcel form they are put into an annealing furnace to be annealed or softened-_i very simple operation, requir- ing care only in knowing and judging when the iron has had 1 as much fire as is needed, without any part being oxidised. The parcels are taken out as they were put in, some bands put round them, levelled, made to look neat, passed over 3 machine as soon as cold, weighed, and the weight marked on, together with the length, width, and thickness. In this form they are called bundles, and are stored in warehouses in readiness to be sent away at the customers' command. Although these sheets are used for hundreds ot purposes, by hundreds .of users, the one I have to introduce you to is the one that converts them into buckets. Such is the marvellous stride labour-saving machinery has made in this class of goods, that where a little over 20 years ago a man and two lads would have considered it a fair day's work if they had made a dozen in ten and a half hours, to-day a man with the assistance of six or eight lads will turn one out every two and a half minutes, or 240 in ten hours. The sheet of iron is taken in hand by the workman, who, with press and dies, cuts a circular piece to form the bottom, the same operation flanging it, and two pieces to form the body or sides. Tne handle and ears are cut by presses into the form and shape required, if for a light bucket. If for a heavy one, the ears and handles are forged. As the sides are pressed they are passed on to a lad (who is as nimble with his lingers as a cat is with her claws), who lays a piece of wire on the side that forms the top of the bucket, brings the edge of it against a small machine, which instantly I laps the sheet . over the wire and makes the round edge. These are passed on to another lad, who bends each end of both pieces, hooks two of them together, hammers the joint to fasten it, and passes it on to another lad, who puts them between rollers which bring them into shape, and the other two ends close, which are hooked, the seam made good and passed on to a youth , who puts it on a block the same size as the bucket he is ' making, taps the flanged bottom in the small end, sets the block revolving, applies a tool, and instantly the two edges are doubled over twice, which makes a strong edge for the 1 bottom of the bucket, and water tight at the same time. i They are again passed on to another youth, who rivets the ears to which the handles are joined on to the bucket, and lso completing the operation really of the manufacture of this useful utensil. Still we cannot leave it in this form. If we did, the moment it was ma in the scullery it would com- mence to rust and waste away, and finally it would go off into a galloping consumption, which would soon bring its whole frame from whence it came—mother earth: To avoid this rapid decay, to give it a bright respectable appear- , once, a surface that is easy to keep clean, and a more healthy constitution, it must go through another operation, which is called "Galvanizing." This consists of the bucket being submerged in a diluted acid bath. After lying in this for a few minutes, it is taken out and thoroughly rinsed in clean water, dried, and for a moment dipped into a bath of molten zinc. It is now taken into the packing room, from whence it find its way into almost every house that is inhabited between the castle and the cottage. • The usual compliments were accorded to Mr. Morris and the Chairman at the close.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.

ANNUAL MEETING. The annual meeting of the above association was held at the Heath Side Schools on Thursdiy evening, for the pur- pose of electing officers, ctc., for the ensuing year, and to hear an address from Mr. C. J. Dawson, B.A , president of the National Union of Elementary Teachers. Mr. D. W. Finney (president of the Warrington Association) occupied the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Edward Wallington, A. Corney, J. S. Kean, James Hamilton, T. W. Jones, F. Wightman, F. W. Ball, S. Barracleugh, W. S. Abraham, William Wallace, Edward Rose (master of the Blue Coat School), A. Brimelow (secretary), and C. J. Dawson, B.A.

THE ACCOUNTS. The PRESIDENT first called upon the treasurer of the association, Mr. Abraham, to read the balance sheet of the association for the past year.—Mr. ABRAHAM stated that they had a balance in hand of £2 Os 81. The income for the year was £5 17s 61 which included a balance of 17s 61 brought forward from 1882, and the total expenditure was £3 16s 101, leaving a. balance in hand of £2 Os 81.—The bAlance sheet was apopted on the motion of Mr. WALLACE, seconded by Mr. ROSE.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS. The election of officers for the ensuing year was then proceeded with. Mr. Finney was unanimously re-elected president, Mr. Rose was appointed vice-president, and Mr. Abraham and Mr. Brimelow were re-elected to the offices of treasurer and secretary respectively, with thanks for past services.—The PRESIDENT said the meeting should appoint someone to represent the Association at the conference of the National Union of Elementary Teachers, which would be held this year at Leicester. Their delegate had up to the present paid his own expenses, but he thought the rail way fare at least should be defrayed by the Association. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BRIMEILOW then proposed that the railway ex- penses be paid by the Association, and this having been seconded by Mr. ROSE, and agreed to, the President was unanimously elected to represent the Association at Leices- ter.

div.head: Ha. DAWSON'S ADDRESS.
div.p: Ha. DAWSON'S ADDRESS.

The PRESIDENT, in introducing Mr. Dawsm to the meet- ing, observed that the latter held the high and honourable position of president of this elementary teachers throughout the country, and the gentleman who occupied such an im- portant post must be very well thought of by his fellow- teachers. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Finney) had seen a good many of the presidents, and he was sure that Mr. Dawson was equal to any of the presidents who had preceded him, and he WAS glad to see him there that evening because he was certain be would tell something worth listening to. (Applause.) Mr. Dawsox, in commencing his address, remarked that he would like to say something as to the particulars of the National Union, its aims, and the work which it had actually accomplished up to the present. If anything was to be accomplished for the good of a body—an individual might do something for himself by acting singly—but if a large number, having common interests and a common work to do, were concerned, they could scarcely be advanced un- less there was unity of action amongst them. That unity of action, as they all knew, was not possible except on the principle that had been expressed in the words "Give and take." He was afraid that some of the difficulties which they found in connection with such a body as the National Union of Elementary Teachers arose from not fully recog- nising the importance and necessity of that principle. Teachers, like other people, were apt to regard merely their individual interest, instead of being willing to sink some of their individuality in the body to which they belonged. (Hear, hear.) If that principle was acted upon entirely they would have less difficulty ill forming associations, and in keeping them together because they would become much stronger, not only in numbers but in the influence which they might exercise on the public. (Hear, hear.) They should remem- ber, too, that in binding themselves together to protect their own interests they were also promoting the education of the people. (Hear, hear.) It was a right step to take, not only because it would help their owo professional interests, but because it would likewise be of service to the State. They c mid give advice and form sound opinions as to the best way of educating children, and what body, he asked, could do that so well as the teachers, who, being actually engaged in the work and coming in contact as they did with parents and children, knew what it was desirable the scholars Should be taught, and how to teach them. The National Union had done a considerable amount of good in convincing the public—or many of them at any rate—that the opinions of teachers were worth consulting and follow- ing, and not only the public, but the heads of the Education Department began to recognise, and had recognised for some time past, that the teachers' opinions ought at any rate to be ascertained so far as they were not purely selfish. They could not give advice as individuals, but by means of a Union such as the National Union of Elementary Teachers they might collect the opinion of teachers from all parts of the country; they could formu- late and arrange them Co as to bring them before the public in a way which was likely to exercise influence. Since the passing of the Act of 1870, which gave occasion for the formation of the Union, various other Acts had been passed to secure the compulsory attendance of children at school. Compulsion in attendance had become the law of the land; but, unfortunately, in many places it was disregarded—in fact some if their appointed guardians of the law, and whose special duty it was to see that that law was carried out—neglected it, and connived at it being disobeyed. That was a matter of importance to the public and also to the teachers, and one part of their work in connection with the Union for some time past had been to make representations to the public and the Department on facts which cime to their knowledge as to the way:school authorities were exer- cising their powers. Not long since a document was sent to all the school authorities of the kingdom calling attention to the defects which existed in the carry ing out of the law, and suggesting remedies. That docu- ment had been received in various fashions. By some au- thorities they had been called impertinent for doing things as they said which did not.concern them, and that they had nothing to do with the matter. They (the teachers), however, knew differently, as it was quite a part of their province to exercise their influence in bringing about a better attend- ance of children. (Hear, hear.) Another portion of their work had been connected with the amendment of the code. The requirements had been so extreme in many districts that it had been hardly possible to meet them, and the work of the Union in that matter had been to endeavour to get those regulations and requirements brought within the range and reach of those who laboured fairly and honestly at their teaching. They had also sug- gested different modifications with a view of securing a better working of the code, and that the education of the ' children should be of a better kind than it had been for- merly. The latest code which had come into operation within the last year or two had been attributed entirely to the teachers, and the faults which existed in it had been stated to have had their origin in the National Union. No. greater mistake could have been made. The National Union had objected to payment by results in the matter of reading, writing, and arithmetic, and they asked that the character of the school should be judged in a different way, and that the higher faculties and talents of the child should be considered rather than those which could be trained

in a mechanical fashion. ( Hear, hear.) If might be said that they had met with failure in their efforts, but why did not those teachers outside their body who knew they were trying to obtain certain alterations help the Union bastead of allowing the work to be done and then grumbling at it afterwards. Ii the Schoolmaster of last week they would find a full account of the representations the Union had made to the Department, So far, he had touched upon school attendance and their work connected with the Code which had to do with the education of the people as well as their own interests, but there were some , other parts of their work which relied upon them merely as teachers„ and in their professional interests. It had been set forth that one of their objects was to raise teaching to the dignity of a profession. (Hear, hear.) Teachers had to do work which required a good education, and a work which, if effective, required the respect of the public generally, and of those with whom they had to deal, arid if that was so he thought they should have a similar position in society as those who belonged to what were termed the liberal professions. (Hear, hear.) The Union had enabled teachers to make their views known, and brought before the public in such a way that it could be seen the same were reasonable and that the teachers knew what they were doing. Mr. Dawson then spoke of the legal protection the Union afforded to teachers. Some, unfortu- nately, knew they could not over-value legal protection, but other teachers who had not fallen into difficulties them- selves thought it was impossible that they ever should, and consequently the advantage of being protected against injustice was of little acconet to them. That was a matter which had occupied a considerable amount of atten- tion on the part of the executive for the past year or two, and a scheme had been drawn up by which the legal assist- ance was made of a more definite kind and more service- fable to the teacher. According to the last report no less than 201 cases had been dealt with by the National Union during 1882. Those were not all cases which came to issue in a court of law, but the majority were dealt with by the secretary writing letters on behalf of the teachers concerned. He next spoke of the qeestion of pensions for teachers, and said that they had issued to all associations a form of memo- rial with a request that it should be brought before the members of Parliament for the different localities and pre- sented through them to the Lords of the Treasury, asking that an increased grant should be made by the Government for pensioning teachers. Speaking of the funds in connec,,- tion with the Union, he said they had a benevolent fund and an orphanage fund. The former had received support to the extent of about £2,500, and already eight teachers had been elected to annuities of £25 to £3O per annum. The orphanage fund had been supported by contributions to the amount of somethieg like £7,000. and 30 or 40 orphans had been elected to allowances of ss. until they were 14 years of age. Those funds deserved the support of every teacher, and instead of their receiving contributions to the amount of 47,000 within five or six years he thought to receive more than that every year, and that could be done with a very little amount of self-sacrifice on the part of teachers. Having spoken of the Provident Society belonging to the Union by which thrift was encouraged he denied the allegation that teachers as a class were improvident. In concluding an able and practical address Mr. Dawson said if they acted in a moderate spirit, but with due professional enthusiasm, and with a real earnest desire to promote the cause of education whilst they were working at the same time for their own interests, they would find that their opinion would become much more valuable, mad by-and-bye teachers throughout the country would be convinced that it was to their ad- vantage to join the Union instead of carping and criticising what the Association did. (Applause.) The PRESIDENT, in the course of a few remarks respect- ing Mr. Dawson's address, said the subject of the pension scheme he looked upon as one of the great evils of the day. Mr. Dawson would bear him out when he said that there were hundreds of teachers who were struggling in the schools from day to day from sheer necessity, and who ought to ire pensioned. Those men were not doing any real service in their school, and the Government were very greatly remiss in not pensioning those teachers—men who had worked 40 or 50 years in their particular schools, and who bad nothing to look forward to but the Workhouse. That was a great shame. (Hear, hear.) As regarded the subject of over-pressure, he reminded them that there were others who suffered from over-pressure as well as children. It was not fair to say it was the teachers own fault. If the Government would allow teachers to withdraw from 10 to 20 of the pupils who were said to be eligible for examina- tion that would relieve it, as they would then be at liberty to present children whom it was desirable to present, and they would withdraw children of whom they knew it would be injurious to present. (Hear, hear.) There was a great deal in the New Code that might be taken objection to, but nevertheless there was a vast amout of good in it, and he thought the great harm came not from the Code it- self, but from the way in which it was administered. (Hear, hear.) He considered no man should be appointed an inspector unless he had had practical experience in a school. Inspectors frequently came into schools knowing very little about them, although he must say they were fortunate in their own district, having a capital inspector in Mr. Cowell. (Hear, hear.)—A vote of thanks having been unanimously passed to Mr. Dawson for his interesting address, on the motion of Mr. WALLACE, seconded by Mr. ;KEAN, Mr. Datatv.Low proposed a similar compliment to the President. and pointed out that the legal defence scheme of the Union deserved the full support of teachers if they wished to protect their own interests.—Mr. Dawson and the "resident haying replied, the meeting separated.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
TEE STRIKE IN NORTH AND NORTH-EAST LANCASHIRE. IMPORTANT DECISION OF THE MASTERS.

Since Tuesday last the manufacturers throughout North and North-Eat Lancashire have become Yery much more united, and a determination to put an end to the strike as speedily as possible has become very strong and wide- spread. The Preston employers have resolved to contribute at the rate of one shilling per loom towards a fund to be placed at the disposal of the Executive Committee for the purpose of assisting the more needy employers. Already the sum contributed is nearly £1,600 per week, and large contributions from other districts are confidently expected. With the exception of the proprietors of two or three thousand looms at Darwen, the whole of the manufacturers in that town have resolved to close their establishments, and there is practically unanimity amongst them. The Executive Committee of the employers have resolved not to summon any more meetings; and it has been determined that none of the mills now standing, or of those which are to be forthwith closed, shall be re-opened until the Whole question of a reduction of wages has been settled.

THE Re-ASSEMBLING O 1 PARLIAMENT.—The following ministers are now in town and are expected to remain until the re-assembling of Parliament :---Earl Granville, Lord Hartington, Lord Narthbrook, Lord Derby, Sir William Harcourt, Mr. Childers, Mr. Chambarlain, and Sir Charles Dilke.

ELOPEMENT OF A MINISTER.—A Ramsgate correspondent reports that the Rev. Thomas E. Cushing, Congregational I minister, of Sandwich, who has a wife and two children, has eloped with a young lady from San lwich. They are said to have gone to London last Saturday, and thence to Liverpool, where they embarked for America. STRANGE CONDUCT OF AN IRISH JUROR—At Clonmel Quirter Sessions, yesterday, during the trial of John Donovan for wounding Matthew Quinlan, a juror called out in a loud voice "I will acquit him." The jury suLsequently disagreed, eleven being for the conviction and one for the acquittal. The prisoner will be re-tried at the naxt assizes.

CHABGE OF MURDER.—At Bow-street Police Court, Lon- don, yesterday, a sailor, named Chrispin, was charge .t en suspicion with the murder of Emily Howell, on the night of December 30, in Westminster. The prisoner, who was arrested in a public-house after he had expressed a hope that the murderer would get oft, was remanded on bail, the magistrate remarking that there appeared to be no ease against him.

TREMBLE ATTACK ON A SALVATIONIST: SCENE MIR- ING, A PEOCESSioN.—During a Salvation Army procession at Peterborough, yesterday, a Salvationist "chucked" a woman under the chin as he passed her in the strret. The woman's husband resenting this liberty, struck the man a blow on the head, from the effects of which he died shortly afterwards. It has since transpired that the WOMill was sister of the deceased,

_ THE ARREST OF A GERMAN " BARON:" FURTHER PAR- TICULARS —Dotective-officer Waller, of the Metropolitan Police, left Sheffield yesterday morning in charge of the gentleman who has been living there for some time as Baron Fritz you Weisenburg. Some time ago the "Baron " was introduced by a confederate, not yet apprehended, to Hamrick liutoch, a German baker in Globe-road, Mile End, London, when the Baron led the baker to believe that he was the nephew of Prince Bismarck, a cousin of Count Waldeck, and related to the Duchess of Albany. His confederate declared him to be a nobleman of great wealth, and that he (the confederate) received £l3 a week for acting as his secretary. Soon after the Baron called alone, discredited his secretary, and aft:red his position to the baker, which he at once accepted. He then began to draw on the baker, and as security left papers and documents purporting to be of great value. Altogether Elemrich advanced him £6OO, .£3,00 of which he had saved, and the remainder he obtained on mortgages. Suddenly his visits ceased, and the baker discovered that he had been duped. The Baron was traced to Sheffield, where he had married a Sheffield lady, kept his carriage, and lived in style in harmony with the position of a German baron. Amongst his papers are a number of unsettled accounts of tradesmen in London and elsewhere. It is alleged that there are ether charges against him.

div.head: ST. MARY'S CHURCH, GREAT SANKEY. OPENING OF A NEW ORGAN.
div.p: ST. MARY'S CHURCH, GREAT SANKEY. OPENING OF A NEW ORGAN.

A new organ which has been erectediTle—;bove church was opened on Monday evening last, in the presence eta very large congregation, many of whom could only obtain standing room. A departure from the "Organ recital " customary on such occasions was ventured upon, and after a short preliminary service a selection of songs and choruses from Handel'e oratorio "The Messiah" was rendered by about 40- members of the Warrington Musical Society, site kindly gave their assistance. T. Mee Pattison, Esq., pre. sided at the organ. The service throughout was an en- joyable one, and highly appreciated by all present. The solos were sung by Miss White (Liverpool), Miss Riley, Mrs. Paterson ; Messrs. Fairclougb, Wallington, and Dell. After service, which concluded a little before nine o'clock, a move was made to the National Schools, which were tastefully decorated for the (=alma, and through the kindness of the Rev. E. H. Vernon, curate, the members of the society, the church officers, and choir were entertained at supper, to which ample justice was done, and thus a very enjoyable evening was brought to a close, not however without a universally expressed wish that it might not be long before the Sankey friends would again provide a similar evening's enjoyment. The opening services will be cont./sued en Sunday next, when two sermons will be preached, in the morning at 10.30, by the Rev. J. W. Diegle, Rural Dean of Childwall, and hi the evening at 6-30 by the Rev. Thomas Chambers, Rotor of Halewood. The organ, which is enclosed in a stained pine case, has been supplied by Messrs. div.head: MARRIAGES.
div.p: MARRIAGES.
